item.title: Five centuries of furniture wood
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Five centuries of furniture wood
In 1904 Percy Macquoid opened *A History of English Furniture* by splitting the craft into four piles of timber. Oak until 1660. Walnut until 1720. Mahogany until 1770. Satinwood after that, into the Regency. The scheme still hangs on gallery labels. It is a useful lie.
It is useful because English fashionable furniture did change color and species in that order, and a buyer walking a country-house corridor can still feel the shift under the hand: the blackened joined oak, the faded oyster walnut, the red-brown chair that wants to be called Chippendale, the yellow card table with a harewood border. It is a lie because farmhouses never got the memo, because Paris ran ahead of London and Philadelphia ran beside it, because Chinese hardwood cabinets were already old when Henry VIII was buying wainscot, and because the wood in a piece is often not the wood on the label.
This series starts here so the later chapters have a room to sit in.
## What a furniture wood is
A furniture wood is a species a shop will spend time on: dry it, saw it to a face, joint it, and show it or hide it. Ship timbers, mine props, and firewood overlap the list. They are not the same list. Beech made Thonet’s café empire and also laundry pegs. Yellow-poplar lined the drawers of Philadelphia high chests and also the cores of cheap veneered suites. The difference is intention and finish, not a moral ranking of trees.
Three behaviors decide whether a wood stays in the shop.
Density and hardness. The USDA Forest Products Laboratory reports side hardness (Janka) and specific gravity at 12 percent moisture in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, 2010, tables 5–3a and following). White oak sits near 1,360 lbf and SG 0.68; black cherry near 950 lbf and 0.50; eastern white pine near 380 lbf and 0.35. Those numbers explain why a pine tavern table dents under a belt buckle and a maple counter does not. They do not explain fashion. Fashion is why cherry was a secondary wood in one decade and a show wood in the next.
Movement. Wood shrinks across the grain as it dries, more tangentially than radially. Quartersawn stock moves less in width and shows rays in oak. A door that was flatsawn in 1710 and hung in a heated apartment in 2010 will tell you this without a hygrometer. The sawing chapter in this series is not a technical aside. It is half of period style.
Workability and finish. Interlocked grain (elm, sapele) tears. Silica (teak) dulls edges. Open pores (oak, ash) drink filler. Fine texture (maple, boxwood) takes a polish that looks like light trapped under glass. Shops chose woods for the tool in hand as much as for the color in the book.
## Trade is the hidden style
English oak furniture of 1550 is not simply “English oak.” Dendrochronology on panels and chests keeps pointing to the south-eastern Baltic — the hinterlands of Gdansk, then Königsberg and Courland — for the slow-grown, radially split boards sold as wainscot (*wagenschot*). Haneca and colleagues (2005) showed how art-historical oak can be provenanced by ring patterns. London joiners mixed that imported stuff with home oak. A linenfold chest can be a North Sea object even when the carving looks local.
Walnut’s English fashion after 1660 rode Dutch and French taste and a veneer technology that wasted less of a scarce, figured log. American black walnut, *Juglans nigra*, did a different job in the colonies: it was a primary solid wood, wide and available, and it still is in the central hardwood belt.
Mahogany’s English story is a statute. Adam Bowett has spent a career killing the old connoisseur’s date (Macquoid’s 1733, Cescinsky’s 1748) for the duty change. The Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722, took the import duty off British West Indian timber. Jamaica wood that had not been worth the freight became, in Bowett’s reading of the port books, cheap enough to use in the solid. Thomas Ripley, advising the Admiralty on a new building, called mahogany cheaper than deal or wainscot when Navy ships carried it freight-free. The rococo splat did not invent mahogany. A tax cut and a sugar island did.
That island story is not a romance. Logging gangs, enslaved labor, and a forest that could be mined like a seam — Bowett’s thesis and the Jamaica trade paper sit on those records. A dining table can be beautiful and still be a receipt from an extractive system. The series will not sand that off.
## The other clocks
Macquoid stopped, more or less, when satinwood and painted decoration had their London hour. Furniture did not.
In the German-speaking lands after the Napoleonic wars, Biedermeier shops made a virtue of pale birch, pear, and cherry. In Denmark a century later, oak and teak and a little rosewood became a national export look. In the United States the Shakers kept a short list — maple, cherry, pine — while Renaissance Revival factories drowned parlors in black walnut. Gustav Stickley and the English Arts and Crafts men dragged quartersawn oak back into the polite room and fumed it with ammonia so the tannins went brown.
Michael Thonet’s No. 14 chair, 1859, is a beech object. Alvar Aalto’s Paimio seating is a birch-laminate object. Charles and Ray Eames’s plywood chairs are a glue-and-veneer object that learned its compound curves on a wartime splint. None of these fit an “Age of Mahogany.” They are still furniture woods.
China’s classical hardwood furniture — huanghuali (*Dalbergia odorifera* and related trade names) and zitan (often *Pterocarpus santalinus*) — belongs in a 500-year survey because European and American collectors spent the late twentieth century treating those pieces as a parallel canon. The trees and the shops are older than that fashion.
## Softwoods were never only poor
Country furniture in pine is not a failed hardwood piece. Scots pine and Baltic deal furnished northern Europe in paint. Eastern white pine furnished New England in paint and in clear varnish. Southern longleaf, the heart pine of floors and some case work, is a different creature: dense latewood, old-growth resin, a naval-stores economy. The Crown’s Broad Arrow reserved large white pines for masts (Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*, and the Massachusetts charter tradition). Furniture shops used what the navy did not take, and later what the cut-over left.
Paint changes the ethics of identification. A blue cupboard from the Connecticut River valley may be pine, poplar, or a mix. The species still matters for repair. It did not always matter for the first owner.
## Substitutes are the modern style
By 1900 Cuban mahogany (*Swietenia mahagoni*) was already a memory in commercial sizes. Honduran mahogany (*S. macrophylla*) took the name, then African *Khaya* and *Entandrophragma* (sapele, utile, sipo) took the sales tag. Teak from Burma and later from plantations filled a mid-century dream of oil and weather. Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) went onto Appendix I of CITES; the rest of *Dalbergia* followed onto Appendix II in 2017. Big-leaf mahogany’s neotropical populations entered Appendix II in 2003.
The honest chapter in this series is the engineered one. Particleboard, medium-density fiberboard, and veneered panels are furniture woods in the only sense that counts: they are what most people now own. They move less than solid flatsawn oak. They fail in water. They can be named without apology. They cannot be named as walnut.
U.S. buyers of imported wood goods also live under the Lacey Act as amended in 2008 and under APHIS’s phased declaration rules (Phase VII, 1 December 2024, sweeping more furniture codes). A species chapter that skips the permit is a period piece.
## How to use what follows
Read the sawing essay next, then the short method piece on how to look at a board. After that, skip. If you own a cherry chest, read cherry. If you are about to specify “mahogany” for a dining table, read mahogany and then sapele. If you like Stickley, read oak and the Arts and Crafts chapter together.
Arkansas sits in this history without needing a costume. White oak, red oak, cherry, walnut, hickory, ash, and pine are the same genera that filled American shops in 1800. The difference is second-growth rings, kiln schedules, and a legal paper trail. Bradley Brand works those hardwoods. The point of the series is to say what the wood will do — swell, dent, darken, take a finish, outlive a fashion — so a designer or a buyer can choose with open eyes.
Macquoid gave us a staircase. The house has more rooms than he drew.
## Sources
Macquoid, *A History of English Furniture*, 1904–08. Bowett, *The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*; “Thomas Ripley and the use of early mahogany,” *Georgian Group Journal* 7 (1997); Naval Stores Act lecture, RFS. Haneca et al., *Journal of Archaeological Science* 32 (2005). USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (2010). CITES appendices and 2003 mahogany press release. USDA APHIS Lacey Act Phase VII. V&A plywood history; V&A Thonet W.31-2011. Albion, *Forests and Sea Power* (1926).

item.title: Quartersawn versus flatsawn
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Quartersawn versus flatsawn
A log is a cylinder of tubes. How you slice the cylinder decides the face you stain, the way a table top cups, and whether an oak chair looks like a cathedral or like a rayed stone. Fashion has picked sides for five hundred years. The physics has not changed.
## Three faces from one tree
Flatsawn (plain-sawn) boards are cut tangent to the rings. On the face you get arches — the “cathedrals” of oak and ash. The width of the board is mostly tangential grain. Tangential shrinkage is the large number in the *Wood Handbook* tables. A flatsawn white-oak board will move more in width, and it will cup so the rings try to flatten. That is not a defect. It is geometry.
Quartersawn boards are cut so the rings run nearly perpendicular to the face. The face is radial. In oak, the medullary rays — ribbons of tissue that ran from pith to bark — show as flakes. English joiners and later Arts and Crafts catalogues called the look “silver grain” or “tiger oak.” Radial shrinkage is smaller. A quartersawn top still moves, but it stays flatter and wears its width change more evenly.
Riftsawn is the compromise: rings at about 30 to 60 degrees, straight stripe, fewer flakes. Chair shops like it for legs that must match. Yield is worse than flatsawing, better than true quartering if the mill is sloppy; worse than both if the mill is honest about the waste.
The USDA *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, ch. 4) treats tangential shrinkage as commonly about 1.5 to 2 times radial for many hardwoods. Species differ. The sawing pattern multiplies whatever the species already wants to do.
## Before the circular saw
Medieval and early modern oak furniture often started as riven stock, not sawn. A wedge follows the rays. The board you get is naturally quartered. That is why a 16th-century linenfold panel can be thin, wide, and stable in a way a cheap 19th-century oak sideboard is not. Baltic wainscot, the *wagenschot* of the Gdansk trade, was typically cleft or sawn to keep the face radial (Haneca et al. 2005; KNOB wainscot literature). Buyers in London and the Low Countries paid for dryness and for that radial cut. “The driest wainscots you know how to get” is a period instruction, not a metaphor.
When pitsaws and later water-powered sash mills took over, flatsawing won on yield. You can get more wide boards by slabbing the log. Fashion and thrift aligned. Walnut veneer in the late 17th century is a flatsawn or rotary-ish slice story of a different kind: the log is too precious to quarter for solidity, so you glue a thin face to a cheaper carcase and let the substrate argue with the weather.
Mahogany in the 18th-century solid — Bowett’s cheap Jamaica wood after 1721 — was often flatsawn simply because the logs were huge and the shops wanted width for dining tables. A two-board mahogany top with matching cathedrals is a flatsaw trophy. Quartersawn mahogany exists; it is quieter, and the ribbon in some *Swietenia* and later in sapele is interlocked grain, not oak-like rays.
## Oak’s public life is a quartered life
Whenever oak is the polite wood, quartering comes back.
Tudor and Jacobean joinery shows ray flake on panels because the stock was riven or chosen. Victorian Gothic revival cut oak any way the steam mill allowed, then stained it black-brown; the flake is there if you look, under the dirt. The Arts and Crafts shop made the flake the point. Gustav Stickley’s *Craftsman* furniture, the English oak of Voysey and Barnsley, the Mission catalogues — they specify quartersawn white oak because the ray is a badge. Fuming (ammonia on tannin) darkens the ray and the fiber at different rates. A flatsawn Mission chair is a cheaper cousin. Collectors still pay the difference.
American white oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group) shows rays more loudly than most red oaks. European oak (*Q. robur*, *Q. petraea*) has the same anatomy. Red oak will quarter; the flake is usually smaller and the pores more open. A designer who wants “that Stickley flash” and specifies red oak flatsawn will get cathedrals and a stain problem.
## Movement in a heated house
Period furniture was built for rooms that went cold at night. Central heating and air conditioning reset the moisture content. A flatsawn oak leaf on a drop-leaf table, glued up in 1780 at a higher average humidity, will shrink across the grain and may split along a glue line or open a rule joint. Quartersawn leaves suffer less cup, not zero movement.
The practical rule in a modern shop is old: allow wood to sit at the humidity of the destination, do not trap a wide flatsawn panel in a rigid groove without room, and prefer quartered stock for frames, stiles, and anything that must stay flat next to glass. The 18th-century frame-and-panel already knew this. The panel floats. The frame is the grown-up wood — often closer to quartered — and the panel, even flatsawn, can shrink inside the groove.
Veneer changes the politics. A crotch mahogany veneer on a yellow-poplar ground (common in American Empire) will check if the ground moves and the glue is hide glue gone brittle. Plywood grounds in the 20th century were a stability invention: cross-banded plies cancel movement. That is why an Eames LCW can be a shaped seat without the splits you would expect from a solid flatsawn slab steamed into a compound curve. The sawing chapter and the plywood chapter are the same argument in two centuries.
## How to see it on a piece you did not make
Look at the end grain. Rings running across the thickness, parallel to the face, mean flatsawn. Rings running through the thickness, end-on, mean quartered. If you cannot see the end, look at the face: cathedrals versus straight stripe plus flake (oak) or ribbon (interlocked tropicals).
Look at wear. Chair seats that were flatsawn cup toward the bark side. Tabletops with breadboard ends: if the pins elongated into slots, someone understood tangential movement. If the breadboard split the top, someone did not.
Look at the period. A 1600 joined chest with ray flake is doing its job. A 1905 sideboard with loud flake is announcing a movement. A 1970 “Mediterranean” oak suite with printed grain on a veneer of unclear species is announcing a factory. Printed grain has no end-grain rings.
## Cost, then and now
Quartering wastes the log. You get narrower boards and more offcuts. That is why Baltic wainscot was dear, why Gillows in Lancaster could pay nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 (Bowett, provincial woods paper), and why a true quartersawn white-oak dining table still costs more per foot than a flatsawn one from the same kiln charge.
Mills now cut “quartered and rift” as a mixed bundle. Designers who want flake must say flake. Designers who want straight grain for a run of doors should say rift, or they will get a surprise cathedral in the middle of a set.
Arkansas white oak quarters well. The rays are the same anatomy they were when a Berkshire joiner opened a Baltic board. The difference is the kiln, the ring width of second growth, and the fact that you can still buy it as a domestic hardwood without a CITES permit. That is not a small fact. It is also not a reason to quarter everything. A flatsawn oak breadboard, a painted pine cupboard, a mahogany table with matching cathedrals — each is a correct use of the cut.
The fashion for one face or the other will swing again. The rings will not.
## A pit, a sash mill, and a pencil line
Picture a 17th-century saw pit first, because the geometry is older than the circular saw. One man stands in the hole. The other walks the log. The saw is a long ribbon of iron with a handle at each end. They are not thinking “quartered.” They are thinking: keep the kerf on the line the joiner scribed, and do not waste a Baltic board that cost freight through the Sound. If the log was riven first, the line already follows the rays. If it was a sawn balk, the men can still rotate the piece and take radial cuts. They usually do not. Width is money. A linenfold panel that is already cleft does not need their help.
A water-powered sash mill changes the arithmetic. The frame saw drops, the carriage advances, and the cheapest way through a cylinder is to slab it. Cathedral faces pile up on the barrow. A shop in Lancaster or Philadelphia in 1760 could still special-order quartered oak. Gillows did, and paid for it (Bowett, provincial woods). Most dining-table mahogany after the 1721 duty change did not get that courtesy. The logs were too wide and too useful as two-board tops. Matching cathedrals from one flitch became a kind of signature: you can still see the pair on a drop-leaf in Winterthur, the arches opening away from a glue line that was once the middle of the tree.
The circular saw, once it is common in the 19th century, leaves its own witness. A skip mark on a backboard — a shallow arc where the blade wandered — tells you the conversion was mill, not pit. Rotary veneer is the flatsawn idea taken to a lathe: the log turns, the knife peels a continuous sheet, and the cathedrals repeat at the circumference. That is how a 1950s bedroom suite can have the same arch every eighteen inches. Quartersliced veneer is a different knife path. The flake in a 1910 Stickley door is usually sliced, not peeled. Look at the repeat. Nature does not clone a ray every foot.
## How a shop decides, piece by piece
FPL-GTR-190, chapter 4, gives the shrinkage ratio — tangential about one and a half to two times radial for many hardwoods. The species notes give hardness and tyloses. They do not choose your cut. If a panel must stay flat, prefer rings on end in the thickness. If a top must show a cathedral, flatsaw and fasten it so the width can move: buttons, slots, a breadboard with pins in elongated holes. If a run of doors must match, rift, and say so on the ticket. “Quartered and rift” as a mixed bundle is a mill convenience, not a specification.
A designer who writes “QS oak” and means Stickley’s silver grain, then accepts red oak from a mixed charge, will get a quieter flake and a stain that floods the open pores. That is the binomial, not the mill cheating. Ribbon stripe in sapele or some *Swietenia* is interlocked grain reversing, not a medullary ray. You can quarter those logs. You cannot get oak flake from them.
Chair legs are the practical case. Rift gives a straight stripe on all four faces, or close enough. A flatsawn leg shows cathedral on two faces and something quieter on the others. Sets do not match. A shop that makes a dozen dining chairs will pay for rift even when the table top is a flatsawn trophy. Yield is worse. Complaints are fewer.
Stand a piece on end when you can. Rings parallel to the face: flat. Rings through the thickness: quartered. No rings, only a photograph: factory. The physics does not care which century you prefer.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (2010), ch. 4 (moisture and shrinkage) and ch. 5 (species notes on oak rays and tyloses). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. Haneca et al. 2005. Bowett, “Furniture woods in London and provincial furniture 1700–1800.” Stickley, *The Craftsman* (fumed oak practice). Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*.
See: `oak-european-and-american`, `arts-and-crafts-oak`, `plywood-veneers-twentieth`, `reading-furniture-wood`.

item.title: How to read a furniture wood
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# How to read a furniture wood
A dealer says mahogany. The drawer sides are a greenish poplar. The back is pine. The beading is a blackened fruitwood. The piece is still “a mahogany chest” in the way a book is “cloth” — by its jacket. Learning to read the woods is learning to read the shop.
This chapter is a method, not a key to every species. The species chapters do that work. Here is how to look so those chapters have somewhere to land.
## Start with the job, not the color
Color is a poor first question. Cherry starts as salmon-pink and goes to liver-brown in the sun. Mahogany ranges from pale salmon to a red so deep the Victorian finishers barely needed pigment. Walnut fades toward chocolate and then toward mud if the windows are cruel. Teak goes silver outdoors and honey under oil. A 1980s stain can make maple look like walnut and oak look like mahogany. Ask instead: what was this part asked to do?
Show surfaces — top, drawer front, splat, door — want a wood that planes, carves or turns, and takes a finish. Secondary woods — drawer sides, dustboards, backboards, glue blocks — want cheap, stable, or both. Chair seats may want a wood that will not split when you drive in legs (elm). Bows want a wood that bends (ash, oak, hickory). Carving wants a wood that holds a cut (lime, close-grained mahogany). Clock cases in New England often want white pine because it is light and takes paint or veneer.
If you name the job first, the short list of species shrinks before you argue about pores.
## Pores, rings, rays
Hardwoods have vessels. On the end grain they are holes. On the face they are grooves or dashes.
Ring-porous woods (oak, ash, elm, teak, hickory) lay a row of large earlywood pores each year. You can count rings with a thumbnail. The face shows a strong grain that filler and stain love and that a fine polish has to negotiate. Diffuse-porous woods (maple, cherry, birch, yellow-poplar, true mahogany in a quieter way) spread smaller pores through the ring. The face can look satiny. Semi-ring-porous woods (walnut) sit between.
Softwoods have no vessels. They have tracheids. Pine shows resin canals and a jump from earlywood to latewood that is loud in southern yellow pine and shy in eastern white pine. If you think you are looking at maple and you see a resin canal, you are not looking at maple.
Rays are the other tell. Oak rays are large enough to be a design element when quartered. Beech and sycamore have crowded rays that speckle a quartered face (European sycamore in the furniture trade is *Acer pseudoplatanus*, a maple; American sycamore is *Platanus*). Boxwood rays are fine; the wood looks almost like a pale meat.
A 10× lens and a cut end grain beat a phone photograph of a finished top.
## Weight and the dent test
Lift the drawer. Yellow-poplar and pine secondary wood make a tall chest possible. Solid oak drawer sides make a chest that fights you. Janka hardness is a laboratory dent test (a steel ball, a measured load). You do not need the machine. A fingernail into an underside arris is crude and useful: pine yields, maple barely does, teak is oily and confusing, old finish lies.
The *Wood Handbook* numbers are averages at 12 percent moisture. A bone-dry antique pine table can feel harder than a damp oak board. Moisture first, then species.
## Tool marks and shop habits
Hand-plane tracks on a drawer bottom, a pit-sawn backboard, a circular-saw skip from a 19th-century mill, a rotary-cut veneer with a wide, repeating cathedral — these date the conversion of the log. They also hint at species. Rotary veneer loves big, cheap logs: lauan, yellow-poplar, Douglas-fir. Sliced veneer is how you get a crown-cut walnut or a quartered oak flake on a door.
Look at the unseen edges. American 18th-century high-style work often uses yellow-poplar (*Liriodendron tulipifera*) for secondary wood in the Mid-Atlantic; New England leans white pine; the South mixes pine and poplar and sometimes cypress. English work uses oak and deal. A “Queen Anne” highboy with MDF dustboards is a marriage, not a birth.
## Finish is a mask and a record
Shellac on mahogany can be French-polished to a depth that looks like standing water. Oil on teak can look like nothing. Milk paint on pine is a crust. Later varnish ambered. Later polyurethane sat on top like a plastic tray.
Cherry’s darkening is oxidation and light, not a finish trick, though finishers have always helped it. If two leaves of a cherry table do not match, ask which one lived under a runner. Walnut’s brown is heartwood color plus time; steamed walnut is a mill practice to even sap and heart, and it is not a sin unless it is undisclosed in a “solid walnut” claim that is mostly sap.
Fumed oak is a chemical reaction (ammonia and tannin), a true finish of the Arts and Crafts shop. A stain trying to fake it sits in the pores and looks dirty.
## Names that mean too many trees
“Mahogany” in a 1760 London bill is likely Jamaican *Swietenia*. In a 1960 American suite it may be *Khaya*, sapele, or a photograph of grain on lauan. “Rosewood” may be *Dalbergia nigra*, East Indian *D. latifolia*, or a stained substitute. “Cedar” in a blanket chest is often *Juniperus virginiana* (eastern redcedar, a juniper). “Cedar” in a Spanish colonial chest may be *Cedrela odorata* (Spanish cedar, a Meliaceae cousin of mahogany). “Sycamore” is a fight between continents.
The species chapters give binomials. Use them when money or law is involved. CITES and the Lacey Act do not care about poetry.
## What you cannot see
Plantation teak and old Burma teak are both *Tectona grandis*. The rings and the oil differ. Second-growth red oak from a fast Arkansas stand is still *Quercus rubra*; the earlywood pores may be wider and the latewood weaker than a tight old tree. The handbook averages still apply. Your board is a sample of one.
Glued-up tops hide the sawing pattern unless you find an end. Engineered cores hide everything except the 0.6 mm face. Reading those pieces is reading an edge. The engineered chapter is written for that edge.
## A short walk around a table
Walk a dining table as a practice.
Top: species and cut. Matching cathedrals — flatsawn pair from one log. Ribbon stripe — quartered interlocked grain, often sapele if the table is postwar and the price was not mahogany-grade. Flake — oak, quartered.
Edge: solid or a lip over ply? A breadboard end? Slot-screwed?
Underside: plane tracks or wide-belt scratches? Pocket screws (late)? Wood shrinks across the width; if the battens are glued tight across a wide flatsawn top, look for splits.
Legs: same species? Often not. A maple leg under a cherry top is a New England habit. A beech leg under a stained “walnut” seat is a factory habit.
Then open a drawer. That is where shops tell the truth.
## Why this comes third
The five-century essay gave you the parade. The sawing essay gave you the geometry. This essay is the field kit. The rest of the series is what you take into the room: oak’s tyloses and the Baltic trade, walnut’s two continents, mahogany’s statute and its substitutes, cherry’s sunburn, maple’s figures, the softwoods that painted the countryside, the tropical woods that law now follows, the plywoods that bent, the fiberboards that do not, and the shops — Windsor, Shaker, Arts and Crafts, Biedermeier, Danish, marquetry — that mixed species because each wood had a job.
Arkansas hardwoods read the same way a Rhode Island shop’s boards did. You look at pores, rays, weight, and the part they play. The brand that mills them is irrelevant to the anatomy. It is not irrelevant to the fact that those species are still in the woods.
## The drawer as a confession
Open the top drawer and do the work the label will not do. Sides first. Yellow-poplar in a Mid-Atlantic chest is a green-tinged, even, diffuse-porous wood that planes like a courtesy and takes a nail. White pine in a New England case is softer, with resin canals if you find an end, and a smell that old varnish cannot quite kill. Oak sides in English work are a different ambition: heavier, ring-porous, sometimes a leftover from the same Baltic parcel that faced the carcass (Bowett’s provincial geography still helps). Cypress in a southern piece is a shop that had a wet-climate wood and used it (Hurst and Prown). MDF or a printed vinyl wrap is a marriage. The dovetails, if they exist, will tell you whether a person or a machine spent the morning here: slight irregularity and a scribe line, or a perfect pin from a spindle jig after the First World War.
Bottoms next. A hand-planed bottom, bevelled to fit a groove, with tracks that catch a fingernail, is older than a plywood panel stapled into rabbets. A rotary-cut veneer bottom with a repeating cathedral is 20th-century conversion. Dustboards, if present, are the same test one storey down. A “Queen Anne” highboy with a fiberboard dustboard was assembled after the form was already a reproduction style.
Then the back. Pit-sawn kerf, a slightly irregular band, is a date before the circular mill was ordinary. Circular-saw arcs are 19th century onward. A single sheet of lauan plywood nailed on is a repair or a factory. Glue blocks in the corners — pine, poplar, sometimes oak — are the shop’s handwriting. They are rarely the wood on the tag.
## Light, a thumbnail, and the name on the tag
Take the piece to a window if you can. Rake light across the show face. Pores that are trenches (oak, ash, elm, hickory, teak) catch the light as lines. A satiny diffuse-porous face (maple, cherry, birch, yellow-poplar, a quiet mahogany) will not. Beech and trade sycamore (*Acer pseudoplatanus*) speckle when quartered — a crowded fleck, not oak’s mirrors (Hoadley; Panshin and de Zeeuw). Softwoods announce themselves with latewood bands and, in pines, resin canals. If you came looking for maple and found a canal, stop. You have a conifer.
The thumbnail on an unseen arris is crude and better than a brochure. Pine yields. Hard maple barely does. FPL-GTR-190’s Janka figures (table 5–3a, 12 percent moisture) are laboratory averages. Your fingernail is not that machine. It still sorts the pile. Moisture lies in both directions. A soaked oak offcut dents. A bone-dry pine tavern table can feel proud of itself until July.
A 1760 London bill that says mahogany is a species claim with a port behind it — Jamaican *Swietenia* in Bowett’s reading of the years after the 1721 duty change, unless the bill is more specific. A 1960 American suite that says mahogany may be *Khaya*, sapele, or a photograph on lauan. CITES and the Lacey Act want binomials. Poetry does not move a container. Glued-up tops hide the cut unless you find the end. A 0.6 mm face hides everything except that edge. Read the edge. The species chapters have a place to sit after that walk.
## Sources
Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*. USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190. Panshin and de Zeeuw, *Textbook of Wood Technology*. Bowett, provincial furniture woods paper (secondary-wood geography in England). Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* (southern secondary woods). CITES Species+; USDA APHIS Lacey Act pages.
See: `five-centuries-of-furniture-wood`, `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`, `engineered-wood-honest`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Oak, European and American
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Oak, European and American
The first piece of furniture most northern Europeans owned that was not a board on trestles was oak. Chests hold that history: boarded six-board chests, then joined chests with panels floating in grooves, then drawers that learned their manners from the chest. The wood was local, or it was Baltic, or it was both in one carcass. Five hundred years later the same genus still makes dining tables in Arkansas. The tree did not become fashionable again. Fashion left and came home.
## Two groups, many trade names
European furniture oak is mostly *Quercus robur* (pedunculate) and *Q. petraea* (sessile), sold as English, French, Polish, Slavonian, Riga, or Danzig oak depending on the port and the century. American furniture oak splits into the white group — *Q. alba* and its cousins (bur, chestnut oak, post, overcup) — and the red group — *Q. rubra*, *Q. falcata*, and the rest. The USDA *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) treats them as groups for good reason: white-oak heartwood pores are usually plugged with tyloses. Liquids stay out. Tight cooperage, ship planking, and a certain kind of outdoor gear follow. Red oak’s pores stay open. You can blow through a red-oak end grain if the piece is straight. Stain floods. Finishers either fill or celebrate the pits.
Hardness is close. White oak: specific gravity about 0.68, Janka about 1,360 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Northern red oak: SG 0.63, Janka about 1,290 lbf (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). European oak sits in the same neighborhood; published Janka figures vary by source and ring width `[CITE NEEDED for a single FPL-equivalent number on Q. robur]`. Slow-grown Baltic oak is often finer and more even than a wide-ringed second-growth red oak from a warm hillside. The binomial does not tell you the ring count.
Both groups are ring-porous. Both quarter to show rays. White oak’s rays are the ones Arts and Crafts catalogues wanted. Red oak will show flake; it is usually less theatrical.
## Workability and finish
Oak planes well if the grain is straight and the irons are sharp. Quartersawn stock can pick up at the rays. Interlocked or wavy boards tear. Steam-bending is a historic use (boat frames, some chair bows) though ash and hickory often took the extreme bends.
Tannin is the chemistry that matters in the shop. Iron and oak make black stains — the old ink, the ruined clamp mark, the fumed Mission finish when ammonia vapor is the iron’s cousin in effect. Water-based finishes can raise the grain into a field of needles. Oil and wax leave the pores open and the flake bright. Filler and pigment stain were the Victorian answer: hide the structure, even the color. A contemporary shop that wants the 17th century back will skip the filler.
Oak moves. Tangential shrinkage is high. Frame-and-panel is not a style choice in oak; it is manners. A wide flatsawn oak slab table in a house with air conditioning is a bet.
## The Baltic board and the English joint
From the late Middle Ages into the 17th century, western Europe imported radially split oak from the south-eastern Baltic. Gdansk (Danzig) dominated the wainscot trade in the 16th century; Haneca et al. (2005) cite Sound Toll figures — 85 percent of wainscots passing Denmark in 1565 shipped from Gdansk, falling as Königsberg and Courland rose. Riga’s name stuck to a grade. Dendrochronology keeps finding that oak in English panels and some furniture. Home oak built the frames; imported boards often made the faces.
This is why “English oak furniture” is a phrase that needs a second sentence. The joinery tradition is English (and Netherlandish, and French). The fiber may be Polish. Victor Chinnery’s *Oak Furniture: The British Tradition* remains the long walk through forms: the court cupboard, the press, the joined stool, the draw-bored mortise and tenon that still holds when the pins have lozenged with time.
Oak did not vanish in 1660 because Macquoid turned a page. It left the fashionable parlor and stayed in the kitchen, the church, the farm. Provincial England kept making oak furniture while London veneered walnut.
## America: the same genus, a different forest
Colonists met a hardwood forest that still had chestnut, and oaks of a size that made the European eye tired. American joined oak exists in the 17th century — the so-called Pilgrim century chests of New Haven and the Connecticut valley — but the colonies also had pine, poplar, and walnut in quantity. Oak became a utility wood: floors, barns, wagon gear, then furniture again when revival and Arts and Crafts wanted it.
Southern and central white oak, including the Ozark and Ouachita timber that Arkansas shops still buy, is cooperage country as much as furniture country. The same tyloses that hold bourbon hold a porch bench if the finish is honest. Red oak became the cheap hardwood of the 20th-century American factory: stained, filled, sold as “golden oak” in the 1890s and as kitchen cabinets in the 1980s. Golden oak was often a finish fashion on quartersawn stock. The 1980s oak kitchen was often flatsawn red oak under a yellow-orange film. Same word. Different ambition.
## Fashion’s returns
Gothic Revival and Renaissance Revival hauled carved oak back into the dining room. Then Morris and the English craft shops, then Stickley, Hubbard, Limbert, made oak the moral wood — honest, quartersawn, fumed or lightly hung with a finish that did not pretend to be mahogany. The Arts and Crafts chapter takes that story. The anatomy is here: they needed white oak’s rays and tannin.
Mid-century taste dropped oak for teak and walnut, then country oak came back as a reproduction style. Danish modern used oak as much as teak; Wegner’s Wishbone is usually oak. The pale northern oak of a 1950s Copenhagen chair and the blackened Jacobean court cupboard are the same genus in different lights.
## Conservation and the living tree
Oak as a furniture species is not a CITES story in the American and European mains. It is a forestry story: high-grading, oak wilt and sudden oak death in some regions, the replacement of oak-hickory stands, the market’s hunger for wide clear boards that second growth does not want to give. European oak prices follow storms and French export policy as much as fashion `[CITE NEEDED for a current price series]`.
Plantation oak exists. It is not Baltic slow-grown wainscot. A designer who wants tight rings must say so on the purchase order, or pay for antique stock.
## What to look for
On an old piece: worm in sapwood, iron stains, replaced hinges that split the stile, a top that was once a chest lid. On a new piece: white versus red (end-grain tyloses, or a water drop that sits versus a water drop that sinks), quartered versus flat, how the finish treats the pore. On a “solid oak” suite from a container: look at the edge. A 0.6 mm oak face on rubberwood or MDF is a legal description in some catalogues. It is not a joined chest.
Arkansas white oak still quarters. The flake on a new table can be the same structure a Gdansk splitter sold to a London joiner. The difference is the kiln ticket and the fact that the tree grew here. That is enough history to be going on with.
## A joined chest and a clamp stain
Start with a 17th-century joined chest because the wood and the joint grew up together. Stiles and rails are mortised. The panel floats in a groove. Pins are draw-bored and, years on, lozenge in the hole as the oak dries. Chinnery walks the forms — court cupboard, press, joined stool — until the construction stops being a mystery and becomes manners. The panel can be Baltic wainscot, radially split, the *wagenschot* Haneca and the KNOB literature keep finding in English work. The frame can be home oak, quicker grown, used where a joiner could hide a wilder ring. “English oak furniture” is that sandwich more often than a gallery label wants to say.
Macquoid’s *Age of Oak* ends, as a fashion story, when walnut veneer takes the polite room after 1660. The kitchen did not read him. Church benches did not. Farm presses did not. Provincial shops kept cutting oak while London laid *regia* oysters on deal. That is not a fall from grace. It is two rooms.
In the shop, tannin is the daily chemistry. A steel clamp left on a damp stile writes a black line that finish will not fully lift. Old iron ink is the same reaction. Fuming — ammonia vapor on the same tannin — is the Arts and Crafts version, a controlled darkening that treats ray and fiber differently (Stickley, *The Craftsman*). Water-based finishes raise the grain into needles. Oil and wax leave the pores open and the flake bright. Victorian filler and pigment hid the structure on purpose. A shop that wants the 17th century back skips the filler and keeps the irons sharp, because quartersawn rays pick up and a wavy board will tear no matter what the catalogue promised.
## What a water drop still tells you
Haneca et al. (2005) and the Sound Toll figures already named above are the port story. Gillows paying nearly mahogany prices for Danzig oak in 1740 (Bowett) is why quartering was never a folk default once mills could slab a log. You waste width. You get flake and a quieter cup. You pay. Albion’s naval oak is context: furniture shops used what the yards and the tannin plants did not take, and later what the steam mill made cheap.
On an old piece, sapwood worm, iron stains at the hinge, a lid that was once a chest top and now a table. On a new piece, the water-drop test on an unseen end: it sits on white oak, it sinks on red, if the finish has not already sealed the question. A container suite stamped “solid oak” wants the edge looked at. A 0.6 mm face on rubberwood or MDF is a legal sentence in some catalogues. It is not a draw-bored stool.
Plantation oak exists. It is not 1565 wainscot. If you want tight rings, say so on the purchase order, or buy antique stock and accept the iron stains. Oak wilt and sudden oak death are forestry facts in some regions `[CITE NEEDED for a current range map if you name counties]`. High-grading of wide clear boards is a market fact everywhere second growth is asked to be old growth. The tree is not a CITES appendix story in the American and European mains. It is a manners story: frame-and-panel, room to move, and a finish that either hides the pore or tells the truth about it.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (oak group notes; table 5–3a). Haneca et al., *JAS* 2005. Chinnery, *Oak Furniture*. Macquoid, *Age of Oak*. Bowett, provincial woods (Danzig oak prices at Gillow). Stickley, *The Craftsman*. Albion, *Forests and Sea Power* (oak as naval timber, context).
See: `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`, `arts-and-crafts-oak`, `windsor-mixed-wood`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Walnut
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Walnut
When Charles II came back in 1660, London’s polite furniture changed color. Oak’s black-brown joinery did not vanish from the kingdom. It vanished from the rooms that wanted to look like the court. Walnut veneer — burl, crotch, oyster, a thin skin over oak or pine — took the light. Macquoid called the years to 1720 the Age of Walnut. French and Italian rooms had already been there. American rooms would stay there longer, because *Juglans nigra* grows like a gift in the central hardwoods and does not need to be sliced to look like money.
## Two walnuts
*Juglans regia* is the European or “English” walnut, also Persian, French, Circassian, Italian, depending on the dealer’s poetry. The heartwood is grey-brown to chocolate with dark streaks. Figure can be wild. The tree is smaller and more crotched than American black walnut; shops used it as veneer because the log asked for that.
*Juglans nigra*, American black walnut, is a taller, straighter gift. Heartwood from light brown to deep chocolate, sapwood creamy and wide on open-grown trees. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) puts it at specific gravity 0.55 and Janka 1,010 lbf at 12 percent moisture — softer than white oak, hard enough for a chair, friendly to tools. The handbook’s species note still reads like a love letter: straight grain, easy to work, stable, takes a natural finish, “much valued for furniture.” About three-quarters of the commercial wood, FPL said, comes from the Central States. Arkansas sits on that belt.
Butternut (*J. cinerea*) is the pale cousin. It stains toward walnut and has never had walnut’s strength. Shops used it for carving and for cheap imitation. It is scarce now, a canker story `[CITE NEEDED for current FPL/USFS status note]`.
## How it behaves
Walnut is semi-ring-porous. The face has a gentle grain, not oak’s trenches. It planes like a courtesy. It carves without the crumbling of coarse red oak or the glass-hard fight of maple. It turns. It glues. The sapwood is the nuisance: pale, and in modern mills often steamed to blend. Purists argue. A board with a sap streak in a 19th-century American piece is ordinary.
The wood darkens, then some of the red goes out in strong sun and you get a flat brown. Old French polish on European walnut can look golden. American oil finishes go deeper. The same species under polyurethane looks sealed-in, like furniture afraid of itself.
Movement is moderate for a hardwood. It is not teak. Wide solid tops still want a proper attachment to their aprons. Veneer on a badly made ground will still check.
Burls and crotches are structural chaos and visual wealth. Oyster veneer — transverse slices laid like shells — used walnut, laburnum, and olive in the late 17th century. That is a walnut-age technique, not a walnut monopoly.
## England: veneer as a worldview
Restoration chairs with cane seats, William-and-Mary high chests, seaweed marquetry on olive and walnut grounds, the first polite card tables — the literature is thick (Bowett, *English Furniture 1660–1714*; Macquoid vol. 2). Dutch taste came with a Dutch king. French taste came because France was the factory of fashion. English walnut trees and imported *regia* fed a veneer trade. The carcase underneath stayed oak or deal. Look at the inside of a drawer from 1690. The truth is pale.
The “walnut famine” of the early 18th century is a connoisseur’s chestnut: frost, or overcutting, or both, and then mahogany. Bowett has been cautious about neat famines. What the port books show is mahogany becoming cheap after the 1721 duty change, and walnut remaining in provincial work. Fashion moved. Supply stories should not be tidier than the ledgers.
## America: walnut in the solid
In the colonies and the early republic, black walnut was a primary wood. Philadelphia and the backcountry, the Shenandoah, Kentucky, later Indiana and Missouri — walnut furniture in the solid, not only as a skin. Queen Anne and Chippendale forms in walnut sit in Winterthur and in county museums. Southern furniture (Hurst and Prown) uses walnut beside cherry and southern pine.
The 19th century made walnut the American parlor wood of the Renaissance Revival and Eastlake years. Factories in Grand Rapids and Cincinnati carved it into a darkness that still fills antique malls. Then taste went oak, then mahogany stain, then blonde. Walnut came back after the Second World War as a mid-century American show wood: dining suites, office desks, the corporate modern that was not teak.
Gun stocks ran parallel the whole time. A furniture shop and a rifle shop want the same dry, stable, figured heartwood.
## Europe after the Age
French *noyer* never needed Macquoid’s permission. Provincial armoires, Parisian veneer work, Italian *noce* — walnut is a European default. German and Austrian shops used it next to oak and pine. Scandinavian modern mostly walked past it toward oak and teak, then rediscovered darker woods later.
Circassian walnut, from the Black Sea and the Caucasus, kept a luxury veneer market into the 20th century. Pianos and dashboards ate the best of it.
## Shop notes
Walnut dust is an irritant for some people; the species is in the same gossip as teak and western redcedar. Work with air.
Stain is rarely required on heartwood and often muddies the grain. If a client wants “even color,” steaming at the mill and a careful sap selection beat a pad of pigment.
Figured walnut veneer is where the law and the ethics get ordinary: know the ground. A 12 mm walnut-veneered MDF panel is a fine kitchen door if named. It is a slight if sold as a solid slab.
## Conservation
Black walnut is a managed American hardwood, not a CITES appendix tree. Demand spikes when interior fashion goes dark; high-grading of figured logs is the quiet harm. *J. regia* in parts of its native and long-naturalized range has been pressured by veneer markets `[CITE NEEDED for a current IUCN or national status]`. Butternut’s decline is the sharper North American conservation story in this genus.
Stolen walnut trees — the backyard-tree-at-night trade — have been a real crime story in the eastern United States in the last twenty years `[CITE NEEDED: specific prosecutions]`. A cheap wide walnut slab from an unnamed seller is a board with a past.
## What to look for
Heart versus sap. Steamed versus raw. Solid versus veneer (the edge, always the edge). European versus American: *regia* often greyer and more streaked; *nigra* often more chocolate and even — until it isn’t. A William-and-Mary piece with a pine carcase and walnut oysters is correct. A 1970s “Mediterranean” suite with printed walnut grain is a poster.
In Arkansas and the Central States the tree is still a neighbor. A new walnut table from that timber sits in a line that does not have to pretend to be English 1680 or Danish 1960. It only has to be dry, honest about sap, and finished so the grain can still be felt.
## Oysters on a card table, pine in the drawer
A William-and-Mary card table is a useful object to stand beside. The show faces are *Juglans regia* — grey-brown, streaked, maybe an oyster of transverse slices laid like shells, maybe a burl that was waste to the sawyer and wealth to the veneer shop. The carcase underneath is oak or deal. Open the drawer. The sides are pale. The grain does not match the top. That is correct (Bowett, *English Furniture 1660–1714*; Macquoid’s second volume). Restoration cane-back chairs, seaweed marquetry on olive and walnut grounds, the first polite high chests: the literature is thick because the rooms wanted to look like the court after 1660, and because Dutch and French taste arrived with people and with prints. English trees and imported *regia* fed a trade that treated the log as a skin. The Age of Walnut is a veneer worldview. It is not a claim that the kingdom stopped owning oak stools.
Oyster work used walnut, laburnum, and olive. The technique is of that moment; the monopoly is not. Crotch and burl are structural chaos. They check if the ground moves and the hide glue goes brittle. A badly made yellow-poplar or pine ground will telegraph. Cross-banding and a proper substrate are the quiet half of the fashion.
The early-18th-century “walnut famine” — frost, overcutting, a neat prelude to mahogany — is a connoisseur’s chestnut. Bowett has been cautious. Port books after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 (in force 1722) show mahogany becoming cheap enough to use in the solid. Walnut stays in provincial shops. Fashion moved. Ledgers are messier than a famine story.
## America in the solid, Grand Rapids in the dark
*Juglans nigra* did not need to be sliced to look like money. Philadelphia and the backcountry, the Shenandoah, Kentucky, later Indiana and Missouri, built Queen Anne and Chippendale forms in the solid. Winterthur holds the high-style end. County museums hold the rest. Southern shops used walnut beside cherry and southern pine (Hurst and Prown). The wood is a primary, not a jacket. A sap streak on a 19th-century American piece is ordinary, not a defect label.
Then the factories. Renaissance Revival and Eastlake parlors in Grand Rapids and Cincinnati carved black walnut into a darkness that still fills antique malls. Gun stocks ran parallel the whole time: the same dry, figured heartwood, a different customer. After the Second World War, walnut came back as American corporate modern — dining suites, office desks — the dark wood that was not teak. Circassian walnut from the Black Sea and the Caucasus kept pianos and dashboards in veneer. Stolen backyard trees — the night trade of the last twenty years — are a real crime file `[CITE NEEDED: named prosecutions]`. A cheap wide slab from an unnamed seller has a past.
## Steaming, sun, and the edge
Heartwood darkens, then some of the red leaves in a south window and you get a flat brown. Old French polish on *regia* can look golden. American oil goes deeper. Polyurethane looks sealed-in. If a client wants even color, mill steaming and sap selection beat a pad of pigment. Disclose the steam. “Solid walnut” that is mostly sap is the slight. Wide tops still want buttons or slots at the aprons. Figured veneer on MDF is a fine kitchen door if named. It is a problem if sold as a slab. A 1970s “Mediterranean” suite with printed grain is a poster. A 1690 oyster table with a pine drawer is a shop telling the truth. The honest buy is still the edge: heart versus sap, steamed versus raw, solid versus a 12 mm jacket.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (black walnut species note; table 5–3a). Macquoid, *Age of Walnut*. Bowett, *English Furniture 1660–1714*; mahogany thesis (on the duty change versus “famine”). Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture*. Winterthur collection practice. Hoadley, *Understanding Wood*.
See: `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `marquetry-picture-of-trees`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`, `five-centuries-of-furniture-wood`.

item.title: Cherry
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Cherry
Leave a newly planed board of American black cherry in a sunny shop for a month, half of it under a scrap of plywood. Take the scrap off. You now have a demonstration that no stain catalogue will beat. The exposed wood has gone toward russet. The masked wood is still the color of a peeled stick. Clients call the dark “cherry.” They mean the sunburn.
*Prunus serotina* is the furniture cherry of North America. *Prunus avium*, wild cherry or gean, is the European cousin. Both are rose-family hardwoods with a fine, diffuse-porous texture and a talent for looking older than they are.
## Numbers and manners
The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) lists black cherry at specific gravity 0.50 and Janka 950 lbf — about walnut’s neighbor, softer than hard maple, harder than poplar. Production, FPL notes, has been centered in the Middle Atlantic States; the range runs from southeastern Canada through the eastern United States. Heartwood is light to dark reddish brown with a luster. Sapwood is nearly white, narrow in old trees, wide in second growth. Machining is “very good.” Shrinkage is moderately high, but the wood is “very dimensionally stable after drying.” That last clause is why cabinetmakers forgive the gum streaks.
Gum pockets and pitch flecks are the species’ handwriting. They are not rot. A shop that fills every one with color-matched putty is making a different product from a shop that leaves them as evidence.
European cherry (*P. avium*) is often a bit paler and pinker in fresh stock, used in French provincial furniture and in German and Alpine work. Trade names wander: cerisier, Kirsche. Neither species is the ornamental flowering cherry of lawns, which is useless as timber.
## Workability and finish
Cherry planes to a surface that wants to be touched. It teases if the grain rolls, as maple does. It turns well. It glues well. It takes a cut for mouldings without oak’s pore-and-splinter argument.
The finishing problem is blotch. Like pine and sometimes maple, cherry can take dye in patches. A washcoat, a dye chosen for evenness, or an oil-varnish that does not push pigment into the soft stripes — each is a school. The other school waits. Light and oxygen will do more than a pad of Van Dyke brown, and they will do it in the direction the wood already wants to go.
UV finishes slow the darkening. Some buyers want that: a kitchen of even pink. Others want the twelve-year color and should be told to keep objects off the top for the first seasons or to accept pale rings forever.
## America: the Federal wood that was not mahogany
Cherry is the show wood of a certain American house: Connecticut, Pennsylvania, western Massachusetts, later Ohio. High-style coastal shops preferred mahogany when they could get it. Inland shops had cherry. Hepplewhite sideboards, tall clocks, Pembroke tables, Shaker stands — cherry reads as polite without being imported.
Winterthur and other collections are full of the type. It was never only “country.” A Lancaster County chest of drawers in cherry can be as exact in its inlay as a Philadelphia mahogany piece, with maple and holly instead of satinwood.
Shaker communities used cherry for the pieces that faced the room. The Shaker chapter comes back to this. The species list is short; cherry is on it because it behaves and because it darkens into dignity.
Southern shops used cherry where it grew. It was never the southern wood the way walnut and heart pine were. It shows up. It does not define the coast.
## Europe: kitchen and Biedermeier, not the court
French provincial armoires in cherry are a tourist truth that happens to be real. German Biedermeier used cherry beside birch and pear when a warmer pale was wanted. English fashionable shops in the 18th century did not make cherry their mahogany. Fruitwood chairs exist; they are not the main London story.
Alpine painted furniture sometimes hides cherry, more often hides pine and fir. Do not trust color.
## The 20th century
American Colonial Revival factories stamped “cherry” on suites that were gum, birch, or maple under a red finish. Sweetgum (*Liquidambar*) has been a stand-in; it is a different anatomy (interlocked, more movement). A lens on an unseen edge ends the argument.
Late-century “Oregon cherry” and other trade names need binomials. Food-industry cherry (the orchard tree) is not a timber supply.
Contemporary American furniture made a cherry decade in the 1990s: reddish dining rooms, clear finishes, a reaction to oak kitchens. Those tables are now in their oxidation middle age. The ones that lived with south windows look like different wood from the ones that lived in apartments with blinds.
## Shop notes
Cherry and steel make marks if you leave a damp chisel. It is not oak’s tannin black, but it is enough to curse.
Thermal darkening: some finishers use heat and light boxes to pre-age. It works, and it can go too far toward brown-black. Tell the client.
Secondary wood in cherry case pieces is often pine or poplar. A cherry drawer side is a luxury, or a small-shop choice.
## Conservation
Black cherry is a commercial U.S. hardwood, not a CITES species. The furniture trade’s pressure is ordinary: clear wide stock from a tree that also has a wildlife and mast value. Black knot and gum are more common in some stands. That is a grading issue, not a moral one.
*P. avium* in Europe is managed and also planted. It is not the conservation emergency that mahogany and rosewood are. It can still be stolen from hedgerows. Provenance is a habit worth keeping.
## What to look for
Gum flecks. Fine diffuse pores. A luster under oil. Sap streaks on the edges of second-growth boards. A color mismatch between leaves of a table (sun). On antiques: oxidized tops and pale interiors. On reproductions: a red dye that sits in the grain and does not match the inside of the drawer.
Arkansas grows cherry in the Ozarks, not in the volumes of Pennsylvania, but the species is the same *P. serotina*. A shop that works it is working a Federal wood that never needed a port. The sun will still finish the job after the truck leaves.
## Inland shops, holly stringing, and a clock case
A Lancaster County chest of drawers in cherry can be as exact in its inlay as a Philadelphia mahogany piece. The difference is the forest out the door. Coastal shops bought *Swietenia* when the duty and the freight allowed (Bowett’s statute story belongs in the mahogany chapter). Inland Connecticut, Pennsylvania, western Massachusetts, later Ohio, had *Prunus serotina*. Hepplewhite sideboards, Pembroke tables, tall clocks with white-pine or poplar works-boxes and cherry hoods — the type fills Winterthur and a hundred town historical societies. Maple and holly stand in for satinwood. The piece is polite. It never saw a Jamaica wharf.
Shaker communities put cherry on the pieces that faced the room: stands, some case fronts, the wood that darkens into a quiet brown while maple stays pale and pine takes paint (Kassay; Rieman and Burks). The species list is short on purpose. Cherry is on it because it machines “very good,” as the *Wood Handbook* still says, and because after drying it is “very dimensionally stable” even though shrinkage is moderately high (FPL-GTR-190). Cabinetmakers forgive the gum streaks for that clause. Southern shops used cherry where it grew. It was never the coast’s defining wood the way walnut and heart pine were (Hurst and Prown). It shows up. It does not brand the tidewater.
European *P. avium* — cerisier, Kirsche, gean — is the kitchen and Biedermeier cousin, often a bit paler and pinker in fresh stock. French provincial armoires in cherry are a tourist sentence that happens to be true. German and Alpine work used it when a warmer pale was wanted next to birch and pear. English fashionable shops in the 18th century did not make it their mahogany. Fruitwood chairs exist. They are not the main London story. Alpine painted furniture sometimes hides cherry and more often hides pine. Do not trust color.
## Gum, blotch, and the runner’s pale ring
Leave a newly planed board in a sunny shop for a month, half under plywood. The demonstration is older than any stain chip. Clients call the dark “cherry.” They mean oxidation and light. UV finishes slow it. A kitchen of even pink is a choice. A buyer who wants the twelve-year color should be told to keep objects off the top for the first seasons or to accept pale rings forever. Two leaves of a table that do not match are often a runner and a window, not two logs.
Gum pockets and pitch flecks are handwriting, not rot. A shop that fills every one with color-matched putty is making a different product from a shop that leaves them. Second-growth sapwood is wide and nearly white; old trees ran narrower sap. A sap streak on the edge of a contemporary board is ordinary. Thermal darkening — heat and light boxes — works, and it can go too far toward brown-black. Tell the client before the box does.
Blotch is the finishing quarrel, shared with pine and sometimes maple (Hoadley). Dye in patches. A washcoat, a dye chosen for evenness, or an oil-varnish that does not shove pigment into the soft stripes: each is a school. The other school waits. Light and oxygen will do more than a pad of Van Dyke brown, and they will do it in the direction the wood already wants to go. Cherry and steel make marks if you leave a damp chisel. It is not oak’s tannin black. It is enough to curse. Secondary wood in cherry case pieces is often pine or poplar. A cherry drawer side is a luxury or a small-shop choice.
The handbook numbers sit next to walnut: specific gravity 0.50, Janka 950 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Softer than hard maple, harder than poplar. Production centered in the Middle Atlantic States; the range runs southeastern Canada through the eastern United States. Fine, diffuse-porous texture. A luster under oil. Neither *P. serotina* nor *P. avium* is the ornamental flowering cherry of lawns, which is useless as timber.
## Factory red, sweetgum, and the 1990s dining room
American Colonial Revival factories stamped “cherry” on suites that were gum, birch, or maple under a red finish. Sweetgum (*Liquidambar*) has been a stand-in: interlocked, more movement, a different anatomy under a lens. An unseen edge ends the argument. Late-century trade names — “Oregon cherry” and the rest — need binomials. Orchard trees for fruit are not a timber supply.
The 1990s made a cherry decade in American dining rooms: reddish tables, clear finishes, a reaction to oak kitchens. Those tops are now in their oxidation middle age. South-window pieces and apartment-blind pieces no longer look like the same wood. Reproductions still push a red dye that sits in the grain and does not match the inside of the drawer. Look there.
Black cherry is a commercial U.S. hardwood, not a CITES species. Clear wide stock from a tree that also has mast and wildlife value is ordinary pressure. Black knot and gum are grading issues. *P. avium* in Europe is managed and planted; it can still be stolen from hedgerows. Provenance is a habit. The species is not mahogany’s emergency. It is a Federal wood that oxidizes after the truck leaves, whether the board came from Pennsylvania volume or a thinner Ozark stand.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (black cherry species note; table 5–3a). Hoadley, *Understanding Wood* (blotch and finishing). Kassay; Rieman and Burks (Shaker). Winterthur / Federal furniture literature. Hurst and Prown (southern context).
See: `shaker-woods`, `maple`, `walnut`, `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Maple
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Maple
A Windsor chair’s legs are often maple because maple turns clean and wears like a tool. A Federal card table’s apron may be birdseye because someone opened a log and found a constellation. A bowling alley is maple because the Janka number is 1,450 lbf and the fiber does not fuzz under feet. Same genus. Three jobs. Fashion only sometimes noticed.
## Hard, soft, and the English “sycamore”
Hard maple is *Acer saccharum* (sugar, rock) and *A. nigrum* (black). The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) gives sugar maple specific gravity 0.63 and Janka 1,450 lbf — among the hardest of the ordinary American furniture woods, in a class with white oak and above cherry and walnut. Heartwood is light reddish brown; sapwood is wide and white. Texture is fine and even. Grain is usually straight until it is not.
Soft maple is mostly *A. rubrum* (red) and *A. saccharinum* (silver). Red maple: SG 0.54, Janka 950 lbf — cherry’s neighbor. It machines well and takes paint and stain. It is not a failed hard maple. It is a different ticket.
European furniture “sycamore” is *Acer pseudoplatanus*, a maple. Quartered, it can be pale and ray-flecked. Dyed grey it became harewood for Hepplewhite and Sheraton inlay. American sycamore is *Platanus occidentalis*, a different family; see that chapter. The word is a trap.
Bigleaf maple (*A. macrophyllum*) on the Pacific coast has its own figured trade. It is a regional story.
## Figure is not a species
Birdseye, curly (fiddleback), quilted, blistered — these are grain deviations, more common in hard maple but not exclusive to it. A shop pays for figure by the leaf. A kitchen island in plain hard maple is still hard maple. Catalogues that say “tiger maple” are selling curl. The Federal inlay tradition used the pale sap and the figure as a substitute for satinwood when satinwood was a ship away.
Figured maple is difficult. Tear-out on curl is a religion of sharp blades and light cuts. Filling birdseye so it does not pit takes patience. The reward is a surface that photographs like water.
## Workability and finish
Plain hard maple is tough on tools and clean in the cut when the irons are right. It turns: tool handles, chair parts, kitchenware. It resists denting. It is a butcher-block wood because it is tight and does not flavor food the way oak’s tannin can.
Blotch in stain is the finishing quarrel, worse on soft maple. Dye and a finish that does not pretend the wood is walnut will treat you better. The mid-century “blonde” maple look was often a clear finish on sapwood, sometimes with a light toner. Colonial Revival “maple” bedroom suites were often a red-orange stain on whatever pale hardwood the factory had.
Maple does not like outdoor life. It has no oak-tyloses story and no teak oil story.
## America: chairs, Shakers, and the blonde dining room
Turned maple is an eastern North American habit from the 17th century on. Chair shops in Philadelphia, New York, and New England bought maple by the wagon. Nancy Goyne Evans’s Windsor work keeps finding maple in the turned members even when the seat is elm or pine and the bow is oak.
Shaker work — Hancock, Sabbathday Lake, Pleasant Hill — uses maple for the pieces that must stay true: chairs, stands, peg rails sometimes, the understructure of tables. Cherry and pine share the load. The aesthetic of pale wood in a clear finish is partly maple’s sapwood.
Federal and Empire shops used figured maple as a show veneer and as solid for smaller forms. A Connecticut cherry chest with maple inlay is a species conversation, not a single-wood object.
The 20th century split. Factory “maple” became a stain color. School furniture and gym floors kept using the real hard maple. Then Scandinavian influence and American blonde modern put pale maple back in the dining room, next to the teak that was getting the magazine covers.
## Europe: pale, dyed, and quiet
Biedermeier used maple when birch was not the local tree. English satinwood-age furniture used harewood (*A. pseudoplatanus* dyed) as a grey field for inlay. French *érable* appears in provincial and in some Parisian work, never as the mahogany of the house.
Thonet is beech. Do not credit maple with the café chair. Maple would have done some of the turning; it would not have been the steam-bent price point in Moravian forests.
## Shop notes
Hard maple and nails are a fight. Predrill. Screws too.
The white sapwood yellows in UV. A “white maple” kitchen in a south window will cream. Water-white finishes slow this; they do not repeal it.
Ambrosia maple — beetle streaks — is a color fashion of the last twenty years. It is wound response, not a separate tree. Fine if you like it. Not an antique grade.
## Conservation
Sugar maple is a managed northern hardwood. Climate and sugar-bush economics affect the furniture log. Soft maple is abundant in many eastern stands. Neither is a CITES species. The conservation conversation is ordinary forestry, and the fashion for wide live-edge slabs that a sugar maple does not want to give.
## What to look for
End grain: diffuse pores, no vessels like oak, no resin canals. Weight: hard maple surprises people who thought “pale means pine.” Figure: look across the light. On Windsors: turned legs that take a crisp bead. On 1940s suites: a color called maple that chips to a different wood.
Arkansas is not Vermont. Hard maple is a northern commercial center (FPL: Middle Atlantic and Great Lakes, about two-thirds of lumber). Soft maple and scattered hard maple still enter southern shops. A designer specifying maple in the South is often specifying shipped stock. Say hard or soft. Say figured or plain. The word alone is a fog.
## Turned legs, an elm seat, and a peg rail
Nancy Goyne Evans keeps finding maple in the turned members of American Windsors even when the seat is elm or pine and the bow is oak. That is a job list, not a species patriotism. Hard maple — *Acer saccharum*, sugar or rock, and *A. nigrum*, black — turns a crisp bead and wears like a tool. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) puts sugar maple at specific gravity 0.63 and Janka 1,450 lbf at 12 percent moisture, among the hardest ordinary American furniture woods, in a class with white oak and above cherry and walnut. Chair shops in Philadelphia, New York, and New England bought it by the wagon from the 17th century on. Soft maple (*A. rubrum*, *A. saccharinum*) is a different ticket: red maple at SG 0.54 and Janka 950 lbf, cherry’s neighbor, a paint-and-stain wood, not a failed hard maple.
Shaker work at Hancock, Sabbathday Lake, and Pleasant Hill uses maple where a piece must stay true: chairs, stands, sometimes peg rails, the understructure of tables (Kassay; Rieman and Burks). Cherry takes the sun. Pine takes paint. The pale clear-finish look that people now call “Shaker” is partly maple sapwood, wide and white, yellowing in UV if you let it. A “white maple” kitchen in a south window will cream. Water-white finishes slow that. They do not repeal it.
Federal and Empire shops used figured maple as show veneer and as solid for smaller forms. A Connecticut cherry chest with maple inlay is a conversation among species, not a single-wood object. Hepplewhite and Sheraton plates call for harewood — *Acer pseudoplatanus* dyed grey — as a field for inlay. That tree is the English furniture “sycamore,” a maple. American sycamore is *Platanus*. The word is a trap already named in this series. Biedermeier used maple when birch was not the local tree. French *érable* appears in provincial work. Thonet is beech. Maple would have turned some parts; it was not the steam-bent price point in Moravian forests.
## Figure, tear-out, and a bowling alley
Birdseye, curly (fiddleback), quilted, blistered: grain deviations, more common in hard maple, not a species. A shop pays for figure by the leaf. Catalogues that say “tiger maple” are selling curl. The Federal tradition used pale sap and figure as a stand-in for satinwood when satinwood was a ship away. Tear-out on curl is sharp blades and light cuts. Filling birdseye so it does not pit takes patience. The surface photographs like water. A kitchen island in plain hard maple is still hard maple. It is allowed to be boring and hard.
Plain hard maple is tough on tools and clean in the cut when the irons are right. Tool handles, chair parts, kitchenware, butcher block: tight fiber, little of oak’s tannin taste. It resists denting. That is why a bowling alley and a gym floor stayed with the real thing while factory “maple” bedroom suites became a red-orange stain on whatever pale hardwood the plant had. Mid-century blonde was often a clear finish on sapwood, sometimes a light toner. Blotch in stain is worse on soft maple. Dye and a finish that does not pretend the wood is walnut will treat you better.
Hard maple and nails are a fight. Predrill. Screws too. The wood has no tyloses story and no teak oil story. It does not like weather. Ambrosia streaks — beetle wound response — are a color fashion of the last twenty years, not a separate tree and not an antique grade. Bigleaf maple (*A. macrophyllum*) on the Pacific coast has its own figured trade. Regional, not a substitute binomial for sugar maple.
## School desks, gym floors, and the word on the tag
The 20th century split the name. School furniture and floors kept using hard maple because the Janka number is not a metaphor. Factory catalogues used “maple” as a color. Scandinavian influence and American blonde modern put pale maple back in the dining room next to the teak that got the magazine covers. End grain still settles arguments: diffuse pores, no oak vessels, no pine resin canals. Weight surprises people who thought pale meant pine.
Sugar maple is a managed northern hardwood. Climate and sugar-bush economics affect the furniture log. Soft maple is abundant in many eastern stands. Neither is CITES. The fashion for wide live-edge slabs asks a sugar maple for a shape it does not want to give. That is ordinary forestry, not an appendix. On a 1940s suite, a color called maple that chips to a different wood is the tell. On a Windsor, a turned leg that takes a crisp bead is the tell. Say hard or soft. Say figured or plain. The word alone is fog, in Vermont or anywhere the stock was shipped.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (hard and soft maple notes; table 5–3a). Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America*. Kassay; Rieman and Burks (Shaker). Sheraton / Hepplewhite plates (harewood). Hoadley.
See: `windsor-mixed-wood`, `shaker-woods`, `sycamore`, `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `satinwood`.

item.title: Ash
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Ash
Ash is the wood that bent. Tool handles, wagon gear, tennis frames, the hoop of a Windsor, the back of a country chair that was steamed in a box and pulled around a form — *Fraxinus* has long fibers and a willingness to move while hot that oak only partly shares and maple mostly refuses. Furniture fashion treated ash as a servant until Mission shops and later pale modern interiors noticed the open grain. Then a beetle from Asia arrived in Michigan in 2002 and the servant’s tree began to die in streets and woodlots across the eastern United States.
## The wood
American white ash (*Fraxinus americana*) and its white-ash group cousins are the furniture and handle woods. The *Wood Handbook* puts white ash at specific gravity 0.60 and Janka 1,320 lbf — oak’s neighbor in hardness, a little lighter in weight. It is ring-porous: a bold earlywood pore line, a face that looks like a quieter oak. Heartwood is light brown; sapwood is wide and nearly white. That pale sap is the “white ash” of table tops in the 2010s.
Black ash (*F. nigra*) is lighter (basic SG in the 0.45–0.48 range, FPL). It is a basket-splint wood, a swamp wood, a veneer wood. It is not the handle grade.
European ash (*F. excelsior*) is the English and continental furniture ash: pale, tough, used for painted chairs and for the bent parts of country seating. Japanese and other ashes exist in trade; the binomial still matters.
Ash has no tyloses story like white oak. It is not a barrel wood. It is not a boat-plank wood of the oak kind. Durability in the ground is poor. Durability in a chair is excellent.
## Workability and finish
Ash planes well, with pore-edge tear if you are careless. It steam-bends in the textbook. It takes stain in the earlywood first, so a dark stain makes a striped, almost oak-revival look. A clear finish on pale sapwood is the modern taste: restaurant tables, Scandinavian-adjacent interiors, the “white oak” look for people who wanted more bounce in the grain.
Open pores want filler if you want a glass top. Most shops now leave them.
The wood is springy. Chair stretchers in ash survive rungs that would snap in a short-fiber species. Baseball bats were white ash until maple and aluminum took shares; the bat factories and the furniture shops bought from the same grade stories.
## Furniture history
English country chairs — the ash and elm combinations of the Midlands and the Thames valley — are older than Macquoid’s parlor ages. Windsor production on both sides of the Atlantic used ash for bows and sometimes for legs. Evans’s American Windsor research and the English vernacular literature agree on the job: bend and toughness.
High-style 18th-century London did not make ash its mahogany. Painted Hepplewhite-style chairs sometimes used beech or birch; ash shows up in the cheaper painted seat. Provincial work is where to look.
Arts and Crafts and Mission shops used ash when oak was dear or when a paler open grain was wanted. Some American factory “oak” of the golden-oak years is ash under a stain. A lens on the end grain: ash rays are finer than oak’s. The flake will not flash the same way.
Mid-century and after: pale ash dining furniture, bent plywood ash faces, the 2010s restaurant boom in ash tables. European designers never abandoned *F. excelsior* for chairs.
## The beetle
Emerald ash borer (*Agrilus planipennis*) was identified in the Detroit area in 2002 (USDA / APHIS and Forest Service timelines). It has since killed ash across a huge part of the species’ North American range. The furniture implication is not “ash is gone from the earth.” It is that urban and woodland salvage has flooded some markets with dead standing timber of uneven quality, that future clear wide stock is a question, and that designers who treat ash as an infinite pale oak substitute are not reading the forest.
Europe has its own ash disaster: *Hymenoscyphus fraxineus*, ash dieback, a different organism, a similar thinning of *F. excelsior* (noted in the chestnut-blight review literature as a parallel introduced-pathogen story). English chair woods are not what they were.
