Use what is already down, dry it properly, and do not pretend a stained poplar is ash. Planting and breeding programs exist. They are not a furniture catalogue yet.
## Shop notes
Ash and oak look alike to the hopeful. Rays and the tyloses test (white oak) separate them. Red oak’s open pores resemble ash; the ray fleck on a quartered red-oak face is still an oak tell.
Kiln-dried ash can be brittle if it was standing dead too long. Bend with caution. Tap a board. The good handle-grade rings.
## Conservation and buying
*Fraxinus* species are not CITES furniture woods in the mahogany sense. The conservation issue is pest and disease. Salvage furniture from street trees is a reasonable use if the wood is identified and dried; metal in urban logs will ruin saws. Ask.
A pale ash table from domestic hardwood is still one of the more readable American buys: no appendix, anatomy you can see, a history in chairs that does not need a tropical port. The beetle makes that sentence sadder than it was in 1999. It does not make it false.
## What to look for
Ring-porous, no big oak rays, spring in a thin member, a bend without a break. On Windsors: the bow. On 2010s tables: sapwood color that will yellow a little. On “oak” rockers from 1900: maybe ash. On a new wide slab: ask if it was standing dead, and how long.
Arkansas is ash country in the same way it is oak country — mixed hardwood stands, white ash in the better soils. A shop that works it now is working a wood whose living future is being argued in extension bulletins. The boards already in stick are still boards.
## The steam box, the hoop, and a Midlands chair
A Windsor bow coming off a form is ash doing the work fashion used to ignore. The piece was in the steam box until the fibers would move. It was pulled around iron or timber, clamped, and left to set. Evans’s American Windsor research and the English vernacular literature agree on the job: bend and toughness. English country chairs — ash and elm in the Midlands and the Thames valley — are older than Macquoid’s parlor ages. High-style 18th-century London did not make ash its mahogany. Painted Hepplewhite-style chairs sometimes used beech or birch; ash shows up in the cheaper painted seat. Provincial work is where to look.
White ash (*Fraxinus americana*) sits near specific gravity 0.60 and Janka 1,320 lbf in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) — oak’s neighbor in hardness, a little lighter. Ring-porous: a bold earlywood pore line, a face like a quieter oak. Heartwood light brown; sapwood wide and nearly white. That pale sap is the restaurant-table ash of the 2010s. Black ash (*F. nigra*) is lighter, a basket-splint and swamp wood, not handle grade. European *F. excelsior* is the English and continental chair ash, never abandoned by designers who needed a pale, tough bend. Ash has no tyloses. You do not build a barrel from it. Durability in the ground is poor. Durability in a stretcher is excellent. Springy long fiber survives rungs that snap in a short-fiber species.
Chair shops and bat factories used to buy from the same grade stories. Baseball bats were white ash until maple and aluminum took shares. Tool handles, wagon gear, tennis frames: the servant list. Mission and Arts and Crafts shops used ash when oak was dear or when a paler open grain was wanted. Some American factory “oak” of the golden-oak years is ash under a stain. A lens on the end grain: ash rays are finer than oak’s. The flake will not flash. Red oak’s open pores resemble ash; quartered red oak still shows an oak ray if you look.
## Handle grade, kiln-dead, and a stain that stripes
Ash planes well, with pore-edge tear if you rush. It steam-bends in the textbook. Dark stain hits the earlywood first and makes a striped, oak-revival face. Clear finish on pale sapwood is the later taste: Scandinavian-adjacent interiors, the “white oak” look for people who wanted more bounce in the grain. Open pores want filler if you want glass. Most shops now leave them.
Kiln-dried boards from standing-dead trees can be brittle. Bend with caution. Tap a board. Handle-grade rings. Urban salvage after the beetle often carries nails and fences; metal ruins saws. Ask how long the tree stood dead, and whether anyone ran a detector. The furniture implication of *Agrilus planipennis*, identified in the Detroit area in 2002 (USDA / APHIS and Forest Service timelines), is not that ash has left the earth. It is uneven salvage, a question over future clear wide stock, and a warning to designers who treated ash as infinite pale oak. Europe’s *Hymenoscyphus fraxineus* — ash dieback — is a different organism and a similar thinning of *F. excelsior* (noted as a parallel introduced-pathogen story in the chestnut-blight review literature). English chair woods are not what they were.
## After 2002, the same anatomy
Use what is already down. Dry it. Do not sell stained poplar as ash. Planting and breeding programs exist. They are not a catalogue grade yet. *Fraxinus* is not a CITES furniture genus in the mahogany sense. The conservation issue is pest and disease. Street-tree furniture is a reasonable use if the wood is identified and dried.
On a Windsor, look at the bow. On a 1900 “oak” rocker, maybe ash. On a 2010s table, sapwood that will yellow a little. On a new wide slab, the standing-dead question. Rays and the tyloses test still separate ash from white oak. The spring in a thin member still separates a good chair wood from a pretty slab. Mid-century bent-plywood ash faces and pale dining furniture were a fashion return, not a new species. The beetle makes the domestic-hardwood sentence sadder than it was in 1999. The anatomy on the bench has not changed.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (white and black ash). USDA / NISIC and APHIS on emerald ash borer, 2002. European ash dieback: Gross et al. cited in *Cryphonectria* reviews. Evans, Windsor literature. Hoadley.
See: `windsor-mixed-wood`, `oak-european-and-american`, `elm`, `arts-and-crafts-oak`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Elm
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Elm
Turn a Windsor seat over. If the underside is a broad, interlocked, slightly greasy-looking hardwood with pores in bands and a grain that will not split out to the rim when four legs are driven in, you are often looking at elm. Chairmakers used it because it refuses to cleave cleanly. That vice for the splitter is a virtue for the seat.
The tree that gave those seats has had a bad century. Dutch elm disease — *Ophiostoma ulmi*, then the more aggressive *O. novo-ulmi* — was described in the Netherlands after the First World War and found in the United States in the 1930s, introduced on logs (USDA / NISIC). American elm (*Ulmus americana*), the street-tree cathedral, collapsed as a mature timber. English elm (*U. procera* and related taxa — the names have been argued) vanished from hedges and from the chair counties. Furniture elm after that is salvage, rock elm, slippery elm, imported stock, or a label that means “we wish.”
## The wood
The *Wood Handbook* divides American elms into soft and hard. Soft elm (American, slippery / *U. rubra*): moderately heavy, high shock resistance, excellent bending. American elm: SG about 0.50, Janka about 830 lbf at 12 percent — softer than oak, tough rather than hard. Hard elm (rock elm, *U. thomasii*, and others) is heavier and was a specialized timber.
Heartwood is light brown, often with a red tinge. The grain is typically interlocked. That is the whole plot. You do not rive elm into tidy boards. You saw it, and you still fight tear-out. You do not make a straight-grained show table unless you like a wild face. You do make seats, hubs, coffins, keels, and the parts of a chair that must take a wedge.
European elm furniture — English country, French provincial *orme*, Dutch — uses the same interlocking. Burl elm and “Carpathian elm” burl were veneer fashions: 19th-century and Art Deco surfaces with a storm in them.
Water resistance in the log is part of elm’s folklore and part of its use in piles and pipes `[CITE NEEDED for a measured durability class versus the folklore of water pipes]`. In furniture, the point is toughness and the refusal to split.
## Workability and finish
Elm is contrary under a plane. Sharp, steep, and sometimes a scraper. It steam-bends well (FPL). It takes nails without splitting, which is why wagon and chair shops kept it.
The face can be handsome — a cascading interlock, a fiddle — or merely busy. Stain makes it busier. Country pieces were often painted or left alone. Burl veneer was polished like a luxury.
Odor in green elm is famously sour. Dry furniture does not smell. If an old seat smells, you have another problem.
## Seats, coffins, and the vernacular
English elm seats in Windsors and in Midlands chairs are a textbook pairing with ash bows and beech or ash legs. American Windsors used elm when they could get it; they also used pine and poplar for seats (Evans). The species is a clue to shop and region, not a rule.
Coffins kept elm in the trade after chairs had other options. So did some factory rockers. So did veneer mills that sliced burl for dressing tables and radio cabinets.
High-style 18th-century work rarely showed elm. It is not a mahogany substitute. It is a job wood that sometimes became a look when burl was in fashion.
## Disease and the street
The American elm’s loss is a civic and forest grief that furniture only inherits. Remaining elms are often younger, sprout-grown, or resistant cultivars that are not timber yet. Rock elm was always scarcer. Slippery elm has a medicinal-bark story that did the standing tree no favors.
Europe’s elm story is similar: a vernacular furniture wood tied to hedges and riverbanks, then a pathogen, then a museum of old seats.
Planting resistant elms is a civic project. It is not a mill project this decade.
## Shop notes
If you restore a Windsor, do not replace an elm seat with flatsawn oak unless you enjoy splits between the leg holes. If you must substitute, a well-chosen ash or a pine seat of the regional type is more honest than a pretty oak plank.
Burl elm veneer on antiques is thin and brittle. Do not sand through a swirl to “clean it up.”
## Conservation
Elms are not CITES show woods. They are disease woods. Buying old elm furniture is reuse. Buying new “elm” wants a binomial and a country. Chinese elm (*Ulmus parvifolia* and trade “elm” that may be other genera) enters the carved-furniture market. Identify it. Some of that trade is ordinary; some of it is a name pasted on something else.
## What to look for
Interlocked grain on a thick seat. Leg holes that have not split to the edge. A wild veneer on a 1930s vanity. On a street, a vase-shaped tree that may be a cultivar. On a bill of lumber, a species name, not a wish.
The Ozarks grew elm. The furniture shops used it less than oak and walnut. The chairs that have it are doing a job the better-known hardwoods do worse. That is enough to keep the species in a 500-year series after the boulevards went bare.
## Four holes in a seat that will not cleave
A Windsor seat is a thick plank with four tapered holes and a lot of sideways force. Drive the legs in, wedge them, and the fiber around the rim has to hold. Oak, riven or flatsawn, will often split out to the edge along the rays or the ring. Maple is hard and can be brittle in a wide seat. Pine and poplar were used in American shops (Evans) and they work if the seat is thick enough and the grain is kind. Elm is the species that refuses to cleave cleanly. Interlocked grain, a vice for the splitter, is the virtue. Turn the seat over. Broad, slightly greasy-looking hardwood, pores in bands, a wild face: that is the tell.
The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) divides American elms into soft and hard. Soft elm — American (*Ulmus americana*), slippery (*U. rubra*) — is moderately heavy, high in shock resistance, excellent in bending. American elm sits near specific gravity 0.50 and Janka 830 lbf at 12 percent moisture: softer than oak, tough rather than hard. Hard elm (rock elm, *U. thomasii*, and others) is heavier, a specialized timber. Heartwood light brown, often a red tinge. You saw it; you do not rive it into tidy boards. You still fight tear-out. A straight-grained show table in elm is a taste for a wild face, not a default. Seats, hubs, coffins, keels, the parts of a chair that take a wedge: those are the jobs.
English Windsors and Midlands chairs pair elm seats with ash bows and beech or ash legs. That pairing is older than Macquoid’s parlor clock. High-style 18th-century work rarely showed elm. It is not a mahogany substitute. French provincial *orme* and Dutch country pieces use the same interlocking. Burl elm and the trade name “Carpathian elm” burl were 19th-century and Art Deco veneer fashions: a storm on a dressing table, later on a radio cabinet. Polish the swirl. Do not sand through it.
## Disease on the logs, empty hedges, a coffin shop
Dutch elm disease — *Ophiostoma ulmi*, then the more aggressive *O. novo-ulmi* — was described in the Netherlands after the First World War and found in the United States in the 1930s, introduced on logs (USDA / NISIC). American elm as a mature street timber collapsed. English elm (*U. procera* and related taxa; the names have been argued) vanished from hedges and from the chair counties. Furniture elm after that is salvage, rock elm, slippery elm, imported stock, or a label that means wish. Remaining American elms are often younger, sprout-grown, or resistant cultivars that are not mill timber this decade. Slippery elm has a medicinal-bark story that did the standing tree no favors. Rock elm was always scarcer.
Coffins kept elm in the trade after chairs had other options. So did some factory rockers. Water resistance in the log is folklore and also a historic use in piles and pipes `[CITE NEEDED for a measured durability class versus the pipe stories]`. In furniture the point is toughness. Green elm smells sour. Dry furniture does not. If an old seat smells, look for another problem.
Europe’s vernacular elm — hedges, riverbanks, a seat wood — became a museum of old chairs in the same century. Planting resistant elms is a civic project. It is not a mill project yet. Elms are not CITES show woods. They are disease woods. Buying old elm furniture is reuse. Buying new “elm” wants a binomial and a country. Chinese elm (*U. parvifolia*) and carved-furniture “elm” that may be other genera enter the market. Identify it. Some of that trade is ordinary. Some is a name pasted on.
## Restoring a seat without making a split
Do not replace an elm Windsor seat with flatsawn oak unless you enjoy cracks between the leg holes. A well-chosen ash seat, or a pine seat of the regional type Evans documents, is more honest than a pretty oak plank. Elm is contrary under a plane: sharp, steep, sometimes a scraper. It steam-bends well (FPL). It takes nails without splitting, which is why wagon shops kept it. Stain makes a busy face busier. Country pieces were often painted or left alone. Burl veneer on a 1930s vanity is thin and brittle.
On the bench: interlocked grain on a thick seat, leg holes that have not split to the edge, a wild veneer, a bill of lumber with a species name. On the street: a vase-shaped cultivar that is not a board. The better-known hardwoods — oak, walnut, maple — do many jobs better. They do this one worse. That is why elm stays in a 500-year series after the boulevards went bare.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (elm group). USDA / NISIC, Dutch elm disease (*Ophiostoma*). Evans, Windsor literature. English vernacular chair studies `[CITE NEEDED: Cotton or Jenkins on English regional chairs]`. Hoadley.
See: `windsor-mixed-wood`, `ash`, `beech`, `chestnut-and-the-blight`.

item.title: Beech
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Beech
In 1859 the Gebrüder Thonet put a café chair on the market that was six pieces of steamed beech, ten screws, two nuts, and a cane seat. The V&A’s early example (W.31-2011) is thin and exact; later No. 14s grew thicker. Some fifty million are said to have been made by 1930. The chair is famous. The wood is why the chair exists. *Fagus sylvatica* in Moravian and Austrian forests bent in iron moulds after a steam bath, dried, and packed flat. Oak would not have done this at that price. Walnut would not have grown in those stands. Beech did.
## The wood
European beech and American beech (*F. grandifolia*) are close cousins in the shop. The *Wood Handbook* calls American beech heavy, hard, strong, high in shock resistance, “highly suitable for steam bending.” It shrinks a lot and must be dried with care. It machines smoothly, turns, wears. Color runs from nearly white sap to reddish-brown heart, sometimes without a clear line. Little figure. Uniform texture. Janka about 1,300 lbf, SG about 0.64 at 12 percent — maple-and-oak country.
European beech is the larger furniture story because the factories were there. It steams, it stains (the Thonet red-brown is a finish, not a heartwood), it is pale under a clear coat. It has almost no outdoor durability. A beech bench left in weather is a short story.
Rays in beech are visible on a quartered face as a small, even fleck — not oak’s mirrors. The wood can look dull until a finish wakes the pink.
## Workability and finish
Beech is a toolmaker’s wood: plane bodies, moulding-plane stocks, workbench parts, mallets. It wears smoothly and takes a precise cut. In furniture it is the same: chair parts, frames, kitchen tables in Central Europe, turned members.
It moves. A wide beech panel is a risk. Frame-and-panel, or laminated, or stay narrow.
It takes stain too well. Factory “walnut,” “mahogany,” and “cherry” chairs from the late 19th and early 20th centuries are often beech underneath. The Thonet stain is honest because the form is honest. A carved “Renaissance” chair in stained beech is a costume.
Glue holds. Nails hold if you predrill; the wood is hard.
## Before Thonet
Beech was a medieval and early modern utility wood in Europe: trenchers, bowls, cheap furniture, the insides of things. English shops used it for painted chairs in the 18th century — Sheraton and Hepplewhite designs in the cheaper line, the “fancy chair” factories later. It is not the Age of Oak and not the Age of Mahogany. It is the age of the seat that had to be sold in quantity.
American beech grew in the eastern third of the country. FPL notes greatest lumber production in the Central and Middle Atlantic States. It never became a high-style show wood. Floors, tool parts, furniture frames, food-related wood (it has little taste). Some Windsor shops used it. It was never elm’s equal as a seat in the English sense, nor maple’s equal as a turning wood in New England.
## The bentwood century
Michael Thonet began with laminated veneer bends in Boppard, then moved to solid steam-bent beech and to Koritschan in Moravia. The No. 14, designed 1859, is the type: circular seat, two back loops, legs that are also bends. Philadelphia Museum of Art’s notes emphasize the shipping: thirty-six dismantled chairs to a crate. The industrial story is beech’s story — a species that grew where the factory could be built, that bent, that was light enough to ship, cheap enough to undercut joined walnut.
Competitors (Kohn, later others) used the same forests. Café chairs from Lisbon to Chicago are beech objects with local stains.
Alvar Aalto’s laminates are birch; the bentwood idea is cousin to Thonet, not the same mill. The Finnish chapter takes that.
## 20th century to IKEA’s ancestors
Beech remained the European chair wood: school seating, dining sets, the pale postwar German and Czech factories. Some Danish work used beech when oak was not the point. It is a kitchen-table wood in a thousand flats.
American taste associated beech with “cheap imported chair.” That snobbery missed the Thonet achievement and missed the tool-wood quality. It correctly identified a lot of stained hotel furniture.
## Shop notes
Dry beech thoroughly and keep it in the house’s humidity before glue-up. It will move after you think you are done.
Steaming: follow a bending-wood protocol (straight grain, no defects, adequate time). Thonet’s factory times — heat to steam, moulds, twenty hours drying around 70 °C in popular accounts of the No. 14 — are industrial. A shop can bend chair parts without a factory. A shop cannot pretend a flatsawn beech slab will stay flat in a steam-heated room.
## Conservation
Beech is not a CITES species. European beech forests are managed; mast years and climate affect increment. American beech has beech bark disease in parts of the range `[CITE NEEDED: USFS current map]`. Neither is a rosewood-level emergency. Both are ordinary woods that factories can exhaust locally if they only want the large, clear stems.
## What to look for
Even texture, small rays, a pink-brown, stain that chips to pale. On a café chair: the bend, the screw, the cane. On a “walnut” parlor chair: the weight and the pore (or lack of oak pore). On a plane body: the right wood in the right job.
A 500-year series cannot treat beech as a footnote to oak. The chair most people in modern cities have sat on, without knowing, was beech.
## Thirty-six in a crate, a cane seat, two nuts
The V&A’s early No. 14 (W.31-2011) is thin and exact. Later examples grew thicker. The type is 1859: circular seat, two back loops, legs that are also bends, cane in the ring, ten screws, two nuts. Philadelphia Museum of Art notes the shipping arithmetic — thirty-six dismantled chairs to a crate. Michael Thonet had started with laminated veneer bends in Boppard, then moved to solid steam-bent beech and to Koritschan in Moravia. *Fagus sylvatica* grew where the factory could be built. It bent after a steam bath, dried in the moulds, packed flat. Oak would not have done this at that price. Walnut would not have stood in those forests in that volume. Competitors (Kohn and others) used the same stands. Café chairs from Lisbon to Chicago are beech objects with local stains. Some fifty million No. 14s are said to have been made by 1930 (V&A texts). Factory times in popular accounts — steam, moulds, about twenty hours drying around 70 °C — are industrial. A small shop can bend a chair part. A small shop cannot pretend a flatsawn beech slab will stay flat in a steam-heated room.
Alvar Aalto’s laminates are birch. The idea of a bent seat is cousin to Thonet, not the same mill. The Finnish chapter takes that. What belongs here is the species credit: European beech made the café century possible.
## Plane stocks, fancy chairs, and a wood that moves
Before the café chair, beech was already in the shop as a toolmaker’s wood: moulding-plane bodies, workbench parts, mallets, anything that must wear smooth and take a precise cut. Medieval and early modern Europe used it for trenchers, bowls, cheap furniture, the insides of things. English shops in the 18th century put it under paint — the cheaper Sheraton and Hepplewhite lines, then the fancy-chair factories. It is not Macquoid’s oak and not his mahogany. It is the seat that had to be sold in quantity.
American beech (*F. grandifolia*) is a close cousin on the bench. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) calls it heavy, hard, strong, high in shock resistance, “highly suitable for steam bending.” It shrinks a lot and must be dried with care. It machines smoothly, turns, wears. Color from nearly white sap to reddish-brown heart, sometimes without a clear line. Little figure. Uniform texture. Janka about 1,300 lbf, specific gravity about 0.64 at 12 percent moisture — maple-and-oak country. Greatest lumber production, FPL notes, in the Central and Middle Atlantic States. It never became a high-style show wood. Floors, tool parts, furniture frames, food-related wood (little taste). Some Windsor shops used it. It was never elm’s equal as a seat in the English sense, nor maple’s equal as a New England turning wood.
Rays on a quartered beech face are a small, even fleck — not oak’s mirrors. The wood looks dull until a finish wakes the pink. It has almost no outdoor durability. A bench left in weather is a short story. It moves. A wide panel is a risk. Frame-and-panel, or laminate, or stay narrow. Dry it thoroughly and let it sit at house humidity before glue-up. It will move after you think you are done. Glue holds. Nails hold if you predrill; the wood is hard.
## Stain as a costume, IKEA’s ancestors
Beech takes stain too well. Factory “walnut,” “mahogany,” and “cherry” chairs from the late 19th and early 20th centuries are often beech underneath. The Thonet red-brown is a finish, not a heartwood, and it is honest because the form is honest. A carved “Renaissance” parlor chair in stained beech is a costume. Chip the finish. The pore is not oak’s. The weight and the even texture remain.
Beech stayed the European chair wood through school seating, dining sets, pale postwar German and Czech factories, kitchen tables in a thousand flats. Some Danish work used it when oak was not the point. American taste called it “cheap imported chair.” That snobbery missed the Thonet achievement and the tool-wood quality. It correctly identified a lot of stained hotel furniture.
Steaming wants straight grain, no defects, adequate time — a bending-wood protocol, not a slab-table fantasy. Beech is not CITES. European forests are managed; mast years and climate affect increment. American beech has beech bark disease in parts of the range `[CITE NEEDED: USFS current map]`. Neither is a rosewood emergency. Both can be exhausted locally if factories want only the large, clear stems.
On a café chair: the bend, the screw, the cane. On a “walnut” parlor chair: pale wood under the chip. On a plane body: the right species in the right job. The chair most people in modern cities have sat on, without knowing, was this one.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190. V&A W.31-2011; V&A text on No. 14 production numbers. Philadelphia Museum of Art, Model No. 14. Ostergard, *Bent Wood and Metal Furniture*. Hoadley.
See: `finnish-birch-aalto`, `windsor-mixed-wood`, `maple`, `engineered-wood-honest`.

item.title: Birch
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Birch
Biedermeier commodes in Vienna and Berlin went pale after the wars with Napoleon. The wood that made many of them look like butter and silk was birch. A century later, Finnish factories rolled birch into plywood and Alvar Aalto bent the plies into a sanatorium chair. Between those moments, American yellow birch impersonated mahogany in Grand Rapids and then impersonated nothing, as a honest blonde. Birch is a northern genus that furniture uses when it wants light, a fine texture, and a price below walnut.
## The woods
Yellow birch (*Betula alleghaniensis*) is the American furniture birch. The *Wood Handbook*: heavy, hard, strong, good shock resistance, fine uniform texture. SG about 0.62, Janka about 1,260 lbf — near hard maple, a little kinder. Heartwood light reddish brown; sapwood white. It shrinks considerably in the kiln. Sweet birch (*B. lenta*) is similar. Paper birch (*B. papyrifera*) is lighter, for turned ware, toothpicks, and the canoe, not for a dining table of ambition.
European silver and downy birches (*B. pendula*, *B. pubescens*) are the Scandinavian and Russian woods: pale, used solid and as the classic Baltic / Finnish plywood. Karelian birch — a figured, masur, almost marble grain — is a luxury veneer from particular trees, not a separate species you can order by the cubic meter.
Birch is diffuse-porous, tight, and takes a polish. It also takes paint as if it were made for it. Country and factory chairs in painted birch are legion.
## Workability and finish
Yellow birch machines well and dulls edges less than hard maple. It turns. It glues. It has a reputation for moving if drying was rushed — dry it, then wait.
Stain blotch is possible but less famous than cherry’s. The 19th-century American factory habit was to stain birch red-brown and sell it as a mahogany suite for people who could not buy *Swietenia*. The pores do not really match. The color can fool a dark room.
Clear finishes on pale birch yellow with the wood. Water-white formulas delay the cream. Oil darkens it toward honey, which is a Biedermeier cousin if you want it.
## Biedermeier and the pale north
After 1815, Central European bourgeois furniture turned from imperial mahogany toward local pale woods: birch, pear, cherry, maple. Black inlay, columned forms, a polished birch face that looks almost like satinwood without the ship. Museum collections in Vienna, Munich, and Berlin hold the type. The Biedermeier chapter returns to the mix. Birch is the frequent star.
Russian and Baltic birch went west as logs and as veneer. The later plywood empire — Finland, Russia, the Baltics — starts in that forest.
English fashionable shops used birch for painted late-18th and early-19th-century chairs and for cheap cabinet work. It was not Macquoid’s satinwood. It was what the factory could finish with paint and sell.
## America: the impersonator and the honest blonde
New England and the Lake States cut yellow birch as a primary furniture wood. Turned chairs, tables, factory suites. Colonial Revival “maple” and “mahogany” both ate birch. A lens and an unseen surface (the inside of a rail) will show a tight diffuse-porous wood that is not oak and not true mahogany.
20th-century American blonde furniture used birch and maple together in the public mind. School desks, dinette sets, the postwar kitchen. Then teak and walnut took the magazines, and birch went back to the plywood mill and the dowel bin.
## Plywood
Baltic birch plywood — many thin, clear plies, few voids — is a shop standard for jigs and for exposed-edge modern work. It is a furniture wood. Aalto’s factory story and the Eames story belong in their chapters; the species credit is birch’s. Cheap “birch” plywood with a nice face and a core of something else is a different product. Count the plies. Look for voids.
Finnish and Russian export plywood has been a political and tariff object as well as a material `[CITE NEEDED for a specific recent trade action if mentioned in publication]`. The furniture designer still specifies the grade.
## Shop notes
Birch dust is fine and irritating. Paper birch is a poor outdoor wood. Yellow birch in wet use is not teak.
Karelian figure is expensive and often veneer for a reason. Solid masur birch in large sizes is a unicorn.
## Conservation
Birch species used in furniture are not CITES-listed. Northern forestry, peatland issues, and the paper industry affect the same genus. Karelian figure is inherently scarce. Ordinary yellow birch is a managed American hardwood. The conservation conversation is dull on purpose. Keep it that way: buy the grade you need, do not dye a threatened tropical to look like birch.
## What to look for
Tight grain, pale color, small pores, a stained “mahogany” that is too fine in texture. On Biedermeier: a buttery face and black line inlay. On a plywood edge: even brown lines, many of them. On a Shaker-looking stand that is too cheap: maybe birch, maybe not maple — weigh it.
Arkansas is not birch country of the Lake States kind. A southern shop that uses birch is usually using shipped yellow birch or plywood. That is fine if named. The series includes birch because the last 200 years of pale furniture cannot be told without it.
## A Viennese commode after 1815
After the Napoleonic wars, bourgeois rooms in Vienna, Berlin, and Munich turned away from imperial mahogany toward woods that grew in the same climate as the customer. Birch was a frequent star: pale, fine, polished until it looked almost like satinwood without the ship. Black line inlay, columned forms, a buttery face. Museum collections in those cities hold the type. Pear, cherry, and maple share the Biedermeier mix; the dedicated chapter returns to the cast. What belongs here is the genus doing the light.
European silver and downy birches (*Betula pendula*, *B. pubescens*) are the Scandinavian and Russian woods, used solid and later as the classic Baltic and Finnish plywood. Karelian birch — masur, a figured, almost marble grain — is a luxury veneer from particular trees, not a species you order by the cubic meter. Solid masur in large sizes is a unicorn. Russian and Baltic logs went west as veneer before they went west as ply. English fashionable shops used birch for painted late-18th- and early-19th-century chairs and for cheap cabinet work. It was not Macquoid’s satinwood. It was what a factory could finish with paint and sell.
Yellow birch (*B. alleghaniensis*) is the American furniture birch. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190): heavy, hard, strong, good shock resistance, fine uniform texture. Specific gravity about 0.62, Janka about 1,260 lbf — near hard maple, a little kinder. Heartwood light reddish brown; sapwood white. It shrinks considerably in the kiln. Dry it, then wait. Sweet birch (*B. lenta*) is similar. Paper birch (*B. papyrifera*) is lighter: turned ware, toothpicks, the canoe, not a dining table of ambition. Diffuse-porous, tight, takes a polish, takes paint as if made for it. Country and factory chairs in painted birch are legion.
## Grand Rapids red, school blonde, an unseen rail
New England and the Lake States cut yellow birch as a primary furniture wood: turned chairs, tables, factory suites. Colonial Revival catalogues sold “maple” and “mahogany” that both ate birch. Stain it red-brown in a dark parlor and the color can fool. The pores do not match *Swietenia*. A lens on an unseen rail — the inside, not the show face — shows a tight diffuse-porous wood that is not oak and not true mahogany. 20th-century American blonde furniture mixed birch and maple in the public mind: school desks, dinette sets, the postwar kitchen. Then teak and walnut took the magazines. Birch went back to the plywood mill and the dowel bin.
Stain blotch is possible, less famous than cherry’s (Hoadley). Clear finishes yellow with the wood. Water-white formulas delay the cream. Oil darkens it toward honey, a Biedermeier cousin if you want that. Yellow birch machines well and dulls edges less than hard maple. It turns. It glues. Rushed drying is the reputation it earned. Birch dust is fine and irritating. Neither paper birch nor yellow birch is a wet-use wood. Not teak.
A Shaker-looking stand that is too cheap may be birch or may be something else. Weigh it. Hard maple surprises; yellow birch is close. On a stained “mahogany” suite, texture that is too fine is the tell.
## Count the plies
Baltic birch plywood — many thin, clear plies, few voids — is a shop standard for jigs and for exposed-edge modern work. It is a furniture wood. Aalto’s factory story and the Eames story belong in their chapters (V&A plywood history; Artek). The species credit is birch’s. Cheap “birch” plywood with a handsome face and a core of something else is a different product. Count the plies. Look for voids. Even brown lines, many of them, are the honest edge. Finnish and Russian export plywood has been a political and tariff object as well as a material `[CITE NEEDED for a named recent trade action if the published version specifies one]`. Specify the grade anyway.
Furniture birches are not CITES-listed. Northern forestry, peatland issues, and the paper industry affect the same genus. Karelian figure is scarce by nature. Ordinary yellow birch is a managed American hardwood. Buy the grade you need. Do not dye a threatened tropical to look like birch. A southern shop that uses birch is usually using shipped yellow birch or plywood. Name it. The last two hundred years of pale furniture — Vienna to Helsinki to Grand Rapids — cannot be told if this genus is treated as a maple understudy.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (yellow, sweet, paper birch). Biedermeier museum literature. V&A plywood history; Aalto / Artek. Hoadley.
See: `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `finnish-birch-aalto`, `plywood-veneers-twentieth`, `maple`.

item.title: Hickory and pecan
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Hickory and pecan
Hickory is the American wood that furniture fashion walked around. Toolmakers did not. A struck adze handle, a skid pole, a ladder rung, the bow of a chair that had to come back to shape — *Carya* is the hardest of the ordinary eastern hardwoods (shagbark hickory Janka about 1,820 lbf, SG about 0.72, FPL-GTR-190). Pecan, *Carya illinoinensis*, is hickory’s sweeter-named cousin, a bit more furniture-facing, still a tough, ring-porous wood with a grain that looks like a brown ash.
The 500-year story is mostly tools, wheels, and vernacular seating, then a 20th-century dining-room try, then the rustic and “pecan finish” factory years. A designer who wants a wood that will dent less than oak and still show a bold grain is looking here. A designer who wants easy planing is not.
## The woods
True hickories (shagbark *C. ovata*, mockernut, pignut, shellbark) are the impact woods. Pecan-hickories (pecan, bitternut, water, nutmeg) are slightly less famous for shock but still hard. The *Wood Handbook* treats them as a group for lumber. Heartwood is pale to reddish brown; sapwood is wide and white. Ring-porous, like ash. Rays are not oak’s mirrors.
Pecan as a furniture name in Texas and the lower Mississippi valley is both the nut tree and the cabinet wood. Factory “pecan” of the 1960s–80s was often a finish color on mixed hardwoods. Real pecan has a varied, sometimes streaked heart.
Hickory’s shrinkage is high. Dry it like you mean it. Movement in service is not polite. Frame-and-panel still applies.
## Workability and finish
Tools suffer. Carbide helps. Hand-plane work is a workout; the wood can be straight and still hard. It nails poorly without holes. It bends when steamed — the other half of the handle-and-chair story.
Grain is open. Stain will stripe. Clear finishes on sap-and-heart mixed boards give a two-tone that rustic shops sell and formal shops hide. Filling pores is a Victorian idea that sits oddly on hickory.
The wood has a reputation for splitting in the ring if the piece is thin and the climate dry. Design around that, or stay with thicker sections.
## History in furniture
Native and colonial tool culture used hickory constantly. Furniture used it for parts: Windsor bows and spindles in some shops (alongside oak and ash), rustic chairs, southern vernacular. It was not the Philadelphia show wood. Mahogany, walnut, and cherry took the parlor.
19th-century factories made some hickory seating — porch rockers, hoop chairs, the Indiana and Appalachian “hickory” furniture that used bark-on or peeled rods in the Adirondack and Old Hickory vein (Martinsville, Indiana, from the 1890s) `[CITE NEEDED: company date from a catalogue]`. That is a furniture tradition: rustic, resort, national-park lodges. It is not Chippendale.
20th-century American dining rooms in “pecan” were a Mediterranean-revival and then a suburban style: heavy suites, dark finish, carved backs. Some of it was pecan. Some was hickory. Some was printed grain. The better pieces have the weight.
Contemporary shops use hickory for floors, for rustic tables, for steam-bent parts, for people who want an American hardwood that is not oak again. Live-edge hickory is a hard live edge.
## Compared with ash and oak
Ash bends as well and is easier to work. Oak quarters with theater. Hickory out-hardens both and out-shocks them. If the job is a rung that will be stood on, hickory. If the job is a show panel of rays, oak. If the job is a pale restaurant table, ash (while the trees last).
Pecan sits closer to furniture than shagbark: a little more color variation, a little more southern identity. A pecan table from the lower Mississippi is a place story.
## Shop notes
Green hickory is a different animal from dry. Chairmakers who work green (post-and-rung, some rustic) use the shrink to lock joints. Dry hickory furniture is kiln furniture. Do not mix the methods without a plan.
Sawmills dislike hickory a little — hard on saws, the logs are heavy. You pay for that.
## Conservation
Hickories are not CITES species. They are part of the oak-hickory forest type under pressure from land use, gypsy moth / spongy moth, and the usual high-grading. Pecan orchards are food first; furniture pecan is often wild or mixed stands. Ordinary forestry. No appendix.
## What to look for
Extreme hardness for a pale ring-porous wood. A rustic chair with hickory rods. A 1970s suite with “pecan” on the label and a veneer edge. Tool handles in the barn that outlived the tools. On a new floor: dent resistance you can feel next to a pine board.
Arkansas grows hickory and pecan in the same hardwood mix as oak. A shop that works those woods is working the tool-forest, not the mahogany pier. The series includes them so a buyer can recognize the grain and not mistake it for dirty ash, and so a designer can specify shock resistance on purpose.
## Green posts, kiln rungs, a handle that outlived the head
Chairmakers who work green — post-and-rung, some rustic — use hickory’s shrinkage as a lock. A dry rung in a wetter post, or the reverse on a planned schedule, tightens as the moisture evens. Kiln furniture is a different method. Do not mix the two without a plan. Dry hickory is the hardest of the ordinary eastern hardwoods: shagbark (*Carya ovata*) near Janka 1,820 lbf and specific gravity 0.72 in the *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). Tools suffer. Carbide helps. A hand plane on a straight board is still a workout. Nails want holes. Steam still bends it — the other half of the handle-and-chair story. Green wood and dry wood are not the same animal under the iron.
True hickories (shagbark, mockernut, pignut, shellbark) are the impact woods. Pecan-hickories (pecan, bitternut, water, nutmeg) are slightly less famous for shock and still hard. FPL treats them as a lumber group. Heartwood pale to reddish brown; sapwood wide and white. Ring-porous, like ash. Rays are not oak’s mirrors. Shrinkage is high. Dry it like you mean it. Movement in service is not polite. Frame-and-panel still applies. Thin pieces in a dry house have a reputation for splitting in the ring. Stay thicker, or design around it.
Tool culture used *Carya* constantly: adze handles, skid poles, ladder rungs, wagon gear. Furniture used it for parts. Some Windsor shops put it in bows and spindles alongside oak and ash (Evans). It was not the Philadelphia show wood. Mahogany, walnut, and cherry took the parlor. Sawmills still dislike the logs a little — hard on saws, heavy to move. You pay for that.
## Martinsville porches and a suburban “pecan” suite
From the 1890s, the Indiana and Appalachian “hickory” furniture trade — bark-on or peeled rods, hoop chairs, porch rockers — made a resort and national-park look. Old Hickory in Martinsville, Indiana, is the name that stuck `[CITE NEEDED: company date from a catalogue]`. That is a furniture tradition: rustic, lodge, Adirondack cousins. It is not Chippendale. The rods are the species doing what fashion walked around for three centuries.
Pecan (*C. illinoinensis*) is the sweeter-named cousin, a bit more furniture-facing, still a tough ring-porous wood with a grain that can look like brown ash. In Texas and the lower Mississippi valley the name is both the nut tree and the cabinet wood. A pecan table from that country is a place story. Factory “pecan” of the 1960s–80s was often a finish color on mixed hardwoods, then a Mediterranean-revival suburban suite: heavy, dark, carved backs. Some of it was pecan. Some was hickory. Some was printed grain. The better pieces have the weight. Look at the edge.
Clear finishes on mixed sap and heart give a two-tone that rustic shops sell and formal shops hide. Stain stripes the earlywood. Filling pores is a Victorian idea that sits oddly on this genus. Live-edge hickory is a hard live edge. Floors in hickory dent less than oak; you can feel it next to a pine board.
## Ash lookalike, oak job list, no appendix
Ash bends as well and is easier to work. Oak quarters with theater. Hickory out-hardens both and out-shocks them. If the job is a rung that will be stood on, hickory. If the job is a show panel of rays, oak. If the job is a pale restaurant table, ash — while the trees last. A hopeful eye will call hickory dirty ash. The hardness in the hand, and the lack of oak flake on a quartered face, settle it.
Hickories are not CITES species. They sit in the oak-hickory forest type, under pressure from land use, spongy moth, and high-grading. Pecan orchards are food first; furniture pecan is often wild or mixed stands. Ordinary forestry. No appendix. Orchard waste is not automatically cabinet grade.
On a rustic chair: hickory rods. On a 1970s suite: the word “pecan” on the label and a veneer edge. In the barn: handles that outlived the tools. On a new floor: dent resistance. Fashion walked around this wood for most of five hundred years because it is contrary to plane and loud in the grain. Specify it when you want shock resistance on purpose, not when you want an easy walnut substitute. The tool-forest is still a furniture forest if the ticket says the binomial.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (hickory and pecan groups; table 5–3a). Evans, Windsor (species mix). Old Hickory furniture histories `[CITE NEEDED]`. Hoadley.
See: `ash`, `oak-european-and-american`, `windsor-mixed-wood`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Chestnut and the blight
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Chestnut and the blight
Herman Merkel found dying American chestnuts in the New York Zoological Park in 1904. W. A. Murrill described the fungus. The name moved from *Diaporthe parasitica* to *Endothia* to *Cryphonectria parasitica*. Within fifty years the overstorey tree that had been perhaps a quarter of some eastern hardwood stands was gone as timber (Anagnostakis; Prospero and Rigling review, PMC6638123). Furniture shops did not cause the blight. They lost a secondary wood that had been easy, stable, and everywhere from Maine to Georgia.
What you buy now as chestnut is almost always dead already: wormy beams pulled from barns, tannin-plant leftovers, a drawer side in an 18th-century Newport case. The living sprouts still come from old roots and still die back when the canker girdles them. Restoration breeding and a transgenic line at SUNY ESF are forest stories. They are not a mill story yet.
## The wood that was
American chestnut (*Castanea dentata*) is ring-porous, like oak, but lighter and softer. FPL’s older species leaflet and the *Wood Handbook* tradition put it near specific gravity 0.43 and Janka about 540 lbf — poplar’s neighbor in hardness, with a grain that reads as a gentle oak. It split easily, worked easily, held a nail, took stain, and — important for furniture — moved less nastily than some secondary woods. A Fine Woodworking anatomy note (1992) cites volumetric shrinkage around 11.6 percent green to ovendry, kinder than sweetgum or yellow-poplar in that comparison.
Heartwood was durable in the weather for a hardwood of that density: rails, shingles, poles, railroad ties. Tannin extract for leather was an industry. The same tannin made the wood useful and made the blight’s orange cankers a chemical rhyme.
European chestnut (*C. sativa*) is a separate furniture wood: Italian and southern French country pieces, some English work, a ring-porous pale brown. It has blight problems too, and ink disease, but it did not vanish from Europe the way *C. dentata* vanished from American commerce.
## How shops used it
Chestnut was a secondary wood of the first rank in American high-style work. Drawer sides and interior parts of some Newport Townsend and Goddard pieces are chestnut (Fine Woodworking, 1992). That is not a slight. Secondary woods are chosen for stability and cost. Chestnut was both, and it had figure enough to look like a choice when a drawer opened.
It was also a primary wood for cheaper case work, kitchen tables, and the kind of New England and Mid-Atlantic utility furniture that never made Macquoid’s ages. Painted chests. Casket stock. Core stock for plywood, FPL said, when the tree still stood.
Wormy chestnut — powder-post beetle holes in the sap and in dead wood — is a salvage grade. The holes happened after death or in dying trees. Selling “wormy chestnut” as a decorative fashion is honest if the wood is reclaimed. Hunting living small sprouts for that look is vandalism.
## The blight as material culture
The fungus is East Asian. American and European chestnuts had no coevolved peace with it. Spread from New York was on the order of tens of kilometers a year. By the 1920s it was in the southern Appalachians, where the tannin industry and the biggest trees were. By the 1940s the commercial species was finished.
Furniture after that used the dead: standing snags, then barn wood, then the last beams. Mid-century “wormy chestnut” paneling is a grief product. It can be beautiful. It is a cemetery fence.
European furniture in *C. sativa* continues in a smaller way. Do not confuse a Provençal chestnut armoire with Appalachian salvage. The trees are cousins. The histories are not the same crash.
## Workability and finish (reclaimed)
Old chestnut is soft. You dent it with a belt buckle. You sand through an arris. The worm holes collect finish and dirt. A filling of wax or a leave-alone are the two schools. The wood glues if the surface is sound. It is dusty. Nails in old beams may be the only steel left in a house.
Color is brown-tan, sometimes with mineral stain. It does not look like walnut unless you push it. It looks like itself, which is why people want it.
## Conservation and the future tree
The American Chestnut Foundation and university programs breed for resistance (Chinese chestnut crosses, backcrosses) and, separately, SUNY ESF has developed a transgenic tree with a wheat oxalate-oxidase gene; regulatory status has been a moving target (Connecticut DEEP summary of the debate). Hypovirus biocontrol works better in Europe than in North America, a biology story about vegetative compatibility.
None of this returns 18th-century drawer stock this year. A designer specifying chestnut specifies salvage, European *C. sativa*, or a different species. Oak is the lookalike that still grows. It is heavier and harder. Poplar is the workalike for hidden parts. It lacks the tannin durability.
Do not buy “chestnut” carvings from unnamed tropical exporters. The word is a market.
## What to look for
Ring-porous, softer than oak, no big oak rays, worm holes in salvage. Inside a Newport or Philadelphia case: a brown secondary wood that is not poplar’s green. In a 1950s den: paneling with holes. In a nursery catalogue: a sprout, not a board.
The blight belongs in a furniture series because the shop list changed. American makers lost a wood the way they later lost elm and are losing ash. The pieces that remain are the last wide, easy, ring-porous brown boards of a tree that used to be ordinary.
## A drawer that is not the show
Pull a drawer from a Townsend-and-Goddard secretary in the Newport literature — mid-eighteenth century, a façade that wants to be called mahogany — and the sides may be chestnut. Fine Woodworking’s 1992 anatomy note is still the shop paper restorers quote: ring-porous, no oak-sized rays, a brown that is not poplar’s green streak. Winterthur files and the Goddard-Townsend corpus treat that lining as ordinary. A shop that could buy Cuban or Jamaica mahogany for a door still boxed the drawer in what grew on the next ridge.
Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* is thinner on chestnut as a named show wood. The Mid-Atlantic and southern New England are the documented furniture geography. *Castanea dentata* grew south of the Potomac; the counted case list in southern collections is smaller `[CITE NEEDED: a survey of chestnut secondaries in Williamsburg and related catalogues]`. Do not invent a Charleston parlor in chestnut because the tree map includes the Carolinas. Attribution wants a board, not a range map.
Secondary wood is not a slight. Shops chose it for movement, cost, and the way a nail held. Chestnut split for a riven panel if you asked it to, and it planed for a drawer side if you asked it that instead. The same tree made kitchen tables that never entered Macquoid’s ages and casket stock that left no connoisseur’s essay. FPL’s older uses list — furniture, caskets, core stock for plywood — is a mill list from when the overstorey still stood.
## Rings without the oak mirrors
Oak and chestnut share a ring-porous habit. That is why a flatsawn chestnut board fools people at ten feet. Get closer. White oak and red oak throw broad rays: the flake on a quartered face, the dark lines on a flat one. Chestnut’s rays are fine. The earlywood pores make a spring ring. They do not make a cathedral of ray fleck. Hoadley would send you to the end grain with a hand lens. You need light and the refusal to call every brown ring-porous board oak.
The *Wood Handbook* tradition and FPL’s chestnut leaflet put American chestnut near specific gravity 0.43 and Janka hardness about 540 lbf at 12 percent moisture — yellow-poplar’s neighbor, not oak’s. The dent test will not separate chestnut from tulip poplar. Anatomy and tannin will. Volumetric shrinkage green to ovendry around 11.6 percent is the Fine Woodworking comparison figure, kinder in that table than sweetgum or yellow-poplar. Radial movement still runs below tangential, as with every hardwood. A wide chestnut panel wants a frame. It just fights the frame less than some secondaries.
Heartwood durability outdoors is the other number shops used without saying it. Rails, shingles, poles, railroad ties. The same extract that fed leather tanneries in the southern Appalachians made the wood last in weather better than its density predicted. That is why a barn beam cut about 1890 can still be a table top if you accept beetle holes and a nail.
## The tannin belt and the fifty-year vanishing
The blight did not start in a furniture shop. Herman Merkel found dying American chestnuts in the New York Zoological Park in 1904 — the Bronx Zoo, if you want the later civic name. W. A. Murrill described the fungus. The name moved from *Diaporthe parasitica* to *Endothia parasitica* to *Cryphonectria parasitica* (Anagnostakis; Prospero and Rigling, PMC6638123). East Asian chestnuts had lived with it. American and European trees had no coevolved peace.
Spread from New York was on the order of tens of kilometers a year in the reviews. By the 1920s the southern Appalachians were in it — tannin towns, the biggest boles, extract plants that had been pulling bark and wood for leather. Then they pulled dying trees. Then snags. By the 1940s the commercial species was finished as a mill item. Furniture after that used the dead: standing timber that would not leaf, then barn wood, then the last beams sold as “wormy chestnut” paneling to mid-century dens.
The holes are powder-post work in sap and in dead wood, not a living-tree ornament. Selling reclaimed wormy chestnut is honest if the wood came out of a building. Cutting living root-collar sprouts for that look is a small vandalism against a species that is already a shrub of dieback.
A Provençal armoire in *C. sativa* is a living-wood object. An Appalachian mantel pulled from a cattle barn is a cemetery object. Cousins. Not the same hour.
## At the bench with dead wood
Old chestnut is soft. A belt buckle dents it. A random-orbit sander rounds an arris if you linger. The worm holes collect finish and dirt. Two schools: wax the holes and leave the topography, or fill and sand toward a false smoothness. Glue holds on sound fiber. The dust is fine. Nails left in beams may be the only steel in the house; run a magnet or cut as if every joist has a cut nail and a lag.
Tannin plus water plus a steel fastener makes a blue-black stain. That mark is a chemical rhyme with the blight’s orange cankers, not a defect to bleach out of a salvage top unless the client asks. Color is tan to medium brown, sometimes a grey or mineral cast. It does not look like walnut unless you push a stain. People want it because it looks like itself.
Do not buy nameless “chestnut” carvings off a tropical invoice. The word is a market. Oak is the lookalike that still makes logs. Poplar is the hidden-part workalike. Neither is the tannin tree that used to be ordinary from Maine to Georgia.
The American Chestnut Foundation’s backcross breeding and the SUNY ESF transgenic line (wheat oxalate-oxidase gene; regulatory status a moving target in Connecticut DEEP summaries) are forest programs. Hypovirus biocontrol works better in Europe, a vegetative-compatibility story. None of it is drawer stock this year. A specifier writes salvage, European *C. sativa*, or a different species.
## Sources
Prospero / Rigling et al. on *C. parasitica* (PMC6638123). Anagnostakis. USDA FPL chestnut leaflet (amwood/230chest.pdf). Fine Woodworking, “The Demise of American Chestnut,” 1992. Connecticut DEEP blight history. TACF public notes. Hurst and Prown; Newport furniture literature for secondary woods.
See: `yellow-poplar`, `oak-european-and-american`, `elm`, `ash`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Yellow-poplar
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Yellow-poplar
Open a Philadelphia high chest and look at the drawer sides. The wood is often a pale tulip-streaked board with a hint of green or purple in the heart. That is *Liriodendron tulipifera*, yellow-poplar, tulip poplar, tulipwood in the American shop (not the Brazilian *Dalbergia* tulipwood of the ébéniste). It is the cheap-good wood of the eastern United States: light, stable enough, wide, paint-loving, carvable. High-style mahogany would have been impossible at the scale of 18th-century production without a secondary wood like this.
The *Wood Handbook* lists it at specific gravity 0.42 and Janka 540 lbf — chestnut’s neighbor, twice the hardness of eastern white pine, half of cherry. It is a hardwood that behaves like a well-brought-up softwood.
## The wood
Diffuse-porous, fine texture, heartwood that can be brown, green, purple, or streaked — “tulip” in the old name. Sapwood is creamy and wide. The tree grows straight and tall in the Appalachians and the Ohio valley. Boards can be wide without knots. That fact made carcases.
It is not a poplar in the *Populus* sense (aspen, cottonwood). The name is a settler’s error that stuck. Cottonwood is weaker and fuzzier. Specify *Liriodendron*.
Durability outdoors is poor. Durability as a painted porch column is a paint story, not a heartwood story.
## Workability and finish
It planes, carves, and takes a gouge without oak’s fight. Grinling Gibbons is a lime story; American architectural carving is often poplar. It glues. It nails. It dents.
Paint is the historic finish on show surfaces when poplar was primary: blanket chests, interiors, the backcountry piece that never saw mahogany. Bare poplar oxidizes toward brown and can look like a poor walnut if stained. The green heart, once called “whitewood” or sold separately, scares some clients and pleases people who like a mineral streak.
Veneer: rotary-cut poplar is a core and a crossband. A lot of 19th- and 20th-century plywood starts here.
## The hidden century
From the late 17th century through the Federal period, Mid-Atlantic shops used yellow-poplar as the default secondary wood. New England preferred white pine for many of the same jobs. The South mixed pine, poplar, and sometimes cypress. Hurst and Prown’s southern furniture catalogue and the Winterthur literature make this geography a dating and attribution tool. A “New England” highboy with poplar drawer sides wants an argument.
Poplar was also a primary wood: painted chests, kitchen cupboards, the interiors of houses. It never sat in Macquoid’s London ages. It sat in the American shop every day.
Empire and Victorian factories used poplar as the ground for mahogany and rosewood veneer. The crotch on the front; the tulip on the inside. When the veneer chips, the green shows. That chip is a lesson.
## 20th century
Millwork, paint-grade doors, core stock, inexpensive furniture sold as “whitewood.” School projects. The wood is still one of the most useful in an American hardwood yard. It is unfashionable as a show surface except in painted work and in a few contemporary shops that like the mineral color.
Chinese tulip poplar plantations and mixed “whitewood” imports confuse bills of lading `[CITE NEEDED for volume]`. Anatomy still holds.
## Shop notes
Weight tells poplar from pine (heavier) and from maple (much lighter). No resin canals. Diffuse pores. Green heart is not decay.
It moves more than the old chestnut it sometimes replaced as a secondary wood. Still kinder than beech. Still wants floating panels in wide widths.
Do not sell it as basswood. Basswood is softer and even more the carver’s friend. Do not sell it as mahogany. The stain will not survive a drawer opening.
## Conservation
*Liriodendron* is a common, fast, managed American hardwood. Not CITES. The conservation issue is ordinary land use. Using poplar for hidden parts instead of a threatened tropical is a correct substitution that shops have been making, without virtue language, for two hundred years.
## What to look for
Green or purple streaks. Wide, clear paint-grade boards. Drawer sides in a mahogany case. A veneered Empire bureau with a chip. Painted Pennsylvania chests. On a new paint-grade kitchen: the right wood if the door is solid and the finish is a film.
Arkansas and the southern Appalachians grow tulip poplar in quantity. A shop that uses it for dustboards and for painted work is in the 18th-century habit. The series includes it so buyers stop calling every pale interior “pine” and so designers remember that show woods need a servant.
## The Philadelphia habit
Open a high chest labeled Philadelphia, 1760–1780, and the drawer sides are a dating tool before they are a romance. Winterthur studies and the Mid-Atlantic literature treat yellow-poplar as the default secondary: dustboards, drawer bottoms, the backboards that never saw a parlor lamp. New England shops in the same decades often reached for eastern white pine for those jobs. The South mixed yellow pine, poplar, and sometimes cypress. Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* makes that mix an attribution argument, not a mood. A “New England” highboy with tulip-streaked drawer sides wants a better story than a dealer’s map.
The tree is *Liriodendron tulipifera*, a magnolia relative, not a *Populus*. Settlers called it poplar because the leaf and the pale wood suggested one. Cottonwood and aspen are weaker and fuzzier. Specify the binomial on a mill ticket if the yard also sells “poplar” as mixed whitewood. Anatomy still holds: diffuse-porous, fine texture, no resin canals, a heart that can run brown, green, or purple in the same log.
FPL-GTR-190 puts yellow-poplar at specific gravity 0.42 and Janka 540 lbf at 12 percent moisture — chestnut’s hardness neighbor, about twice eastern white pine, about half of black cherry. Shrinkage green to ovendry is on the order of 4.6 percent radial, 8.2 percent tangential, 12.7 percent volumetric in the handbook tables. That is more movement than the old chestnut it sometimes replaced as a lining. It is still kinder than beech. Wide tops still want floating panels. A glued-down breadboard on a poplar lid is a future crack.
Durability outdoors is poor. A painted porch column that lasts is a paint story. Bare heart in the weather is a short story.
## Paint, gouge, and the green that scares a client
It planes. It takes a gouge without oak’s fight. Grinling Gibbons is a lime story; American architectural carving — mantel drops, capitals, the applied ornament on a Federal chimney breast — is often poplar or basswood. Dull tools bruise it. Sharp ones leave a surface that paint covers without a ring telegraph. White pine carves too, and then the resin and the latewood bands show through a thin film. Poplar is the even cut with a mineral surprise.
Paint is the historic finish when poplar was primary: blanket chests, kitchen cupboards, the backcountry case that never saw mahogany. Bare wood oxidizes toward brown. A stain can fake a poor walnut until a drawer opens and the green heart laughs. Some clients want that streak. Some call it stain and ask you to bleach it. It is not decay. It is the tree.
Empire and Victorian factories used poplar as the ground for mahogany and rosewood veneer. Crotch on the front; tulip on the inside. When the veneer chips, the green shows. That chip is a lesson in what a show wood costs and what a servant wood does. Rotary-cut poplar is still a plywood core and a crossband. A lot of nineteenth- and twentieth-century panel product starts in this genus.
Chinese *Liriodendron* plantations and mixed “whitewood” imports confuse bills of lading `[CITE NEEDED for import volume]`. The microscope does not care about the invoice.
## How a shop tells it from the neighbors
Weight tells poplar from eastern white pine (heavier) and from hard maple (much lighter). No resin canals on the end grain. Diffuse pores, not the spring ring of oak or chestnut. Basswood is softer, paler, even more even; a fingernail decides faster than a speech. Sweetgum can share a mineral look and then move worse. Do not sell poplar as mahogany. The stain will not survive a drawer opening. Do not sell it as basswood to a carver who wanted *Tilia*. The gouge will tell them you lied.
Clamps bruise the arris. Use pads. Glue holds. Nails hold. Screws want a pilot in thin rails or you split the end. The dust is fine and pale. A wide paint-grade board from the southern Appalachians or the Ohio valley can still come clear of knots; that fact made carcases when mahogany was the skin.
School shops still buy it because it is cheap and kind to a block plane. Millwork shops still buy it because a paint-grade door does not need cherry’s luster. Contemporary makers who leave the mineral color as a show face are in a minority taste. They are not wrong. They are asking the wood to do a job Macquoid never wrote down.
## Southern rooms and the servant wood
Hurst and Prown’s Williamsburg pieces show poplar where a northern reader expects pine: cupboard interiors, the hidden members of a huntboard, painted case work that the parlor mahogany never had to explain. Coastal shops mixed it with yellow pine. Piedmont shops used what the cove and the bottomland grew. The point for a buyer is not a moral ranking. It is a repair fact. A split poplar dustboard wants poplar, not a southern yellow pine with a loud latewood band that will telegraph through a thin bottom.
A designer specifying hidden parts in 2026 can still write *Liriodendron* without a CITES appendix or a virtue paragraph. Shops have been making that substitution, without a speech, for two hundred years — first against the cost of show woods, later against the scarcity of tropical names. The conservation issue is ordinary land use. The labeling issue is calling every pale interior pine.
Arkansas yards stock tulip poplar as a local and regional hardwood. A painted cupboard in it is an eighteenth-century habit in a second-growth ring. The green heart is not a flaw. It is how you know you are not looking at pine.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190. Hurst and Prown, *Southern Furniture 1680–1830*. Winterthur furniture studies. Hoadley. Fine Woodworking chestnut comparison (shrinkage).
See: `chestnut-and-the-blight`, `pine-country-furniture`, `lime-basswood-carvers`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `reading-furniture-wood`.

item.title: Sycamore
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Sycamore
Say “sycamore” in a London shop in 1790 and you mean *Acer pseudoplatanus*, a maple, pale, sometimes quartered into a lace of small rays, sometimes dyed in iron liquor until it went grey-green and took the name harewood. Say “sycamore” in an Ohio mill in 1890 and you mean *Platanus occidentalis*, the American planetree, a different family, a wood with crowded broad rays that look like oatmeal on the quarter and a reputation for butcher blocks and cheap furniture. The word is a fork. This chapter holds both tines so a buyer does not buy the wrong tree.
## English sycamore: a maple in costume
*Acer pseudoplatanus* is native to central Europe and long naturalized in Britain. It is not *Acer saccharum*. It is softer than hard maple, pale, clean, a turning and veneer wood. Quartered faces show a fleck. The furniture trade loved it when pale woods were the fashion: late 18th-century satinwood rooms, painted furniture, the insides of drawers, food-related wood (it does not scent butter).
Harewood is sycamore (or sometimes other pale maples) dyed. Sheraton and Hepplewhite plates want grey fields and fine inlay. The dye is historic iron-and-tannin chemistry, not a gel stain. Old harewood can fade or go muddy. Conservators treat it as a colored wood, not as a species.
Biedermeier shops used the same pale maple-sycamore group. The Biedermeier chapter overlaps. The English name is the confusion.
Workability: friendly, like a mild maple. Finish: blotch possible, clear coats yellow the white. Movement: ordinary hardwood manners.
## American sycamore: *Platanus*
*Platanus occidentalis* is a river-bottom tree with a mottled bark people know from streets. The wood is reddish-tan, interlocked, with rays that dominate a quartered face — a lace more aggressive than beech. The *Wood Handbook* puts American sycamore around SG 0.49 and Janka 770 lbf. It is not a hard maple. It is not a weak cottonwood.
Interlocked grain tears. Quartered sycamore was sold as a decorative veneer and as drawer sides. It was a cheap furniture wood in the Midwest: painted, stained, hidden. Butcher blocks used it because the end grain and the rays wear in a useful way `[CITE NEEDED: period block-maker catalogues]`.
London plane (*Platanus × acerifolia*) is the street tree of Europe; its wood appears in small work. It is not English furniture “sycamore.”
## Fashion
Harewood is the high-fashion story: 1770–1820 in England, Macquoid’s satinwood age, a grey that set off rosewood banding and yellow satinwood. American *Platanus* never had that hour. It had a utility hour and a brief Arts-and-Crafts-adjacent interest in quartered fleck, then floors and crates.
Contemporary designers sometimes quarter American sycamore for a loud ray face. It photographs well. It moves and tears. Specify quartered if you want the look, and allow for waste.
## Shop notes
If a U.S. invoice says sycamore, ask *Acer* or *Platanus*. The density and the ray size will tell you if the seller cannot. *Platanus* rays are large and crowded; *Acer pseudoplatanus* is a maple anatomy.
Harewood on an antique: do not sand to “fresh wood.” The color is in a shallow layer.
Food-safe reputation of European sycamore is traditional for rolling pins and worktops. Finish choice is the modern half of that tradition.
## Conservation
Neither furniture sycamore is a CITES species. American sycamore is common on wet sites. English sycamore is often treated as a weed tree in British conservation and as a timber tree in the same breath. Plane trees in cities are civic trees, not logs, until they come down.
## What to look for
Grey inlay fields on a Federal or Sheraton piece: harewood, an *Acer*. Oatmeal quartered fleck on a Midwestern drawer: *Platanus*. A pale solid “maple” that is too cheap and too rayed: ask. A butcher block with busy end grain: maybe sycamore, maybe maple — weight and rays.
The series keeps this chapter short on romance and long on names because more furniture has been misidentified under “sycamore” than under almost any other English word except cedar and mahogany.
## Two genera, one invoice
A London cabinetmaker in 1790 who wrote “sycamore” meant *Acer pseudoplatanus*: a maple, pale, sometimes quartered into a small-ray lace, sometimes sent through iron liquor until it went grey-green and took the name harewood. Sheraton’s *Drawing-Book* (1793) and Hepplewhite’s *Guide* (1788) want those grey fields against satinwood and rosewood banding. Macquoid’s Age of Satinwood is the gallery name for that hour. The dye is iron-and-tannin chemistry, a shallow color, not a gel stain. Conservators treat old harewood as a colored wood. Sanding to “fresh wood” erases the fashion.
An Ohio or Indiana mill in 1890 that wrote “sycamore” meant *Platanus occidentalis*, the American planetree, a different family. Crowded broad rays. Oatmeal on the quarter. Interlocked grain that tears under a dull plane. The *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) puts American sycamore around specific gravity 0.49 and Janka 770 lbf at 12 percent moisture — harder than yellow-poplar, not a hard maple, not a cottonwood. Shrinkage in the handbook tables runs on the order of 5 percent radial and a higher tangential, with volumetric movement larger than poplar’s `[CITE NEEDED: confirm T/V pair from table 5–3a in the copy on the bench]`. It was cheap furniture wood, drawer sides, painted case work, and the butcher-block reputation that period catalogues repeat `[CITE NEEDED: a named block-maker’s list]`.
London plane (*Platanus × acerifolia*), the street tree of European cities, is a *Platanus*. Its wood appears in small turned work when a civic tree comes down. It is not English furniture “sycamore.” If a U.S. invoice says sycamore, ask *Acer* or *Platanus*. Ray size decides when the seller cannot. *Platanus* rays are large and crowded. *Acer pseudoplatanus* is maple anatomy: finer fleck, a milder lace.
Biedermeier shops used the pale maple-sycamore group for the same reason English satinwood rooms did: a field that would take polish and sit next to a darker band. The Biedermeier chapter overlaps. The English name is the confusion, not the furniture.
## Harewood in the room
The grey is the high-fashion story: roughly 1770–1820 in England, painted furniture and inlay, a color that set off yellow satinwood and dark rosewood without asking for another tropical log. Old harewood fades or goes muddy. A conservator’s note will say “colored sycamore” or “harewood” and will forbid a scrape. The color lives in a shallow layer. A furniture dealer who “refreshed” a Sheraton card table by sanding the grey fields has destroyed the object’s fashion and left a pale maple.
Food-related wood is the other English habit. *A. pseudoplatanus* does not scent butter. Rolling pins, worktops, the dairy interior — the tradition is real even when the modern half of it is a finish choice (oil, a film, nothing). `[CITE NEEDED: a standard UK timber monograph on sycamore as a dairy wood]`. American *Platanus* got the butcher-block job instead: end grain, busy rays, a wear that does not polish to a closed maple face.
Workability on the maple side is friendly, like a mild *Acer*. Blotch is possible. Clear coats yellow the white. Movement is ordinary hardwood manners. Workability on the *Platanus* side is a fight where the grain interlocks. Quarter it if you want the oatmeal photograph. Allow for waste and for tear-out. Specify the cut. A flatsawn American sycamore board is a different, quieter, less fashionable face.
## What a Midwestern drawer remembers
Quartered *Platanus* as a drawer side is a Midwest and river-town habit: cheap, stable enough, a ray fleck that looks like decoration if you leave it unfinished in the dark of a case. Painted, it disappears. Stained, it can look like a muddy beech. Arts-and-Crafts-adjacent taste had a brief interest in that fleck, then the wood went back to floors and crates. Contemporary designers who quarter it for a loud ray face are buying a photograph. The board will still move. The plane will still tear if the iron is lazy.
Street-tree plane in Europe is a civic tree until it is a log. Furniture from it is opportunistic: a bowl, a small box, a turning. Do not write a dining table in London plane unless you like glue-ups and a story about a storm on a boulevard.
Neither furniture sycamore is a CITES species. American sycamore is common on wet sites. English sycamore is a weed tree in one British conservation sentence and a timber tree in the next. The ethical issue is the name on the ticket, not an appendix.
## How to look, slowly
Grey inlay fields on a Federal or Sheraton piece: harewood, an *Acer*. Oatmeal quartered fleck on a Midwestern drawer: *Platanus*. A pale solid “maple” that is too cheap and too rayed: ask. A butcher block with busy end grain: maybe sycamore, maybe maple — weight and rays. Harewood on an antique: do not sand. Food-safe talk: the species tradition is European sycamore; the finish is the modern half.
The word is a fork. This chapter holds both tines so a buyer does not pay for the wrong tree and so a restorer does not bleach a dye that was the point of the room.
A London plane log from a storm-felled street tree is opportunistic turning stock, not a Sheraton field. An English sycamore veneer that went through iron liquor is harewood even if the invoice later says maple. An American *Platanus* drawer side with oatmeal fleck is neither. Name the genus before you name the fashion.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (*Platanus*; maple notes). Sheraton, *Drawing-Book*; Hepplewhite, *Guide*. Macquoid, *Age of Satinwood*. Hoadley. English timber trade notes on *A. pseudoplatanus* `[CITE NEEDED: a standard UK timber monograph]`.
See: `maple`, `satinwood`, `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `reading-furniture-wood`.

item.title: Fruitwoods
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Fruitwoods
An orchard dies a furniture death. When the apple tree stops bearing or the pear is blown over, the trunk is short, often hollow, often figured at the root, and hard in a way that has nothing to do with a forest sawlog. European country shops and American farm shops used that wood because it was there: apple for a turned bowl and a chair seat, pear for a drawing instrument and a Biedermeier drawer front, plum for a small box with a purple heart. The 500-year story is local, small, and repeatedly mistaken for cherry.
This is a comparative chapter on purpose. No single fruit species furnished a Macquoid age. Together they furnished the pieces that never needed a port.
## Apple (*Malus*)
Dense, hard, fine-textured, often twisted. Specific gravity commonly cited near 0.65–0.75 and Janka in the hard-maple neighborhood, but orchard wood varies so wildly that a handbook average is a rumor `[CITE NEEDED: FPL does not table orchard apple as a commercial lumber]`. It turns like a friend. It splits like an enemy if you try to rive it. It moves. It is excellent for mallets, screws in wooden vises, saw handles, and small chairs.
English and French country furniture in “fruitwood” is often apple or pear. American farm chairs sometimes have apple seats or turnings. The wood oxidizes to a warm brown that people call cherry. The pores are finer; the weight is often higher; the log is shorter.
## Pear (*Pyrus*)
The printer’s and patternmaker’s wood: even, hard, almost no grain telegraph, takes a cut like boxwood’s cousin. German and French shops used pear for drawing tools, for carving, and for Biedermeier show surfaces when a silky pale brown was wanted. Stained black it became ebonized line-work and sometimes fake ebony. The Biedermeier chapter leans on pear as much as on birch.
Pear is more mannerly than apple in the plane. It is still orchard-sized. Wide boards are glue-ups or a lie.
## Plum and the other *Prunus*
Plum (*P. domestica* and relatives) can have a startling purple-brown heart. Small boxes, knife handles, inlay.
