Wild cherry is in the cherry chapter; orchard cherry is usually too small and too valuable as fruit to be a timber. Apricot and peach appear in southern European small work. None of these are a dining table unless the table is a fraud or a mosaic.
## How shops thought
Fruitwood is a farm and provincial category. Inventories say “fruitwood” because the clerk did not care which tree in the hedge. Attribution now wants a lens: cherry vs apple vs pear vs alder (often painted and thrown in the same bin). Weight, pore, and smell in the cut help. Pear is even; apple is wilder; cherry has gum flecks and a luster.
High-style Paris used fruitwoods in marquetry as colors: light brown, pink, a stained green. The Riesener chapter of this series (marquetry) is the court version of the orchard.
American high-style used cherry, which is a *Prunus* and a forest tree, not an orchard leftover. Do not collapse *P. serotina* into “fruitwood.” It is a commercial lumber.
## Finish and aging
Fruitwoods take a polish to a closed, almost metallic surface. Oil darkens apple toward mahogany-in-miniature. Pear stays paler unless stained. Old French polish on pear is a Biedermeier signature.
Worm likes some fruit sapwood. Orchard trees are often full of metal: nails, fence wire, a forgotten hook. The first cut is a saw-risk.
## Fashion
Never a London decade of apple. Always a countryside constant. Biedermeier made pear polite. Arts and Crafts sometimes used fruit for inlay and small cabinets. Mid-century ignored them except as bowls. Contemporary makers pay orchardists for a trunk and make a bench that is one tree wide and four feet long. That is the honest scale.
## Conservation
Orchard fruitwoods are agricultural waste or a second crop. Using them is not a forest threat. Wild *Pyrus* and *Malus* in hedges are another matter if you strip a hedgerow for “character wood.” Buy trees that were coming down. CITES is silent here.
Watch for tropical woods sold as “fruitwood finish.” That is a stain name from factory catalogues, often on rubberwood (*Hevea*) or mixed hardwoods. Rubberwood is a plantation rubber tree, a legitimate furniture wood with its own story, not an apple.
## What to look for
Short billets, wild grain, hardness, a provincial chair, a German drawer front like satin, a purple plum box. A catalogue that says “fruitwood” on an eight-foot dining table: read the edge.
Arkansas orchards are not Normandy, but apple wood still turns up from farm removals. A shop that uses it is in the old habit: the tree that fed people then furnished them. Cherry from the woods remains the forest *Prunus*. Keep the words apart.
## When the orchard stops bearing
A trunk comes off a farm on a wagon because the apples have gone to canker or the pear blew in a March wind. The bole is short, often hollow, often figured at the root flare, and hard in a way that has nothing to do with a forest sawlog. European country shops and American farm shops used that wood because it was there. No port book records a cargo of cider trees. The 500-year story is local, small, and repeatedly mistaken for cherry.
Inventories say “fruitwood” because the clerk did not care which tree in the hedge. Attribution now wants a lens. Apple (*Malus*) is dense, often twisted, a friend on the lathe and an enemy if you try to rive it. Specific gravity is commonly cited near 0.65–0.75 and Janka in the hard-maple neighborhood, but orchard wood varies so wildly that a handbook average is a rumor. FPL-GTR-190 does not table orchard apple as a commercial lumber `[CITE NEEDED: a measured table for apple and pear hardness]`. Pear (*Pyrus*) is even, hard, almost no grain telegraph, the printer’s and patternmaker’s wood. Plum (*Prunus domestica* and relatives) can throw a purple-brown heart in a small box. Wild black cherry (*P. serotina*) is a forest tree and a commercial lumber; it has its own chapter. Do not collapse it into the orchard leftover.
Roubo’s *L’Art du menuisier* lists workshop woods with a craftsman’s economy. Pear shows up where a cut must hold and not shout. The Wallace Collection’s Riesener notes treat fruitwoods as marquetry colors: light brown, pink, a stained green. That is the court version of the same hedge. High-style Paris used the orchard as a palette. American high-style used cherry from the woods. Keep the words apart.
## Apple at the bench
It turns. Bowls, mallet heads, the wooden screw in a vise, saw handles, a chair seat that will take a lot of sitting. It splits if you ask it to be a riven panel. It moves. Oil darkens it toward a mahogany-in-miniature that people then call cherry. The pores are finer than *P. serotina*; the weight is often higher; the log is shorter. English and French country furniture sold as “fruitwood” is often apple or pear. American farm chairs sometimes have apple seats or turnings. The oxidization is warm brown. A catalogue that says fruitwood on an eight-foot dining table is reading a stain name or telling a lie.
Orchard trees hold metal. Fence wire, a hook, a nail driven for a clothesline in 1940. The first cut is a saw-risk. Worm likes some fruit sapwood. The heart can be sound and the sap a lace of holes. Design for the defects. They are the tree.
## Pear, plum, and the polite drawer
German and French shops used pear for drawing instruments, for carving, and for Biedermeier show surfaces when a silky pale brown was wanted. Stained black it became ebonized line-work and sometimes a stand-in for ebony. The Biedermeier chapter leans on pear as much as on birch. Pear is more mannerly than apple in the plane. It is still orchard-sized. Wide boards are glue-ups or a fiction.
Old French polish on pear is a Biedermeier signature: a closed, almost metallic surface. Apple will take the same polish and then look warmer. Plum wants to be a small object — knife scales, a box, an inlay slip. Apricot and peach appear in southern European small work `[CITE NEEDED: a regional monograph naming those species in furniture]`. None of these are a dining table unless the table is a mosaic.
Weight, pore, and the smell of a fresh cut help when the label says fruitwood and the piece might be alder painted brown. Pear is even. Apple is wilder. Cherry has gum flecks and a luster. Alder is lighter and takes stain like a servant. Holly and maple do the pale inlay jobs that pear sometimes shares.
## Fashion that never took a London decade
There was never a Macquoid Age of Apple. There was always a countryside constant: provincial chairs, a Norman armoire, a farm stool, a German drawer front like satin. Arts and Crafts shops used fruit for inlay and small cabinets. Mid-century factories ignored them except as salad bowls. Contemporary makers pay orchardists for a trunk and make a bench that is one tree wide and four feet long. That is the honest scale.
Watch the factory phrase “fruitwood finish.” It is a stain name, often on rubberwood (*Hevea brasiliensis*) or mixed hardwoods. Rubberwood is a plantation rubber tree, a legitimate furniture wood with its own story, not an apple. CITES is silent on orchard *Malus* and *Pyrus*. Using a tree that was coming down is not a forest threat. Stripping a hedgerow of wild crab and perry pear for “character wood” is another matter.
Arkansas orchards are not the Calvados hedge. Apple still turns up from farm removals. A shop that uses it is in the old habit: the tree that fed people then furnished them. Name the genus if you can. If you cannot, say orchard fruitwood and do not say cherry.
## Sources
Hoadley (anatomy). Biedermeier collection catalogues. Wallace Collection, Riesener (fruitwoods in marquetry). Roubo, *L’Art du menuisier* (period workshop woods). `[CITE NEEDED: a measured table for apple and pear hardness]`.
See: `cherry`, `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `marquetry-picture-of-trees`, `boxwood`, `lime-basswood-carvers`.

item.title: Lime, basswood, and the carver
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Lime, basswood, and the carver
Grinling Gibbons cut lime. The cascades of lacewood flowers at Hampton Court and St. James’s — the ones that look like they would bruise — are *Tilia*, the European lime, not the citrus. American basswood is the same genus, *Tilia americana*: pale, light, even, a wood that holds a knife cut and does not fight the grain. Furniture uses it where the show is the carving or the paint, not the pore.
The *Wood Handbook* puts basswood at about SG 0.37 and Janka 410 lbf — among the softest commercial hardwoods, pine’s neighbor, softer than yellow-poplar. It is not a chair-seat wood unless the chair is painted and the sitter is kind. It is a carver’s wood, a Venetian-blind wood, a honey-section wood, a piano-key (some grades) and drawing-board wood.
## The wood
Diffuse-porous, almost invisible grain, sap and heart both pale. Soft enough to dent with a fingernail. Straight logs. Cheap in the American yard relative to walnut. European lime (*T. cordata*, *T. platyphyllos*) is the historic carving timber of Britain and the Low Countries. German *Linde* is the same idea.
It dries with little trouble for a hardwood. It moves less dramatically than beech. It has no outdoor life.
## Workability and finish
Gouges love it. It cuts across the grain without crumbling like a cheap pine and without the muscle of maple. Undercuts stay crisp if the tool is sharp. Dull tools bruise it.
Paint and gesso were the court finishes: frames, applied ornaments, the carved drops that were glued onto oak or pine carcases. Bare lime yellows. Stain is blotchy and pointless. Gilding over gesso is the high finish.
In American factories basswood was a core, a painted bedroom-suite wood, a cheap drawer side. It still is a carving-class wood and a model-maker’s wood.
## History
Medieval polychrome sculpture in northern Europe is often lime or oak, depending on region. Baroque decorative carving in England after the Restoration made lime famous because Gibbons and his shop used it at a scale that still stops people in doorways. The V&A and the royal palaces hold the evidence. The carcase behind the lace may be oak or pine. The lace is lime.
American architectural carving — capitals, mantel ornaments — used basswood and yellow-poplar. Ship carvers used whatever was light and available; white pine is the other half of that sentence.
Furniture in the solid basswood that shows the wood is rare in high-style work. Painted country pieces exist. A “solid walnut” Victorian bed with basswood applied carvings is a factory ordinary.
## Compared with poplar and pine
Yellow-poplar is harder and has mineral color; it carves well but not as indulgently. White pine carves well and is even softer in some grades; it has resin and rings that telegraph through paint. Lime/basswood is the even, ringless cut. Boxwood is the opposite: hard, tiny, for the finest detail. Carvers keep both.
## Shop notes
Basswood dust is fine. The wood bruises in clamps. Use pads. Glue holds. Nails hold too well and crush.
Do not use it for a table top that will see keys and plates. Do use it for a carved crest that will be gilded.
European lime from urban trees can hide nails and a life of pollution. Same as orchard fruitwood: cut carefully.
## Conservation
*Tilia* species in commerce are not CITES. American basswood is a managed northern hardwood. European limes are street and park trees as much as forest trees. Using a taken-down civic lime for carving is a good death. Stripping a double row of limes for a kitchen island is a bad joke; the wood is wrong for the island anyway.
## What to look for
Pale, even, soft, carved lace, gesso, a painted suite that dents. Gibbons-style drops. A model airplane. A drawer side that is too soft to be poplar. On an invoice: basswood vs aspen vs poplar — weight and a fingernail.
The series includes the carver’s woods so a reader who only thinks in oak and mahogany can see why a palace door has a different genus glued to it. Arkansas yards may stock basswood as a northern import. The carving habit does not require a local tree. It requires a cut that holds a leaf.
## Gibbons and the lace that would bruise
Grinling Gibbons cut lime. The cascades at Hampton Court — the King’s Apartments, the drops that look as if a sleeve would crush them — are *Tilia*, the European lime, not the citrus. St. James’s, the choir at St. Paul’s, the Carved Room at Petworth, college work at Oxford and Cambridge: the V&A and the royal palaces hold the evidence. The carcase behind the lace may be oak or pine. The lace is lime. David Esterly’s modern reconstructions and the palace conservation files are the shop literature for how those undercuts still read `[CITE NEEDED: a named conservation paper on lime sculpture and Gibbons restorations]`.
Medieval polychrome sculpture in northern Europe is often lime or oak, depending on region. German *Linde* and the lime of the Low Countries are the same idea: a wood that holds a knife cut, takes gesso and paint, and does not fight the grain the way oak’s rays will. Baroque decorative carving in England after the Restoration made the genus famous because Gibbons and his shop used it at a scale that still stops people in doorways. The fashion was the applied drop: carved in the round, glued onto a structural wood, gilded or left the color of pale bread.
American architectural carving — capitals, mantel ornaments, the applied fruit on a Victorian bed — used basswood (*Tilia americana*) and yellow-poplar. Ship carvers used whatever was light; white pine is the other half of that sentence. Furniture in solid basswood that shows the wood is rare in high-style work. Painted country pieces exist. A “solid walnut” factory bed with basswood applied carvings is ordinary.
## What the handbook allows
FPL-GTR-190 puts American basswood at about specific gravity 0.37 and Janka 410 lbf at 12 percent moisture — among the softest commercial hardwoods, eastern white pine’s neighbor, softer than yellow-poplar’s 540. Shrinkage green to ovendry is not as timid as the carving reputation suggests: radial and tangential figures in the handbook are higher than poplar’s, with volumetric movement in the mid-teens `[CITE NEEDED: quote table 5–3a radial/tangential pair from the bench copy]`. It dries with little trouble for a hardwood. It has no outdoor life. It is not a chair-seat wood unless the chair is painted and the sitter is kind.
Diffuse-porous, almost invisible grain, sap and heart both pale. Straight logs. Cheap in the American yard relative to walnut. European lime (*T. cordata*, *T. platyphyllos*) is the historic carving timber of Britain and the Low Countries. Uses in the FPL tradition include carving, drawing boards, piano keys and actions in some grades, Venetian blinds, apiary sections, and painted millwork. The wood is a servant that became famous only when a carver asked it to be lace.
Gouges love it. It cuts across the grain without crumbling like a cheap pine and without the muscle of maple. Undercuts stay crisp if the tool is sharp. Dull tools bruise it. Paint and gesso were the court finishes. Bare lime yellows. Stain is blotchy and pointless. Gilding over gesso is the high finish. In American factories basswood was a core, a painted bedroom-suite wood, a cheap drawer side. It still is a carving-class wood and a model-maker’s wood.
## Lime, poplar, pine, box
Yellow-poplar is harder and has mineral color; it carves well but not as indulgently. White pine carves well and is even softer in some grades; resin and rings telegraph through paint. Lime and basswood are the even, ringless cut. Boxwood is the opposite pole: hard, tiny, for the finest detail and for a knob that must survive a hand. Carvers keep both. Roubo’s carving-wood remarks belong on the same shelf as the V&A Gibbons labels.
Basswood dust is fine. The wood bruises in clamps; use pads. Glue holds. Nails hold too well and crush the fiber. Do not use it for a table top that will see keys and plates. Do use it for a carved crest that will be gilded. European lime from urban trees hides nails and a life of street grit, the same saw-risk as orchard fruitwood. Cut slowly.
A drawer side that is too soft to be poplar may be basswood. Weight and a fingernail decide faster than a speech. Aspen is in the same pale, soft conversation and then felts under a tool. Specify *Tilia* if the job is a leaf.
## Civic trees and the kitchen-island joke
*Tilia* species in commerce are not CITES. American basswood is a managed northern hardwood. European limes are street and park trees as much as forest trees. Using a taken-down civic lime for carving is a good death. Stripping a double row of limes for a kitchen island is a bad joke; the wood is wrong for the island anyway. Arkansas yards may stock basswood as a northern import. The carving habit does not require a local tree. It requires a cut that holds a leaf and a shop that will gild it or paint it instead of asking it to be walnut.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (basswood). V&A / Hampton Court Gibbons literature. Hoadley. Roubo (carving woods). `[CITE NEEDED: a conservation paper on lime sculpture]`.
See: `fruitwoods`, `yellow-poplar`, `boxwood`, `pine-country-furniture`.

item.title: Alder
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Alder
Red alder (*Alnus rubra*) is the Pacific Coast’s paint-grade and stain-grade hardwood: light, even, a little like a soft cherry when finished, a little like birch when left pale. European alder (*A. glutinosa*) is an older furniture and clog and pile wood, a riverside tree whose timber turns from white to orange when you cut it and then to a dull brown. Neither alder furnished a court style. Both furnished a lot of chairs and a lot of kitchen doors, and American factory catalogues in the late 20th century made “alder” a bedroom-suite word.
## The wood
Red alder: the *Wood Handbook* puts it near SG 0.41 and Janka 590 lbf — between poplar and cherry, closer to poplar. Fine, even texture. Heart and sap not strongly parted. It takes stain with a willingness that made it a cherry impersonator in western factories. It is not durable outdoors. It is not a structural oak.
European alder is similar in hardness, famous for underwater piles (Venice’s folklore and some fact `[CITE NEEDED: a measured durability note]`) and for smoking, clogs, and cheap furniture. The fresh-cut color change is a shop tale every mill knows.
## Workability and finish
Alder machines easily. It dents. It glues. It is a dream for painted millwork and a temptation for stained “cherry” doors. The blotch is milder than cherry’s, the hardness lower, the pores still diffuse.
A clear finish on red alder is a warm, quiet brown-pink. It will never have cherry’s luster or oxidation drama. Selling it as cherry is a stain crime. Selling it as alder is a correct kitchen.
## History
European alder in furniture is vernacular: painted rural pieces, interiors, the hidden parts. It does not have a Macquoid chapter.
Red alder’s furniture hour is 20th-century West Coast: plentiful, fast-growing after logging, a hardwood where the other commercial trees were Douglas-fir and hemlock. Cabinet shops in Oregon and Washington used it as their poplar. Then nationwide factories discovered it as a stain-grade suite wood. “Alder bedroom” in a 1990s catalogue is a real specification.
Arts and Crafts shops in the Pacific Northwest sometimes used alder when oak had to be shipped in. It is not quartersawn white oak. It should not be asked to be.
## Shop notes
Weight and hardness separate alder from cherry (lighter, softer) and from maple (much softer). No gum flecks. Even grain. Pin knots in lower grades are the character some kitchen lines sell.
It is a poor outdoor wood and a poor wet-bath wood unless painted and maintained.
## Conservation
Red alder is an abundant, nitrogen-fixing pioneer on the Pacific Coast. Using it is ordinary forestry, often a feature of the stand, not a raid. European alder is common on wet ground. Not CITES. The ethical issue is labeling: alder as alder, not as cherry, not as “solid hardwood” hiding an MDF core with an alder frame.
## What to look for
A stained cherry look on a western door that dents too easily. Painted millwork. A Pacific kitchen. European painted country furniture that is not pine. On an invoice from the West: a correct default hardwood.
Arkansas does not grow red alder. A southern shop using it has shipped it, which is fine. Local equivalents for paint-grade are poplar and soft maple. The series includes alder so the stain-name era has a species under it.
## A western hardwood where the woods were fir
Red alder (*Alnus rubra*) is the Pacific Coast’s answer to yellow-poplar: light, even, paint-grade and stain-grade, a hardwood in a forest that sold Douglas-fir and hemlock to the structural trade. After logging, alder comes in as a pioneer. Nitrogen-fixing roots, fast growth, a mill log in decades rather than centuries. Cabinet shops in Oregon and Washington used it as their default secondary and then as a show wood when a kitchen wanted paint or a mild stain. Nationwide factories in the late twentieth century made “alder bedroom” a catalogue specification. That is a real species line, not a mood.
FPL-GTR-190 puts red alder near specific gravity 0.41 and Janka 590 lbf at 12 percent moisture — between poplar and cherry, closer to poplar. Shrinkage in the handbook tables is moderate for a hardwood (radial about 4.4 percent, tangential about 7.3 percent, volumetric about 12.6 percent green to ovendry). Fine, even texture. Heart and sap not strongly parted. It takes stain with a willingness that made it a cherry impersonator in western factories. It is not durable outdoors. It is not a structural oak. It is not cherry.
European alder (*A. glutinosa*) is the older furniture and clog and pile wood: a riverside tree whose timber turns from white to orange when you cut it and then to a dull brown. Every mill that has opened a log knows that color change. Underwater piles are the folklore and some of the fact of Venice and other wet cities `[CITE NEEDED: a measured durability note, not a guidebook sentence]`. Smoking, clogs, cheap painted furniture — vernacular, not a Macquoid chapter.
## Stain crimes and kitchen doors
Alder machines easily. It dents. It glues. It is a dream for painted millwork and a temptation for stained “cherry” doors. The blotch is milder than cherry’s. The hardness is lower. The pores are still diffuse. A clear finish on red alder is a warm, quiet brown-pink. It will never have cherry’s luster or oxidation drama. Selling it as cherry is a stain crime. Selling it as alder is a correct kitchen.
Weight and hardness separate it from cherry (lighter, softer) and from maple (much softer). No gum flecks. Even grain. Pin knots in lower grades are the “character” some kitchen lines sell on purpose. A steel screw without a pilot can split a thin rail. Paint hides a multitude of pin knots and a multitude of dents. A wet bath is a poor place for bare alder; maintain the film or pick a different wood.
Arts and Crafts shops in the Pacific Northwest sometimes used alder when quartersawn white oak had to be shipped in. It is not fumed oak. It should not be asked to be. The open-grain theater of Stickley’s face is a different genus and a different chemistry.
## How the factory found it
The furniture hour is twentieth-century West Coast first, then national. Plentiful, fast, a hardwood where the other commercial trees were softwoods. Then stain-grade suites: bedroom collections, entertainment walls, the 1990s catalogue page that said alder and meant it. Some of those pieces are honest solid frames. Some are an alder face on a particleboard box. The engineered chapter takes the box. The ethical issue here is labeling: alder as alder, not as cherry, not as “solid hardwood” hiding an MDF core with an alder stile.
European painted country furniture that is not pine is sometimes alder. Interiors, hidden parts, a rural chair. It does not have a court style. It has a river.
West Coast mill grades and WCLIB practice sort alder for millwork and furniture `[CITE NEEDED: a WCLIB or similar grade note]`. Pin-knot “character” grade is a marketing decision as much as a forest one. Clear paint-grade is the older shop wish.
## A southern shop and a shipped board
Arkansas does not grow red alder. A southern shop using it has paid freight, which is fine. Local paint-grade equivalents are yellow-poplar and soft maple. If the job is a stained door that must survive a client who owns cherry furniture, say so and pick cherry, or say alder and keep the stain honest. *Alnus* species in commerce are not CITES. Using red alder is ordinary forestry, often a feature of the stand. The conservation argument is land use and labeling, not an appendix.
Look for a stained cherry look on a western door that dents too easily. Painted millwork. A Pacific kitchen. European painted country furniture that is not pine. On an invoice from the West: a correct default hardwood. On a bill that says cherry and weighs like poplar: ask.
## A mill ticket and a kitchen stile
Walk a Portland or Tacoma millwork shop in the 1970s and the rack that is not fir is often alder. Door stiles, drawer fronts, a face frame for a painted box. The plane takes a long shaving. The arris bruises if you stack boards without stickers. Fresh-cut European alder flashes orange on the saw and then settles; red alder is quieter about that change but still pinks as it oxidizes. Hoadley would send you to the end grain: diffuse pores, no gum, no oak ray. A client who wants “cherry grain” will be disappointed. A client who wants a painted door that machines clean will not.
Turned alder legs show in factory suites more often than in high-style work. They dent at the foot where a vacuum hits. That is the hardness number doing what FPL said it would do. Birch is paler and a little harder in many grades; poplar has the mineral streak; maple fights the stain. Alder sits in the middle and takes the spray booth’s cherry toner without a fight. The honest shop writes the species on the ticket. The dishonest one writes the toner name.
Clogs and smoked fish are the European vernacular pair that never needed a parlor. Pile work in wet ground is the other old job. Furniture from *A. glutinosa* in a North German painted cupboard is the same riverside tree doing a drier task. Do not force a Venice-foundation speech onto a kitchen door. The chemistry of wet durability and the chemistry of a stain-grade bedroom are not the same sentence `[CITE NEEDED: a measured pile-durability note]`.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (red alder). Hoadley. West Coast mill practice `[CITE NEEDED: a WCLIB or similar grade note]`.
See: `cherry`, `yellow-poplar`, `birch`, `engineered-wood-honest`.

item.title: Yew
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Yew
The English longbow is the famous yew object. The Welsh stick chair and the country Windsor that used a yew bow or a yew stick are the furniture objects. *Taxus baccata* is a softwood that behaves like a hard, elastic hardwood: tight rings, a warm orange heart, a cream sap, a willingness to bend and return. It grows slowly, often in churchyards and on limestone, and the furniture that came from it is almost always vernacular, small, and now expensive.
Pacific yew (*T. brevifolia*) is a different history — a bow wood, a tool wood, then a cancer-drug bark story (taxol) that had nothing to do with chairs. European yew is the furniture species of this chapter.
## The wood
Closed grain, no vessels (it is a conifer), hardness often compared to hard maple in anecdotal shop tests; published Janka figures sit in a high range for a “softwood,” around 1,500 lbf in secondary compilations `[CITE NEEDED: confirm a primary FPL or equivalent number]`. Density is high. The heartwood is orange to russet, sometimes with purple streaks; sapwood is sharply pale. That two-tone is the furniture look: a Windsor bow with a ribbon of sap, a slab stool with a white edge.
It is durable. Churchyard trees and outdoor gates have used that fact. The foliage and seed (not the aril) are poisonous to livestock; the wood in a chair is not a poison story for sitters.
## Workability and finish
Yew planes to a glass surface and can tear where the grain swirls around knots — and yew is knots. It turns beautifully. It scrapes. It takes a polish that looks like a hard varnish even under oil.
Bending: the bowyer’s art and the chairmaker’s. Steam or heat, a form, a restraint. English Windsors and Welsh chairs used yew for the parts that had to be tough and pretty. Not every shop could get it. Ash did the same job more often.
The dust and the sawing of old churchyard yew can include metal and grit. Cut slowly.
## Furniture history
Medieval and early modern England used yew for small joined work, for inlay, and for the occasional fine box. The main furniture tradition is country seating from the 18th and 19th centuries: the yew-wood Windsor, prized now out of proportion to its original farmhouse status. Collectors pay for the color and for the romance of the churchyard tree. Chinnery’s oak book is the wrong shelf; vernacular chair books are the right ones `[CITE NEEDED: Cotton, Jenkins, or Dunn on Welsh chairs]`.
French and Alpine work used yew in small doses. Italian *tasso* appears in inlay. It was never mahogany.
American furniture rarely shows *T. baccata*. Pacific yew is too scarce and too small for case work. A “yew” dining table from a catalogue is likely veneer of European yew on a cheaper ground, or a stained impostor.
## Fashion
Always a minority taste. The late 20th century made yew veneer a boardroom and hotel-desk fashion in Britain — a burled, golden surface that is a slice, not a stick chair. That veneer can be handsome. It is a different object from a 19th-century Windsor.
## Shop notes
Dry yew moves less than its hardness suggests, but knots check. Design for the defects; they are the tree.
Do not confuse yew with osage-orange (*Maclura*), another orange bow wood, American, with a different anatomy (a hardwood, ring-porous). Osage shows up in American rustic work and tool handles.
## Conservation
*Taxus baccata* is not a typical CITES furniture listing; local felling rules and churchyard sentiment are the real limits. Old trees are cultural monuments. Furniture should come from windthrows and managed cuts, not from a raid on a medieval churchyard. Pacific yew was pressured by the taxol harvest before synthesis; it was never a furniture supply.
## What to look for
Orange heart, white sap, tiny rings, a bent bow, a Welsh chair, a hotel desk with yew burl veneer. Weight. A polish like stone. On a cheap “yew” suite: the edge.
The series includes yew so the country chair is not collapsed into “oak or elm,” and so the longbow’s tree gets its domestic life. Arkansas does not grow *T. baccata*. A southern shop meets it as an antique or as a veneer. The local elastic hardwoods are hickory and ash. Different color, same job in a bend.
## The chair, not only the bow
The English longbow is the famous yew object. The furniture objects are smaller and closer to the ground: a Welsh stick chair with a yew arm, a country Windsor whose bow is a steamed *Taxus* stick with a ribbon of cream sap against orange heart. *Taxus baccata* is a conifer that behaves like a hard, elastic hardwood. Tight rings. No vessels. A warm orange to russet heart, sometimes with a purple hint. Sapwood sharply pale. That two-tone is the furniture look. Collectors pay for it now out of proportion to the farmhouse status the chair had when it was new.
Vernacular chair books are the right shelf. Chinnery’s oak volume is the wrong one. Cotton, Jenkins, and Dunn on Welsh and country seating are the names restorers reach for `[CITE NEEDED: pin the chair monograph you have on the bench]`. English Windsors used yew when the shop could get it; ash did the same bending job more often. Not every Thames-valley or High Wycombe shop had churchyard thinnings and limestone-hill stools in the rack.
French and Alpine work used yew in small doses. Italian *tasso* appears in inlay. It was never mahogany. American furniture rarely shows *T. baccata*. Pacific yew (*T. brevifolia*) is a bow wood and a tool wood, then a taxol-bark story that had nothing to do with chairs. It was never a case-work supply. A catalogue “yew” dining table is likely European yew veneer on a cheaper ground, or a stained impostor. Look at the edge.
## Softwood numbers, hardwood manners
Closed grain, no pores. Hardness in secondary compilations sits high for a “softwood,” around 1,500 lbf Janka `[CITE NEEDED: confirm a primary FPL or equivalent number; FPL-GTR-190 does not treat yew as a commercial furniture lumber in the domestic tables]`. Density is high. The wood planes to a glass surface and tears where the grain swirls around knots — and yew is knots. It turns. It scrapes. It takes a polish that looks like a hard varnish even under oil. Dry yew moves less than its hardness suggests. Knots check. Design for the defects. They are the tree.
Bending is the bowyer’s art and the chairmaker’s. Steam or heat, a form, a restraint. The elasticity that made a war bow makes a Windsor hoop that comes back. Churchyard trees and outdoor gates used the durability of the heart. The foliage and seed (not the red aril) are poisonous to livestock. The wood in a chair is not a poison story for sitters. Old churchyard logs hide metal and grit. Cut slowly.
Do not confuse yew with osage-orange (*Maclura pomifera*), another orange bow wood, American, a ring-porous hardwood. Osage shows up in rustic work and tool handles. Anatomy decides: vessels versus none.
## Two yew objects that are not the same
Medieval and early modern England used yew for small joined work, for inlay, and for the occasional fine box. The main furniture tradition is country seating from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The late twentieth century made a third object: yew burl veneer on boardroom desks and hotel case goods in Britain, a golden sliced surface that is not a stick chair. That veneer can be handsome. It is a different object. Do not restore a 1980s pedestal desk as if it were a Welsh armchair.
Fashion was always a minority taste. Price now is a collector’s taste. The romance of the churchyard tree is real and also a hazard. Old trees are cultural monuments. Furniture should come from windthrows and managed cuts, not from a raid on a medieval yard. Local felling rules and sentiment are the real limits; *T. baccata* is not a typical CITES furniture listing. Pacific yew was pressured by the taxol harvest before synthesis. It was never a furniture supply.
## How to look
Orange heart, white sap, tiny rings, a bent bow, a Welsh chair, a hotel desk with yew burl veneer. Weight. A polish like stone. On a cheap “yew” suite: the edge. On a southern bench: you are probably looking at an antique or a veneer, not an Arkansas log. The local elastic hardwoods for a bend are hickory and ash. Different color. Same job if the part must come back to shape.
Tap a dry stick. The good bow-grade rings. Standing-dead churchyard wood can be brittle. Bend with caution. A thin long span will snap where a new ash bow would complain first.
A Windsor bow in yew wants a clean steam and a form that matches the stick, not a fight against a knot that will open on the outside of the bend. High Wycombe and other English chair districts used ash when yew was dear or short; the mixed-wood Windsor chapter takes that shop list. Inlay slips of yew in a walnut or oak ground are the small high-style use: a warm line, not a field. Italian *tasso* in a cabinet is the same idea. If the invoice says yew and the panel is eighteen inches wide without a glue line, look again. The tree does not offer that board.
## Sources
Hoadley (softwood anatomy). English vernacular chair literature `[CITE NEEDED]`. Bowyer literature for mechanical comparisons. Wood Database compilations for hardness (secondary). Chinnery (limited).
See: `windsor-mixed-wood`, `elm`, `ash`, `hickory-and-pecan`.

item.title: Boxwood
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Boxwood
A boxwood rule does not wear out in a hurry. Neither does a wood-engraving block cut on the end grain, the kind Thomas Bewick made ordinary and the 19th-century press made industrial. *Buxus sempervirens* is a shrub-tree of tiny rings, a specific gravity that can exceed 0.9, and a hardness that secondary tables put near or above 2,800 lbf `[CITE NEEDED: primary mechanical test]`. Furniture uses it the way a jeweler uses gold: stringing, banding, knobs, chess pieces, the pale line in a dark walnut veneer. Nobody makes a press cupboard of box.
## The wood
Pale yellow, closed, almost no visible pore on the face, a silky end grain. European box from the Mediterranean and the Caucasus, English garden box that took a century to make a billet, later East London “box” that was often *Buxus* from the Black Sea trade. African box (*B. macowanii*) and other hard pale woods filled the engraving trade when Turkish and European box ran short `[CITE NEEDED: 19th-c. engraving-trade supply notes]`.
It is a hardwood, diffuse-porous, so dense it sinks in some pieces. It does not like wide flats. The tree does not make them.
## Workability and finish
Turns like ivory’s cousin. Files, scrapers, a polish with its own dust. Hand planes can do small faces. Tools must be sharp; the wood is abrasive in a fine way.
It moves less than its density might scare you into thinking, in small sections. In a humid swing, a wide glue-up of box would still be a mistake. There are no wide glue-ups; there is no stock.
Finish is often wax or oil or nothing. The wood is already a finish.
## Furniture and the trades
Marquetry and parquetry: the pale string. William-and-Mary and later walnut furniture uses box lines the way a drawing uses a highlight. French ébénistes used it with ebony and brass. The marquetry chapter returns to this.
Turned knobs, finials, chess sets, musical-instrument fittings, textile-block printing, the engraving trade — boxwood’s main life was not chairs. A 17th-century English table with box inlay is using the tree correctly.
American furniture used boxwood less because the tree is not an American forest species. Imported box served the same inlay jobs. Substitute pale woods (holly, maple, sometimes holly’s lookalikes) did the cheap stringing. Holly (*Ilex*) is the other Federal inlay white; it is not as hard.
## Fashion
Always a minor wood by volume, a major wood by eye. When pale classical furniture wanted a sharp line, box or holly provided it. When Victorian engravers wanted a block that would print a thousand times, box provided it. When the block trade collapsed, the furniture inlay trade did not take up the slack; it had already moved to other whites.
## Shop notes
Box dust is fine and can irritate. Old engraving blocks are historical objects; do not cut them for knobs. Garden box from a ripped-out hedge is full of dirt at the collar and small in diameter. Use it for what it is.
Do not confuse boxwood with “box elder” (*Acer negundo*), a soft maple with red stain streaks. The names share a syllable and nothing else.
## Conservation
*Buxus sempervirens* in European gardens has been hit by box blight and box-tree moth in the last decades — an ornamental crisis, not a CITES furniture listing `[CITE NEEDED: current CABI or forestry notes]`. Wild box in the Mediterranean and Caucasus has been pressured by historic trade. Buy small, old, or clearly garden-salvage stock. Do not specify box for surfaces that holly or maple stringing can do.
## What to look for
A pale hard line in walnut or ebony. A turned knob that feels like stone. An engraving block, end-grain, 19th century. A “boxwood” large table: a lie or a veneer.
The series includes boxwood because 500 years of fine furniture are drawn in pale lines, and those lines have a genus. Arkansas does not grow *Buxus* as timber. A southern shop meets it as inlay stock. The local pale hard wood is maple. Different scale, related job.
## A rule, a block, a pale line
A boxwood rule does not wear out in a hurry. Folding rules from the nineteenth-century tool trades — boxwood with brass joints — outlived the men who carried them in an apron. Thomas Bewick made end-grain box the ordinary wood-engraving block; the press then made it industrial. *Buxus sempervirens* is a shrub-tree of tiny rings. Specific gravity can exceed 0.9. Secondary hardness tables put Janka near or above 2,800 lbf `[CITE NEEDED: a primary mechanical test; FPL-GTR-190 does not table European box as a commercial American lumber]`. Furniture uses it the way a jeweler uses gold: stringing, banding, knobs, chessmen, the pale line in a dark walnut veneer. Nobody makes a press cupboard of box. The tree does not make the board.
European box from the Mediterranean and the Caucasus, English garden box that took a century to make a billet, later East London “box” that was often *Buxus* from the Black Sea trade. African box (*B. macowanii*) and other hard pale woods filled the engraving trade when Turkish and European box ran short `[CITE NEEDED: 19th-c. engraving-trade supply notes]`. It is diffuse-porous, so dense some pieces sink. Pale yellow, closed, almost no visible pore on the face, a silky end grain. Wide flats do not exist. Anyone selling a “boxwood” table top is selling a veneer or a different tree.
## At the bench: ivory’s cousin
It turns. Files, scrapers, a polish with its own dust. Hand planes can do small faces if the iron is sharp; the wood is abrasive in a fine way. It moves less than its density might scare you into thinking, in small sections. In a humid swing, a wide glue-up of box would still be a mistake. There are no wide glue-ups. There is no stock. Finish is often wax or oil or nothing. The wood is already a finish.
Box dust is fine and can irritate. Old engraving blocks are historical objects; do not cut them for knobs. Garden box from a ripped-out hedge is full of dirt at the collar and small in diameter. Use it for what it is. Do not confuse boxwood with “box elder” (*Acer negundo*), a soft maple with red stain streaks. The names share a syllable and nothing else. Holly (*Ilex*) is the other Federal inlay white; it is not as hard. Maple stringing is the cheap pale line. Box is the line that survives a fingernail.
## Marquetry, William-and-Mary, and the trades that were not chairs
William-and-Mary and later walnut furniture uses box lines the way a drawing uses a highlight. French ébénistes used it with ebony and brass. Roubo and the Wallace Collection marquetry notes put pale *Buxus* in the same kit as dyed greens and the dark woods. The marquetry chapter of this series returns to that picture. A seventeenth-century English table with box inlay is using the tree correctly: a line, not a field.
Turned knobs, finials, chess sets, musical-instrument fittings (recorders, some guitar and violin parts in small bits), textile printing blocks, the engraving trade — boxwood’s main life was not seating. American furniture used imported box for the same inlay jobs because the tree is not an American forest species. Substitute pale woods did the cheap stringing. When the wood-engraving trade collapsed, the furniture inlay trade did not take up the slack. It had already moved to other whites.
Fashion: always a minor wood by volume, a major wood by eye. When pale classical furniture wanted a sharp line, box or holly provided it. When Victorian engravers wanted a block that would print a thousand times, box provided it.
## Blight, moth, and the small buy
*Buxus sempervirens* in European gardens has been hit by box blight and box-tree moth in recent decades — an ornamental crisis, not a CITES furniture listing `[CITE NEEDED: current CABI or forestry notes]`. Wild box in the Mediterranean and Caucasus has been pressured by historic trade. Buy small, old, or clearly garden-salvage stock. Do not specify box for surfaces that holly or maple stringing can do. A forestry monograph on the historic *Buxus* trade belongs on the source shelf when you can put a hand on it `[CITE NEEDED]`.
Look for a pale hard line in walnut or ebony. A turned knob that feels like stone. An engraving block, end-grain, nineteenth century. A “boxwood” large table: a lie or a veneer. Arkansas does not grow *Buxus* as timber. A southern shop meets it as inlay stock. The local pale hard wood is maple. Different scale. Related job.
A wood-engraving block is cut on the end grain so the tool meets a field of tiny rings, not a long fiber. Bewick’s school and the later London trade depended on that cut. Furniture stringing is the long-grain cousin: a slip planed thin, glued into a rebate, scraped flush. The same density that held a thousand impressions on a press holds a fingernail on a drawer front. Chessmen and rule joints are the turning shop’s share. Musical-instrument fittings are another small life — a recorder beak, a guitar bridge pin — not a furniture volume. Keep the objects in scale. A “boxwood” dining surface is still the wrong scale.
## Sources
Hoadley. Bewick and wood-engraving histories. Roubo; Wallace Collection marquetry notes. Wood Database (secondary hardness). `[CITE NEEDED: a forestry monograph on Buxus trade]`.
See: `marquetry-picture-of-trees`, `walnut`, `satinwood`, `lime-basswood-carvers`.

item.title: Pine and country furniture
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Pine and country furniture
A six-board chest in eastern white pine, painted oxblood, is not a failed oak chest. It is a different idea of furniture: light enough to move, cheap enough to own, soft enough to dent, and honest about paint. Northern Europe and eastern North America furnished more rooms in pine than in walnut. The fashionable histories under-count it because pine was often painted out of the story.
This chapter is the country habit. Heart pine and Baltic deal have their own essays. They overlap. They are not the same trees.
## The woods people meant
Eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*) — Weymouth pine in England — is the New England and Great Lakes furniture pine: SG about 0.35, Janka about 380 lbf (FPL-GTR-190). Soft, even, low shrinkage, easy to kiln. Heartwood light brown with a red hint; it darkens in air. The *Wood Handbook* still lists furniture among its uses. Old-growth clear white pine is a vanished grade; second growth is knotty and fine for paint.
Scots pine (*P. sylvestris*) is the European furniture and joinery pine, the redwood or red deal of the British trade when it came from the Baltic and Scandinavia. Harder than white pine in many grades, with a stronger ring.
Southern yellow pines (*P. taeda*, *P. echinata*, and kin) are denser, with a loud latewood band. They appear in southern country furniture and in later factory work. Longleaf heart pine is the next chapter.
Knots are not a defect in country pine. They are the tree. A knot that holds is a feature; a knot that falls out is a hole you plug or paint.
## Workability and finish
Pine planes easily and bruises easily. Resin in yellow pines gums cutters and finishes. White pine is kinder. All pines take paint as if they were born for it. Stain blotches: the earlywood drinks, the latewood refuses. A “honey pine” finish is often a toner and a varnish arguing with the rings.
Nails hold in pine as well as in any furniture wood; the fiber crushes and grips. Glue holds if the resin is not on the surface.
Movement is modest in white pine compared with oak. A wide pine board still cups. Breadboard ends and battens are old answers.
## Country, not “primitive” as an insult
Painted pine furniture is the furniture of people who had trees and brushes: New England blanket chests, Pennsylvania schranks that are not all walnut, Scandinavian peasant cupboards, Alpine painted armoires, English boarded pine of the farmhouse. The Metropolitan, Winterthur, and Nordic museums hold the best of it. Most of it lived harder lives and did not survive.
Shaker pine is a subset: clear finish or light paint, maple and cherry beside it. The Shaker chapter takes the mix. The pine there is a chosen pale, not a last resort.
Southern pine country pieces — huntboards, pie safes, cupboard tops — may be yellow pine, poplar, or both. Hurst and Prown teach the reader to look.
## The knotty-pine century
20th-century American dens and kitchens paneled in knotty pine, often *P. strobus* or western pines, made a fashion of the grade that old-growth millers would have rejected for furniture. Colonial Revival “Early American” factories made pine dining rooms with machine distress. Some of it is charming. Some of it is a cartoon of a 17th-century board chest.
Mid-century taste hid pine, then country taste brought it back, then oak and cherry took the 1990s. Pine never left the painted cupboard.
## Shop notes
A steel screw in pine without a pilot can split a thin rail. Glue and a peg are older and often better.
Old paint may be lead. That is a conservation and health fact, not a style note.
Do not call every pale American secondary wood pine. Poplar is greener and heavier. Basswood is even softer and more even.
## Conservation
The pines in this chapter are not CITES species. White pine’s old-growth was taken for masts and for clear lumber (Albion; the Broad Arrow tradition). Second-growth furniture is a different material. Using plantation and managed pine for painted work is ordinary. Using remaining old-growth for a suburban table is a waste of a scarce grade.
## What to look for
Dents, paint layers, knots, resin canals on the end grain, light weight. A chest you can lift. A “mahogany” factory piece with a pine back. A Shaker stand that is maple and pine together.
Bradley Brand works pine among other Arkansas woods. A painted pine cupboard from southern yellow pine is a country object in a line that does not need to apologize to walnut. It needs a finish that expects dents, and a buyer who does not mistake softness for a mistake.
## Six boards and a brush
A six-board chest is a lesson in what pine is for. Two sides, a bottom, a lid, a front and back — nailed or pegged, often a till inside, often painted oxblood or blue or a green that has gone black in the folds. Eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*) made the New England version light enough to drag to a wall. You can lift a chest that would be a two-person oak object. That is not a failed hardwood piece. It is a different idea of furniture: cheap enough to own, soft enough to dent, honest about paint.
FPL-GTR-190 puts eastern white pine at about specific gravity 0.35 and Janka 380 lbf at 12 percent moisture. Shrinkage is low for a commercial wood: on the order of 2.1 percent radial, 6.1 percent tangential, 8.2 percent volumetric green to ovendry. That stability, and the old-growth clears that used to come off the lake states and New England, made furniture and interior joinery. The *Wood Handbook* still lists furniture among its uses. Second growth is knotty. Knots are not a defect in country pine. A knot that holds is a feature. A knot that falls out is a hole you plug or paint.
Scots pine (*P. sylvestris*) is the European furniture and joinery pine, the redwood or red deal of the British trade when it came from the Baltic and Scandinavia. Harder than white pine in many grades, with a stronger ring. Southern yellow pines (*P. taeda*, *P. echinata*, and kin) are denser, with a loud latewood band. They appear in southern country furniture and in later factory work. Hurst and Prown teach the reader to look: a huntboard or pie safe may be yellow pine, poplar, or both. Longleaf heart pine has its own chapter. Baltic deal has its own. They overlap. They are not the same trees.
England called *P. strobus* Weymouth pine. The Broad Arrow reserved large white pines for masts (Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*; the Massachusetts charter tradition). Furniture shops used what the navy did not take, and later what the cut-over left. Old-growth clear white pine is a vanished grade for ordinary yards. Using remaining old-growth for a suburban table is a waste of a scarce clear. Using managed and plantation pine for painted work is ordinary.
## Paint as construction
Pine planes easily and bruises easily. Resin in yellow pines gums cutters and finishes. White pine is kinder. All pines take paint as if they were born for it. Stain blotches: the earlywood drinks, the latewood refuses. A “honey pine” finish is often a toner and a varnish arguing with the rings. Nails hold; the fiber crushes and grips. Glue holds if the resin is not on the surface. A steel screw without a pilot can split a thin rail. Glue and a peg are older and often better. Breadboard ends and battens are old answers to a wide board that still cups.
Painted pine is the furniture of people who had trees and brushes: New England blanket chests, Pennsylvania schranks that are not all walnut, Scandinavian peasant cupboards, Alpine painted armoires, English boarded pine of the farmhouse. The Metropolitan, Winterthur, and Nordic museums hold the best of it. Most of it lived harder lives and did not survive. Old paint may be lead. That is a conservation and health fact, not a style note. Overpaint is a palimpsest. Stripping a cupboard to “natural pine” is often a 1960s taste, not an eighteenth-century one.
Shaker pine is a subset: clear finish or light paint, maple and cherry beside it. The Shaker chapter takes the mix. The pine there is a chosen pale, not a last resort.
## The knotty-pine room and the factory distress
Twentieth-century American dens and kitchens paneled in knotty pine — often *P. strobus* or western pines — made a fashion of the grade that old-growth millers would have rejected for furniture. Colonial Revival “Early American” factories made pine dining rooms with machine distress. Some of it is charming. Some of it is a cartoon of a seventeenth-century board chest. Mid-century taste hid pine, then country taste brought it back, then oak and cherry took the 1990s. Pine never left the painted cupboard.
Do not call every pale American secondary wood pine. Yellow-poplar is greener and heavier. Basswood is even softer and more even. End grain shows resin canals in pine. That is the tell when a dealer says “all original pine” and the drawer side is tulip-streaked.
The pines in this chapter are not CITES species. Second-growth furniture is a different material from mast-grade clears. A painted southern yellow-pine cupboard is a country object in a line that does not need to apologize to walnut. It needs a finish that expects dents, and a buyer who does not mistake softness for a mistake.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (eastern white pine; southern pines). Albion, *Forests and Sea Power*. Forman; Hurst and Prown. Shaker catalogues (Kassay; Rieman and Burks). Hoadley.
See: `heart-pine-longleaf`, `baltic-deal-painted-pine`, `shaker-woods`, `yellow-poplar`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Heart pine and longleaf
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Heart pine and longleaf
Before the longleaf pine was a floor, it was a tar tree. The naval-stores belt of the American South — North Carolina to Texas, a fire forest of *Pinus palustris* — fed pitch, tar, turpentine, and masts to Atlantic shipping (Outland, *Tapping the Pines*; Earley, *Looking for Longleaf*). The heartwood of old trees, dense with latewood and resin, became the “heart pine” of southern houses: joists, floors, the occasional press and table. Furniture was a side use. The side use is what this chapter is for.
## The wood
Longleaf is a southern yellow pine. The *Wood Handbook* lists longleaf at about SG 0.59 and Janka 870 lbf at 12 percent — more than twice the hardness of eastern white pine, in the neighborhood of teak’s number and below oak. The face is a loud stripe of hard latewood and softer earlywood. Old-growth heartwood is red-orange to brown, resinous, and heavy. Sapwood is paler. What dealers call heart pine is that old heartwood, often reclaimed from mills and warehouses.
Slash pine (*P. elliottii*) and other yellow pines overlap in the salvage market. Anatomy does not always give you the species on a painted joist. The grade is the density and the heart.
Resin will bleed through finishes for years if the kiln work was shy. Old heart is more stable than a wet new yellow-pine 2×10. It is still a pine: it dents less than white pine, more than maple.
## Workability and finish
Hard latewood and soft earlywood make a corrugated plane feel if the iron is dull. Carbide and sharp handsaws. Nails in old heart can bend. Predrill.
Oil finishes wake the red. Film finishes sit on the resin and sometimes peel. Shellac as a sealer is an old answer to bleed. Water-based finishes can fail on resinous stock.
The grain is too strong for a delicate stain. People who want “oak” should buy oak. Heart pine looks like itself or it looks like a gym floor.
## Southern furniture
Coastal and backcountry shops used yellow pine as a primary wood for painted and stained case work and as a secondary wood under walnut and mahogany. Huntboards, safes, cupboard interiors, bedsteads. Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* is the place to see the mix. A Charleston parlor might show mahogany; the passage and the kitchen did not.
19th-century mills cut longleaf into a national structural lumber. Furniture factories used it when they wanted cheap and strong. School desks, pews, mill-town tables.
20th-century depletion of old-growth longleaf (agriculture, logging, fire suppression that stopped the forest’s own regeneration) made heart pine a salvage fashion. Flooring companies pulled warehouses. Dining tables from 19th-century joists became a late-century product. Some of those tables are honest reuse. Some are new yellow pine stained orange.
## Naval stores and the Crown
The Naval Stores Act tradition and the Broad Arrow are white-pine and Baltic stories as much as longleaf, but the southern pitch industry is the economic pair to New England masts. Longleaf was a strategic tree. Furniture shops lived on the leftovers and on the domestic build. Reading a heart-pine table without the tar kiln is like reading mahogany without Jamaica.
## Shop notes
Metal in reclaimed joists: nails, plaster keys, a bolt. Scan or cut slowly.
Old heart can be brittle. A thin long span will snap where a new oak board would bend.
Insect holes in sapwood are common; heart is less tasty. Do not buy powder that is still coming out.
## Conservation
Longleaf restoration is one of the serious American forest projects: fire, wiregrass, red-cockaded woodpecker. Earley’s book is the public narrative. Furniture should use certified new longleaf if you want new wood (the tree is being planted again), or documented salvage. It should not use the last old trees for a coffee table.
Not CITES. The Lacey Act still applies to imported pine that might be mixed in a container of “heart pine.” Ask for the country and the species.
## What to look for
Loud latewood, orange heart, weight, resin, a southern house floor, a joist mortise in the underside of a table. A light, even “heart pine” from a big-box aisle: probably not.
Arkansas is on the edge of the old longleaf map; shortleaf and loblolly are the more local yellow pines. A shop that works southern pine is in the right region. True old-growth longleaf is a salvage or a specialty order. Name it honestly.
## Tar first, then the floor
Before the longleaf pine was a floor, it was a tar tree. The naval-stores belt of the American South — North Carolina to Texas, a fire forest of *Pinus palustris* — fed pitch, tar, turpentine, and masts to Atlantic shipping. Robert B. Outland III’s *Tapping the Pines* (2004) is the industry book. Lawrence S. Earley’s *Looking for Longleaf* (2004) is the forest book. Furniture was a side use. The side use is what this chapter is for. Reading a heart-pine table without the tar kiln is like reading mahogany without Jamaica.
The Naval Stores Act tradition and the Broad Arrow are white-pine and Baltic stories as much as longleaf (Albion). The southern pitch industry is the economic pair to New England masts. Longleaf was a strategic tree. Shops lived on leftovers and on the domestic build: joists, floors, the occasional press and table, painted case work in the passage and the kitchen while a Charleston parlor showed mahogany.
FPL-GTR-190 lists longleaf at about specific gravity 0.59 and Janka 870 lbf at 12 percent moisture — more than twice the hardness of eastern white pine, in the neighborhood of teak’s handbook number and below oak. Shrinkage green to ovendry is on the order of 5.1 percent radial, 7.5 percent tangential, 12.2 percent volumetric. The face is a loud stripe of hard latewood and softer earlywood. Old-growth heartwood is red-orange to brown, resinous, and heavy. Sapwood is paler. What dealers call heart pine is that old heart, often reclaimed from mills and warehouses. Slash pine (*P. elliottii*) and other yellow pines overlap in the salvage market. Anatomy does not always give you the species on a painted joist. The grade is the density and the heart.
## At the bench with resin
Hard latewood and soft earlywood make a corrugated plane feel if the iron is dull. Carbide and sharp handsaws. Nails in old heart can bend. Predrill. Oil finishes wake the red. Film finishes sit on the resin and sometimes peel. Shellac as a sealer is an old answer to bleed. Water-based finishes can fail on resinous stock. Resin will bleed through for years if the kiln work was shy. Old heart is more stable than a wet new yellow-pine 2×10. It is still a pine: it dents less than white pine, more than maple.
The grain is too strong for a delicate stain. People who want “oak” should buy oak. Heart pine looks like itself or it looks like a gym floor. Metal in reclaimed joists — nails, plaster keys, a bolt — will ruin a saw. Scan or cut slowly. Old heart can be brittle. A thin long span will snap where a new oak board would bend. Insect holes in sapwood are common; heart is less tasty. Do not buy powder that is still coming out.
## Southern shops and the salvage century
Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* is the place to see yellow pine as a primary wood for painted and stained case work and as a secondary wood under walnut and mahogany. Huntboards, safes, cupboard interiors, bedsteads. A Charleston parlor might show mahogany; the passage and the kitchen did not. Nineteenth-century mills cut longleaf into a national structural lumber. Furniture factories used it when they wanted cheap and strong: school desks, pews, mill-town tables.
Twentieth-century depletion of old-growth longleaf — agriculture, logging, fire suppression that stopped the forest’s own regeneration — made heart pine a salvage fashion. Flooring companies pulled warehouses. Dining tables from nineteenth-century joists became a late-century product. Some of those tables are honest reuse. A joist mortise in the underside is a good tell. Some are new yellow pine stained orange. A light, even “heart pine” from a big-box aisle is probably not.
Longleaf restoration is one of the serious American forest projects: fire, wiregrass, red-cockaded woodpecker. Earley’s book is the public narrative. Furniture should use certified new longleaf if you want new wood (the tree is being planted again), or documented salvage. It should not use the last old trees for a coffee table. Not CITES. The Lacey Act still applies to imported pine that might be mixed in a container of “heart pine.” Ask for the country and the species.
Arkansas sits on the edge of the old longleaf map. Shortleaf and loblolly are the more local yellow pines. A shop that works southern pine is in the right region. True old-growth longleaf is a salvage or a specialty order. Name it honestly. Weight, resin, loud latewood, orange heart — those are the tells. A joist mortise under a table is better evidence than a hang-tag.
A fire forest wants fire. Earley’s narrative and the restoration literature agree on that much: without periodic burn, hardwoods and loblolly take the ground, and longleaf fails to recruit. Furniture does not restore a stand. It can refuse to spend the last old boles on a coffee table and it can name salvage as salvage. Turpentine faces and boxed hearts in a reclaimed joist are industrial marks, not rustic decoration. Leave them if they are stable. Do not sand them into a gym-floor cartoon.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (longleaf). Outland, *Tapping the Pines* (2004). Earley, *Looking for Longleaf* (2004). Hurst and Prown. Albion (naval context).
See: `pine-country-furniture`, `baltic-deal-painted-pine`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Baltic deal and painted pine
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Baltic deal and painted pine
English joiners said “deal” the way they said “wainscot”: a traded size and a quality, not a botanical mood. Deal was a sawn softwood board, often Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*) or spruce (*Picea abies*), shipped from Norway, Sweden, Finland, and the Russian Baltic. It built floors, shop fittings, the carcases under walnut veneer, and whole painted interiors. The furniture of northern Europe that is not oak is, a great deal of the time, this wood with a brush on it.
## The trade
The Dutch and the English ran on Baltic timber as they ran on Baltic oak. Sound Toll registers and later timber-auction records at the Zaan and in London are the paper trail (the same KNOB and Haneca world as wainscot, with different cargoes). “Yellow deal” and “red deal” were color and port grades of pine. White deal was often spruce. A London cabinetmaker’s bill that says deal means the cheap, stable, imported board — the yellow-poplar of Britain.
Gillows and other northern English firms bought Baltic oak and Baltic deals on the salt-and-cloth return voyages (Bowett, provincial woods). Furniture in Lancaster could be mahogany show and deal hide, or painted deal throughout.
## The wood
Scots pine in northern, slow-grown grades is an even, resinous, workable furniture pine, harder than *P. strobus*. Spruce is lighter, less resinous, a painter’s friend and a soundboard wood. Both dent. Both take nails. Both move less than oak.
Identification on a painted antique is a scraped edge and a resin-canal search. Do not scrape a museum piece. On a house-owned cupboard, a chip in the back tells you.
## Paint as the species
Scandinavian and North German painted furniture — rosemaling, blue-grey Gustavian, the peasant cupboard — is a finish tradition on local and traded pine and spruce. The Gustavian pale grey of late-18th-century Sweden is a classical fashion in paint, a Baltic answer to satinwood that does not need satinwood. Russian and Finnish painted work belongs here too.
English painted pine of the 18th and early 19th centuries — dressing tables, cheap chairs, later the “fancy chair” — used deal and beech and birch. Sheraton’s cheaper cousins lived here.
The paint is linseed, milk, distemper, later industrial enamel. Lead in old layers. Overpaint is a palimpsest. Stripping a Gustavian cupboard to “natural pine” is a period error unless you like 1960s taste.
## Under the veneer
William-and-Mary and Georgian carcases: oak for strength, deal for backs and dustboards. A walnut oyster box with a deal inside is correct. An English “oak coffer” that is deal throughout with oak graining is a different, later, and common object. Graining is a skill. It is also a disguise.
## 19th and 20th centuries
Steam-sawn Nordic pine became the whitewood of Europe’s factories. Thonet is beech; the packing crates were deal. IKEA’s ancestors are this forest: painted, stained, then foil-wrapped. The engineered chapter takes the foil. The tree under the early cheap furniture was still *Pinus* and *Picea*.
## Shop notes
Deal in old English houses can be wide and slow-grown — a grade you cannot buy new. Repair with the closest northern pine, not with southern yellow pine’s loud latewood, unless you want the patch to shout.
Knots in furniture-grade Baltic were once selected against. Knotty Nordic is a modern taste.
## Conservation
Boreal forestry is a climate and old-growth argument, not a CITES appendix. FSC and PEFC appear on Nordic pine for a reason. Antique deal is reuse. New “reclaimed Baltic pine” should have a story that is not a container of mixed softwood.
## What to look for
Paint layers, light weight, a London carcase, a Swedish grey cupboard, yellow/red deal in a joiner’s account. Graining that follows a fantasy oak. A spruce drawer bottom that is still bright after two hundred years in the dark.
The series splits pine into three chapters because a Connecticut blanket chest, a Savannah heart-pine floor, and a Stockholm painted cupboard are not one material. They share dents and paint. They do not share ports.
## Deal is a cargo word
English joiners said “deal” the way they said “wainscot”: a traded size and a quality, not a botanical mood. Adam Bowett’s work on furniture woods in London and the provinces is the place that keeps the two words from collapsing. Wainscot is oak — often slow-grown Baltic oak, radially split, the *wagenschot* cargo of Gdansk and the eastern ports. Deal is a sawn softwood board, often Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*) or spruce (*Picea abies*), shipped from Norway, Sweden, Finland, and the Russian Baltic. Different cargoes. Sometimes the same sea. Do not invent a named voyage or a price; the Sound Toll registers and later timber-auction records at the Zaan and in London are the paper trail (the KNOB and Haneca world of wainscot studies, with different manifests).
“Yellow deal” and “red deal” were color and port grades of pine. White deal was often spruce. A London cabinetmaker’s bill that says deal means the cheap, stable, imported board — the yellow-poplar of Britain. Gillows and other northern English firms bought Baltic oak and Baltic deals on the salt-and-cloth return voyages (Bowett, provincial woods). Furniture in Lancaster could be mahogany show and deal hide, or painted deal throughout. Floors, shop fittings, the carcases under walnut veneer, whole painted interiors: northern Europe that is not oak is, a great deal of the time, this wood with a brush on it.
Ports in the ordinary timber literature include Drammen and other Norwegian outlets, Gothenburg and Stockholm, Riga, and the Russian Baltic yards `[CITE NEEDED: pin a named cargo series to a year only when you have the register page]`. Albion’s naval-timber book is the strategic pair. Furniture shops lived on the joinery grade, not the mast.
## Pine, spruce, and a scraped edge
Scots pine in northern, slow-grown grades is an even, resinous, workable furniture pine, harder than *P. strobus* in many parcels. Spruce is lighter, less resinous, a painter’s friend and a soundboard wood. Both dent. Both take nails. Both move less than oak. FPL notes on Scots pine as an imported wood belong beside the domestic pine tables where the handbook tables them `[CITE NEEDED: confirm the imported-woods chapter entry in the bench copy of FPL-GTR-190]`.
Identification on a painted antique is a scraped edge and a resin-canal search. Do not scrape a museum piece. On a house-owned cupboard, a chip in the back tells you. Repair old English house-joinery with the closest northern pine, not with southern yellow pine’s loud latewood, unless you want the patch to shout. Knots in furniture-grade Baltic were once selected against. Knotty Nordic is a modern taste. Deal in old English houses can be wide and slow-grown — a grade you cannot buy new.
William-and-Mary and Georgian carcases: oak for strength, deal for backs and dustboards. A walnut oyster box with a deal inside is correct. An English “oak coffer” that is deal throughout with oak graining is a different, later, and common object. Graining is a skill. It is also a disguise.
## Paint as the species
Scandinavian and North German painted furniture — rosemaling, blue-grey Gustavian, the peasant cupboard — is a finish tradition on local and traded pine and spruce. The Gustavian pale grey of late-eighteenth-century Sweden is a classical fashion in paint, a Baltic answer to satinwood that does not need satinwood. Russian and Finnish painted work belongs here too. Museum catalogues in Stockholm and the Nordic collections are the object record.
English painted pine of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries — dressing tables, cheap chairs, later the “fancy chair” — used deal and beech and birch. Sheraton’s cheaper cousins lived here. The paint is linseed, milk, distemper, later industrial enamel. Lead in old layers. Overpaint is a palimpsest. Stripping a Gustavian cupboard to “natural pine” is a period error unless you like 1960s taste.
Steam-sawn Nordic pine became the whitewood of Europe’s factories. Thonet is beech; the packing crates were deal. IKEA’s ancestors are this forest: painted, stained, then foil-wrapped. The engineered chapter takes the foil. The tree under the early cheap furniture was still *Pinus* and *Picea*.
Boreal forestry is a climate and old-growth argument, not a CITES appendix. FSC and PEFC appear on Nordic pine for a reason. Antique deal is reuse. New “reclaimed Baltic pine” should have a story that is not a container of mixed softwood.
Look for paint layers, light weight, a London carcase, a Swedish grey cupboard, yellow or red deal in a joiner’s account. Graining that follows a fantasy oak. A spruce drawer bottom that is still bright after two hundred years in the dark. A Connecticut blanket chest, a Savannah heart-pine floor, and a Stockholm painted cupboard share dents and paint. They do not share ports.
A London joiner’s account that lists deals by the hundred is buying a size. Bowett’s provincial-woods essays keep that cargo language next to wainscot so a reader does not hear “pine” and “oak” as moods. Repair a dustboard with northern pine of similar ring and resin, not with a loud southern yellow-pine patch, unless the shout is the point. On a Gustavian grey cupboard, the paint is the fashion. The deal is the servant. Scrape a hidden edge if you must name the tree. Leave the show face alone.
## Sources
Bowett, provincial furniture woods (deal vs wainscot geography). KNOB wainscot/deal market literature. Albion. FPL notes on Scots pine as imported wood where tabled. Gustavian and Nordic museum catalogues. Hoadley.
See: `pine-country-furniture`, `heart-pine-longleaf`, `oak-european-and-american`, `walnut`.

item.title: Cedar
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Cedar
“Cedar” on a furniture label is a family reunion that invited strangers. A moth chest in Pennsylvania is usually eastern redcedar, *Juniperus virginiana*, a juniper with purple heartwood and a kitchen-spice smell. A Spanish colonial chest or a cigar-box lining may be *Cedrela odorata*, Spanish cedar, a Meliaceae cousin of mahogany, soft, fragrant, the wood Cuban cigar factories still want. A Pacific blanket chest may be western redcedar, *Thuja plicata*, a true thuja, light, durable, not a furniture show wood of the parlor kind. Three genera. One English word. This chapter keeps them in separate drawers.
## Eastern redcedar (*Juniperus virginiana*)
The *Wood Handbook* lists eastern redcedar around SG 0.47 and Janka 900 lbf — harder than you think for a “cedar,” a match for cherry’s neighborhood. Heartwood is dull red to purple-red; sapwood is cream and sharp. The odor is the point of the linen chest. Whether the volatiles still deter moths in a 40-year-old chest with a worn surface is a question shops over-claim `[CITE NEEDED: a current entomology note]`. Fresh heartwood is the traditional belief.
The wood is knotty. Clear grades are small. It is used for chests, closet lining, small boxes, pencils (the pencil trade also used incense-cedar, *Calocedrus*). It works easily, takes a polish, and will stain a damp shirt if the finish is thin.
American furniture: the cedar chest as a 19th- and 20th-century factory object (Lane and others) is a cultural form — dowry, storage, a smell. Earlier, small southern and Mid-Atlantic boxes. Not a Chippendale wood.
## Spanish cedar (*Cedrela odorata*)
Soft, mahogany-like grain, fragrant, the traditional lining of humidors and the secondary wood of some tropical and colonial furniture. It is in the mahogany family. It machines like a mild *Swietenia*. It is not durable in all grades the way teak is; it is durable enough for many interiors.
*Cedrela* species have moved onto CITES listings (populations and annotations have changed; check Species+ at publication — *C. odorata* has been App. III and subject to later uplisting proposals). A humidor factory and a furniture importer live under different paperwork than a Missouri redcedar mill.
Colonial Spanish and Portuguese furniture used *Cedrela* and related woods because they grew in the same empires as mahogany. English shops used it less as a show wood.
## Western redcedar (*Thuja plicata*)
SG about 0.32, Janka about 350 lbf — a true light, durable, outdoor and shingle wood. Furniture use is porch, garden, the occasional chest, contemporary outdoor benches. The odor is different from juniper. The hardness is not a table-top hardness unless you like dents.
## Other “cedars”
Aromatic “Spanish cedar” is not incense-cedar. White cedar (*Thuja occidentalis*) is a northern white, canoe and fence, almost no furniture. Port-Orford-cedar (*Chamaecyparis lawsoniana*) is a Pacific specialty, a Japanese-export wood, a boat wood. Yellow-cedar (*Callitropsis nootkatensis*) is another Pacific specialty. None of these should be sold as the Pennsylvania moth chest.
## Shop notes
Juniper dust and splinters irritate some people. The purple heart will fade in sun toward brown. A finish slows the smell and the fade; a chest meant to smell should not be plastic-coated inside.
Do not put a western redcedar outdoor bench finish on a juniper linen chest. Different jobs.
## Conservation
Eastern redcedar is a pasture invader in parts of the Midwest and a timber tree in others — not scarce. Spanish cedar is a tropical hardwood with a genuine harvest and permit story; look up the current appendix. Western redcedar old-growth is a Pacific conservation fight; second-growth and certified stock exist. The word “cedar” on an import invoice is not enough for Lacey. The binomial is required.
## What to look for
Smell, purple vs mahogany-tan vs chocolate-weathered grey. Knots in juniper. A cigar box. A Lane chest. A porch bench that is too light to be oak. A “cedar” dining table: ask which genus, then sit down.
Arkansas grows *Juniperus virginiana* on glades and old fields. A chest from that wood is a local object. It is not Spanish cedar and does not need to be. The series includes all three so a buyer can follow a nose to the right tree.
## A linen chest in a January room
Open a late-nineteenth-century Pennsylvania or Shenandoah Valley chest in January and the first fact is smell. Eastern redcedar heartwood carries a kitchen-spice note shops still sell as moth insurance. The *Wood Handbook* already put the species near specific gravity 0.47 and side hardness 900 lbf at 12 percent moisture — cherry’s neighborhood, not pine’s. That hardness is why a lid can take a sitting child and why a knot, left proud, will print a shirt.
The object is a household form before it is a timber form. Farm boxes in the Mid-Atlantic, factory Lane chests after the First World War (Altavista, Virginia, and the catalogues that followed), closet lining nailed over pine studs: American shops treated juniper as a smell and a color, not as a parlor show wood. Chippendale never asked for it. A joiner making a small box in 1840 did.
