The purple-red heart and the cream sapwood make a striped interior that owners learned to leave unfinished so the volatiles could move. A film finish inside a chest is a decision against that habit.
Knots are not defects in this wood; they are the tree. Eastern redcedar on glades and old fields is often limby. Clear cuttings are short. A shop that wants a clean lid glue-up is selecting, not milling a forest sawlog. Hoadley’s anatomy pages will show you a juniper, not a mahogany: no vessels, a distinct heart, a smell you can still get off a fresh pencil shaving if the pencil was the older incense-cedar trade (*Calocedrus decurrens*) rather than this one.
## Havana lining and the mahogany cousin
Kukachka’s imported-woods paper (FPL-125) and the *Wood Handbook*’s imported chapter treat *Cedrela* as a light, fragrant utility hardwood, not as a structural oak. Compiled Janka figures sit well below Honduran mahogany’s commonly cited 800 lbf; specific gravity is often given in the high 0.3s `[CITE NEEDED: the exact FPL or Kukachka row for *C. odorata*]`. It machines like a mild mahogany. Watch the softness on arrises. The fragrance is a selling point and a finishing complication; some film finishes trap it, some owners want it. It is not teak-durable in every grade. Interior work is the honest job.
Colonial Spanish and Portuguese furniture in the Caribbean and Brazil used *Cedrela* and related woods because they grew in the same empires as mahogany. English fashionable shops used it less as a show face. When it appears in a London or Philadelphia piece it is often a drawer lining, a cigar cabinet, or a later repair. Ports that handled it sat on the same sugar-and-log routes Bowett mapped for *Swietenia*: Kingston and the Spanish islands, then the continental entrepôts. Do not invent a particular ship. The customs category is the evidence, and a named port-book line that separates *Cedrela* from mahogany is still a research note `[CITE NEEDED]`.
*Cedrela* listings have moved. Populations have sat on Appendix III and have been the subject of later uplisting proposals. Species+ at publication is the living page. A Missouri redcedar mill and a furniture importer of tropical *Cedrela* do not share a legal file.
At the bench, *Cedrela* versus *Swietenia* is smell, softness, and a slightly more open, cedar-family fragrance rather than the flatter mahogany odor. A lens on an unseen rail still helps. A humidor that smells right and a dining table sold as “Spanish cedar” are not the same specification.
## Puget Sound boards and the porch
Old-growth *Thuja* on the British Columbia and Washington coasts is a conservation argument with its own literature. Second-growth and certified stock exist. A crate that says only “cedar” on an import invoice fails Lacey the same way a crate that says only “mahogany” fails it. The binomial is the specification.
Port-Orford-cedar (*Chamaecyparis lawsoniana*) left Coos Bay and related Pacific ports as a specialty: boat wood, a Japanese-export timber, a mill rarity after root disease cut the commercial forest `[CITE NEEDED: a dated note on *Phytophthora lateralis* and the Port-Orford trade]`. Yellow-cedar (*Callitropsis nootkatensis*) is another Pacific specialty. White cedar (*Thuja occidentalis*) is canoe-and-fence in the Northeast. None of these are the Pennsylvania moth chest. A shop that lumps them on a sales tag is selling a smell.
Western redcedar heartwood’s durability is a tropolone story in the wood-science literature — thujaplicins and related extractives that discourage fungi `[CITE NEEDED: the FPL durability class row and a named extractives paper]`. That chemistry is why a shingle lasts and why a garden bench can be left unfinished to go silver. It is not a reason to build a dining table and then be surprised by dents.
## How a shop works each genus
Juniper: glue is ordinary hide or PVA on clean, dry heart; knots want to be accepted or cut out, not filled and forgotten. *Cedrela*: treat it as a secondary mahogany. Sharp tools, modest feed, a finish chosen for the job (oil if you want smell; a film if you want a humidor that wipes clean). Watch end-grain checking on thin box sides. The wood will take a stain that makes it look more like *Swietenia* than it is. Refuse that trick on a piece you will later have to name. *Thuja*: fasteners should be stainless or bronze if the piece lives in weather. End grain drinks finish; the flats can look dry a week later. That is the wood, not a failed product.
Incense-cedar belongs in the pencil trade more than in the furniture rack. If a pencil and a hope chest share a word, they do not share a genus. A shop that keeps one bin labeled CEDAR will eventually sell the wrong tree to a careful customer. Three bins, three binomials.
## Movement, fade, and the shirt test
Eastern redcedar’s shrinkage numbers in the *Wood Handbook* are modest for a wood of its density; the practical movement problem is not a table top — it is a lid that was flatsawn through a knot and then hung over a heat register `[CITE NEEDED: the exact radial/tangential pair from FPL table 4–3 or 5–3 if you quote them]`. Spanish cedar, being a tropical hardwood of low density, is often well behaved in small boxes and less so if you treat a wide board as if it were quartersawn oak. Western redcedar moves, but the bigger outdoor failure is design that holds water against end grain.
Fade is a juniper fact. A chest left under a south window will lose the purple and keep the smell a little longer than the color. Owners who want the 1910 interior should keep the lid down. Owners who want a coffee-table top from a recycled chest should accept brown.
The shirt test is crude and useful: a damp cotton rag rubbed on unfinished juniper heart will often pick up color. *Cedrela* is less of a dye and more of a scent. *Thuja* can leave a tea-colored wet mark on stone. None of this is a laboratory ID. It is a shop habit that keeps the three words from collapsing.
A “cedar” dining table on a container invoice is still the question this chapter opened with. Ask which genus. Then sit down. The moth chest, the Havana box, and the porch bench can share a showroom wall. They should not share a species line.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (eastern redcedar; western redcedar; imported *Cedrela* notes). CITES Species+ (*Cedrela*). Hoadley. Cigar and humidor trade practice.
See: `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `cypress`, `cites-lacey-buying`, `pine-country-furniture`.

item.title: Cypress
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Cypress
Baldcypress (*Taxodium distichum*) stands in water and makes a furniture wood that southern shops used for pieces that had to live with damp: pie safes, cupboard bottoms, plantation shutters, the occasional chest, later a porch and garden furniture. The *Wood Handbook* puts baldcypress around SG 0.46 and Janka 510 lbf — soft, light, a cousin to the cedars in manners if not in family. Heartwood is brown to reddish, sometimes with a greasy look; it has a reputation for decay resistance that made it a tank, flume, and greenhouse wood as much as a parlor wood.
It is not the Italian cypress of graveyards (*Cupressus*). It is not the northern white-cedar. It is a deciduous conifer of the Mississippi valley, the Gulf Coast, and the drowned forests that salvage loggers still pull from river mud.
## The wood
Even, relatively straight, with a grain that can be plain or gently figured. Old-growth “sinker” cypress from river bottoms is darker, oilier, and sold as a precious grade. Second-growth is paler and milder. Pecky cypress — fungal pockets in the living tree — is a decorative salvage look, like wormy chestnut, with the same need for honesty.
Workability is easy. It planes, nails, takes paint. It can feel greasy to glue; wipe and use the right adhesive. Finish: oil on old heart is the current fashion; paint is the historic one for a lot of utility pieces.
The odor is mild, not juniper. The durability is the selling point for outdoor and wet-adjacent interiors. It is not teak. It will still weather grey and it will still fail if designed as a sponge.
## Southern furniture
Cypress appears in Hurst and Prown’s world as a secondary and sometimes primary wood: coastal and riverine shops, painted case work, pieces that sat on brick floors. New Orleans and the sugar-country houses used it because it grew there and because the climate punishes maple.
It never became a Federal show wood. Mahogany and walnut took those rooms. Cypress took the closet, the safe, the shutter, the cistern cover, then the Craftsman porch.
20th-century pecky cypress paneling is a Florida and Gulf fashion. Some of it is handsome. All of it is a fungus pattern, not a species you can plant for pecky on purpose in a short rotation.
## Sinker logs
Deadheads and buried logs in southern rivers are a real supply and a real regulation story (state ownership of submerged timber varies) `[CITE NEEDED: a specific state statute example]`. The wood can be spectacular. The ethics are: permits, not night diving, and no fairy tale about infinite sunken forests.
## Shop notes
Baldcypress and yellow-poplar can look similar in a painted piece. Weight and the softwood anatomy (no vessels) separate them. Cypress has no oak pores.
Outdoor cypress furniture wants design that drains, not a finish that claims immortality.
## Conservation
Old-growth baldcypress swamps are a conservation habitat (birds, water, the trees themselves). Furniture should prefer certified second-growth or documented sinker. Not CITES. Lacey still wants the right name on imports of “cypress” that may be other *Cupressaceae* from other continents.
Mexican and Central American “cypress” in trade may be *Cupressus* or mixed softwoods. Binomials.
## What to look for
A southern safe, a shutter, pecky paneling, a sinker slab with dark oil, light weight, soft dent, no vessels. A “cypress” dining set from a container: ask.
Arkansas grows baldcypress in the Delta and in wet bottoms. A shop that uses it is using a southern wet-site wood, not an Ozark oak. The series includes it so the hardwood belt is not the only southern story.
## A pie safe on a brick floor
Picture a coastal Louisiana or low-country cupboard standing on brick, summer air coming through a shutter, a pie safe with punched-tin panels and a soft brown case. Hurst and Prown’s southern furniture world is full of pieces that had to live with damp. Baldcypress (*Taxodium distichum*) took that job because it grew in the same climate that punished maple. New Orleans shops, river-town joiners, plantation outbuildings: the wood is a Gulf and Mississippi-valley fact, not a Federal show wood.
Mahogany and walnut took the polite rooms when they could be had. Cypress took the closet, the safe, the shutter, the cistern cover, then — much later — the Craftsman porch and the pecky paneling of a Florida room. A painted case from the sugar country may be cypress, yellow-poplar, or pine; weight and a lens decide. Cypress has no vessels. Poplar does. That single anatomical fact will save a restorer who was about to treat a cupboard as a hardwood and then wonder why the arris crushed.
The *Wood Handbook* already put baldcypress near specific gravity 0.46 and Janka 510 lbf — soft, light, a cousin to the cedars in manners if not in family. Heartwood is brown to reddish, sometimes with a greasy look. The durability reputation made it a tank, flume, and greenhouse wood as much as a parlor wood. Furniture inherited that reputation. It did not inherit teak’s silica or teak’s oil.
## Old growth, second growth, and pecky faces
Old-growth “sinker” cypress from river bottoms is darker, oilier, and sold as a precious grade. Second-growth is paler and milder. The difference is not a romance; it is ring width, extractives, and time in mud or water that excluded oxygen. Salvage loggers still pull deadheads from southern rivers. The wood can be spectacular. The ethics are permits, not night diving, and no fairy tale about infinite sunken forests.
State ownership of submerged timber varies. A Louisiana or Mississippi statute is the local law; this draft will not pretend one sentence covers the Gulf `[CITE NEEDED: a specific state statute example]`. A shop buying a slab should ask for the permit paper the way a tropical importer asks for a binomial. Existence of a log in a river is not title.
Pecky cypress is a fungal pocket pattern in the living tree, sold as a decorative salvage look, like wormy chestnut. You cannot plant a short-rotation stand and harvest pecky on a schedule. A 1950s Florida den paneled in pecky boards is a fashion. Some of it is handsome. All of it is a fungus, not a species you can order by the truckload from a nursery.
Workability is easy. It planes, nails, takes paint. It can feel greasy to glue; wipe and use the right adhesive. Finish: oil on old heart is the current fashion; paint is the historic one for a lot of utility pieces. The odor is mild, not juniper. Outdoor pieces want design that drains. A finish that claims immortality on a sponge-shaped bench is a label, not a wood.
## Anatomy against poplar, pine, and “cypress”
Baldcypress is a deciduous conifer. Under a hand lens you see earlywood and latewood, no pores, a softness that dents with a thumbnail more readily than white oak and less romantically than eastern white pine. Yellow-poplar (*Liriodendron*) in a painted piece can look similar in color once the paint is on. Weight, the vessel lines on an unseen edge, and the way a chisel crushes the end grain separate them. Pine shows resin canals; cypress does not, not in the pine sense.
Italian cypress (*Cupressus sempervirens*) is a graveyard and garden tree, not this wood. Mexican and Central American “cypress” in trade may be *Cupressus* or mixed softwoods. Northern white-cedar is *Thuja occidentalis*. A container dining set stamped CYPRESS is a binomial question. Lacey wants the right name. The series keeps this chapter so the hardwood belt is not the only southern story, and so a Gulf shutter is not sold as a Mediterranean tree.
Durability of baldcypress heartwood is real enough that the *Wood Handbook* and older naval-stores and tank literature treat it as a wet-service timber `[CITE NEEDED: the FPL durability class listing for baldcypress heartwood]`. Sapwood is another matter. A shop that uses a wide sap streak on a porch floor is building a shorter story than the heartwood catalogues promised.
## Southern shops, shutters, and the cistern
Hurst and Prown keep returning to secondary woods and to pieces that sat on brick. Cypress appears as a primary wood more often in coastal and riverine work than in Piedmont walnut country. Plantation shutters — louvered, painted, swollen in August — are a cypress job when the shop had the tree. So are cupboard bottoms that faced a damp floor, cistern covers, and later greenhouse benches. None of these objects needed a splat carved in the solid. They needed a board that would not sulk after a flood week.
20th-century pecky paneling and porch furniture pulled the wood into a Craftsman and then a Florida-resort vocabulary. Some contemporary outdoor furniture still specifies baldcypress. The honest comparison is white oak (tyloses, heavier) and western redcedar (lighter, different odor), not teak. A designer who wants teak’s outdoor manners in a domestic wet-site wood is looking at cypress or white oak, not at a stain called “cypress finish” on rubberwood.
Arkansas grows baldcypress in the Delta and in wet bottoms. A Bradley Brand shop that uses it is using a southern wet-site wood, not an Ozark oak. The rings will be second-growth unless the slab is a documented sinker. That is enough history for a porch bench. It is not enough history to call a container table cypress and stop.
## Working wet-site wood
Sharp tools, a light cut, nails that do not split the way oak splits. Glue: wipe the grease, then ordinary PVA or a polyurethane if the piece will see weather. Outdoor fasteners should be stainless or hot-dip; tannin-family stains are milder than oak’s but wet steel still leaves a mark `[CITE NEEDED: a measured extractives or fastener-stain note]`. End grain in old heart can look oily and still drink a first coat.
Paint was the historic finish for utility pieces because paint is a climate tool in the South. Oil on sinker heart is a late fashion that shows the grain and the grease. Neither finish will save a joint that holds water. Design the bench to drain; then choose a color.
If you restore a painted safe, do not strip to “find the cypress” unless the client has asked for a different object. The paint is often the period surface. If you must patch, match softness as well as color: a hard-maple dutchman in a cypress stile will read as a scar in a year.
Identification in a mixed southern cupboard is a lens and a weight test, not a romance of the swamp. No vessels, light weight, a soft dent, sometimes a greasy heart, sometimes pecky pockets. A “cypress” dining set from a container: ask. The drowned forest is finite. The word on the crate is not.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (baldcypress). Hurst and Prown. Hoadley. Sinker-log regulation `[CITE NEEDED]`.
See: `cedar`, `heart-pine-longleaf`, `yellow-poplar`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Mahogany and the substitutes
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Mahogany and the substitutes
Thomas Ripley told the Admiralty that mahogany would be cheaper than deal or wainscot if Navy ships brought it home (Bowett, *Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). That sentence still surprises people who were raised on Macquoid’s luxury. The Naval Stores Act of 1721, in force 1722, stripped the duty from British West Indian timber. Jamaica wood that had not been worth the freight became, in the port books, a furniture wood you could carve in the solid. The splat of a mid-century London chair is a tax story, a sugar-island story, and only then a style story.
## Three *Swietenia* and a crowd of names
*Swietenia mahagoni* — Cuban, Santo Domingo, West Indian — is the fine, often darker, tighter mahogany of the early trade and of the Spanish islands. Commercial sizes were exhausted early. *S. macrophylla* — Honduran, big-leaf, “genuine mahogany” in later trade — ranges from Mexico to the Amazon. The *Wood Handbook* describes American mahogany as pale pink to dark reddish brown, generally straighter than African *Khaya*, easy to dry, dimensionally stable, durable, easy to work, a premier veneer wood. Plantations exist. Wild old trees of furniture grade are a different market.
*S. humilis* is a Pacific-dry-forest species, listed and scarce.
Janka for Honduran mahogany is commonly cited near 800 lbf, SG near 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods chapter / Kukachka tradition). It is softer than white oak, kinder than maple, strong enough in the right section for a slender chair — the quality R. W. Symonds and others credited with English rococo (Bowett quotes and complicates this).
“African mahogany” is *Khaya*. Sapele, utile, sipo are *Entandrophragma*. Philippine “mahogany” was lauan/meranti. Spanish cedar is *Cedrela*. Toon is *Toona*. The substitutes chapter in the series (`african-mahogany-sapele-khaya`, `lauan-meranti-okoume`) picks them up. This chapter is the true *Swietenia* and the moment the word escaped the genus.
## Workability and finish
Mahogany planes, carves, and takes a moulding without oak’s pores or maple’s hardness. Crotch and curl are the show veneers. Ribbon stripe appears when the grain interlocks and the board is quartered — more famous later in sapele than in all *Swietenia*.
It finishes like a gift: oil, French polish, a film that looks deep. Old oxidized mahogany is brown; refinishers who sand to pink and then dye fire-engine red are making a 1900s dining-room idea, not an 1760 one.
Movement is modest for a tropical hardwood of this density. Wide tables still need to float.
## Jamaica, the Bay, and Cuba
Bowett’s thesis (*The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*) is the backbone: little evidence of a furniture trade before 1700; the 1660 Book of Rates lists other West Indian woods (ebony, lignum vitae, fustic) and not mahogany; after 1722 the values in the customs accounts jump. Jamaica dominated the early furniture supply. Honduras “bay-wood” became a large, cheaper, often coarser supply later in the century. Cuban and Hispaniola woods had quality reputations and Spanish-imperial politics. The 1795 duty schedules treated sources differently (Bowett, Jamaica/Gillow paper).
Gillow of Lancaster bought Jamaica wood as a provincial firm in a port world, not only as a London satellite. Chippendale’s *Director* (1754) assumes mahogany. Harewood House paid Chippendale with money that sat on West Indian estates — Bowett’s opening image. The chair and the plantation are the same economy.
Enslaved labor logged and milled. That belongs in the caption, not in a footnote the reader can skip.
## America
Coastal American shops used mahogany when they could get it: Newport, Philadelphia, Charleston, New York. Inland shops used walnut and cherry. A high chest with mahogany drawer fronts and poplar sides is the type. Later, Empire factories drowned the country in crotch mahogany veneer over pine and poplar.
20th-century “mahogany” suites are where the word breaks. *Khaya*, sapele, stained birch, printed lauan — see the other chapters.
## Conservation
Neotropical *S. macrophylla* went onto CITES Appendix II (decision 2002, in force 15 November 2003), annotation covering logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood (CITES press release 11 Nov. 2003). Finished furniture may fall outside that annotation; the sawn wood in the factory does not. *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* are also listed. Plantation mahogany exists; illegal wild mahogany also exists. TRAFFIC and Chatham House have tracked the trade.
U.S. Lacey Act (2008 amendment) makes illegally harvested plant product a crime regardless of the appendix. APHIS declarations now reach more furniture HTS codes (Phase VII, 1 Dec. 2024).
Buyers: Species+, a named country, a named species, a chain of custody. “Genuine mahogany” is an ad. *Swietenia macrophylla*, Guatemala, FSC, is a specification.
## What to look for
On an 18th-century chair: carved splat, oxidized brown, secondary wood of the region. On a Victorian table: redder finish, maybe still *Swietenia*. On a 1960s suite: probably not. On a new table: the invoice binomial. Ribbon that looks like sapele: read the sapele chapter.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A southern shop that wants that color in a domestic wood is looking at cherry after ten years of sun, or at walnut, or at a named African substitute with its own manners. The honest sentence is the species name.
## After 1722: a London splat and a Kingston log
Adam Bowett’s thesis (*The English Mahogany Trade 1700–1793*) is the backbone this chapter already named: little evidence of a furniture trade before 1700; the 1660 Book of Rates lists ebony, lignum vitae, and fustic, not mahogany; after the Naval Stores Act of 1721 — in force 1722 — the values in the customs accounts jump. Jamaica dominated the early furniture supply. Thomas Ripley, advising the Admiralty, called mahogany cheaper than deal or wainscot if Navy ships carried it freight-free (*Georgian Group Journal*, 1997). Macquoid’s 1733 and Cescinsky’s 1748 are connoisseur dates. The statute is the date.
A mid-century London chair with a carved splat in the solid is therefore a tax object before it is a style object. Chippendale’s *Director* (1754; third edition 1762) assumes mahogany. Gillow of Lancaster bought Jamaica wood as a provincial firm in a port world, not only as a London satellite (Bowett’s Jamaica/Gillow paper). Harewood House paid Chippendale with money that sat on West Indian estates — Bowett’s opening image. The chair and the plantation are the same economy. Enslaved labor logged and milled. That belongs in the caption.
Honduras “bay-wood” became a large, cheaper, often coarser supply later in the century. Cuban and Hispaniola woods had quality reputations and Spanish-imperial politics. The 1795 duty schedules treated sources differently (Bowett again). Do not invent a particular voyage or a price. The port books and the duty tables are the evidence; the splat is the residue.
*Swietenia mahagoni* — Cuban, Santo Domingo, West Indian — is the fine, often darker, tighter mahogany of the early trade. Commercial sizes were exhausted early. *S. macrophylla* — Honduran, big-leaf, “genuine mahogany” in later trade — ranges from Mexico to the Amazon. *S. humilis* is a Pacific-dry-forest species, listed and scarce. Plantations of *S. macrophylla* exist. Wild old trees of furniture grade are a different market.
## What the handbook measures
The *Wood Handbook* describes American mahogany as pale pink to dark reddish brown, generally straighter than African *Khaya*, easy to dry, dimensionally stable, durable, easy to work, a premier veneer wood. Janka for Honduran mahogany is commonly cited near 800 lbf, specific gravity near 0.45–0.50 (FPL imported-woods chapter / Kukachka FPL-125). It is softer than white oak, kinder than maple, strong enough in the right section for a slender chair — the quality R. W. Symonds and others credited with English rococo. Bowett quotes and complicates that credit. The wood made the carving possible. The duty cut made the wood ordinary enough to carve in the solid.
Movement is modest for a tropical hardwood of this density. Wide tables still need to float. Crotch and curl are the show veneers. Ribbon stripe appears when the grain interlocks and the board is quartered — more famous later in sapele than in all *Swietenia*. It finishes like a gift: oil, French polish, a film that looks deep. Old oxidized mahogany is brown. Refinishers who sand to pink and then dye fire-engine red are making a 1900s dining-room idea, not a 1760 one.
At the bench the plane likes mahogany. Moulding profiles stay crisp without oak’s pore and without maple’s fight. Interlock, when it appears, wants a scraper. Dust is milder than rosewood’s sensitizing dust, which is not a reason to skip collection. Glue is ordinary if the surface is clean; oily patches are less a teak problem than a finish-contamination problem.
## Newport, Philadelphia, Charleston, New York
Coastal American shops used mahogany when they could get it. Newport’s Townsend-Goddard circle, Philadelphia’s high-chest shops, Charleston’s humid rooms, New York’s later Empire factories: the secondary woods tell the town. A high chest with mahogany drawer fronts and yellow-poplar sides is the Mid-Atlantic type. A Charleston piece may hide cypress or pine where Philadelphia hid poplar. Inland shops used walnut and cherry because the log was local and the import was a coastal luxury.
Later, Empire and then factory suites drowned the country in crotch mahogany veneer over pine and poplar. That is still *Swietenia* when the face is true. It is already a substitute economy when the face is *Khaya*, sapele, stained birch, or printed lauan. The 20th-century stamp MAHOGANY is where the word breaks. See `african-mahogany-sapele-khaya` and `lauan-meranti-okoume`.
Bowett’s 18th-century Jamaica wood did not consent to those later names. Honest specification now is the binomial, the country, the cut. *Swietenia macrophylla*, Guatemala, FSC, quartersawn, is a specification. “Genuine mahogany” is an ad.
## 2003, Lacey, and the warehouse aisle
Neotropical *S. macrophylla* went onto CITES Appendix II (decision 2002, in force 15 November 2003), annotation covering logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood (CITES press release, 11 November 2003). Finished furniture may fall outside that annotation; the sawn wood in the factory does not. *S. mahagoni* and *S. humilis* are also listed. TRAFFIC and Chatham House have tracked the trade. Illegal wild mahogany exists beside legal plantation wood. Species+ is the living page.
The U.S. Lacey Act as amended in 2008 makes illegally harvested plant product a crime regardless of the appendix. APHIS declarations now reach more furniture HTS codes (Phase VII, 1 December 2024). A crate that says only MAHOGANY fails the declaration the way a crate that says only CEDAR fails it.
In a warehouse aisle the substitutes stand next to the true boards. *Khaya* is often a bit more interlocked, a staple of interwar and postwar case work. Sapele (*Entandrophragma cylindricum*) shows the ribbon that architects now mean when they say mahogany. Utile and sipo sit in the same genus confusion. Philippine “mahogany” was lauan. Spanish cedar is *Cedrela*. Toon is *Toona*. Santos mahogany is *Myroxylon*, denser, a different family. The client who wants a Chippendale splat should hear that sapele is harder to carve and historically wrong in species, even if the color sings.
Arkansas does not grow *Swietenia*. A southern shop that wants that color in a domestic wood is looking at cherry after ten years of sun, or at walnut, or at a named African substitute with its own manners. The honest sentence is still the species name. The 1721 Act made Jamaica wood cheap enough to carve. The 2003 listing made big-leaf mahogany a permit wood. Those two dates belong on the same shop wall.
## Sources
Bowett, thesis 1997; Ripley 1997; Jamaica/Gillow; RFS Naval Stores Act notes. Macquoid, *Age of Mahogany* (use as periodization, not as duty date — he said 1733). Chippendale, *Director*. USDA FPL imported woods. CITES 2003 mahogany release; Species+. USDA APHIS Lacey Phase VII. TRAFFIC/Chatham House five-taxa paper.
See: `african-mahogany-sapele-khaya`, `walnut`, `five-centuries-of-furniture-wood`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Teak
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Teak
Teak feels oily because it is. *Tectona grandis*, a ring-porous tree of India, Burma (Myanmar), Thailand, and the old East Indies, lays down a heartwood that the *Wood Handbook* describes as yellow-brown to golden brown, aging to a richer brown, coarse, usually straight, with excellent dimensional stability and a very high natural durability. Silica in the fiber dulls tools. The same heartwood does not corrode iron the way oak’s tannin does, which is why shipbuilders and the fittings on deck wanted it. Furniture wanted it for the same oil and for a color that mid-century Denmark turned into a world export.
## Numbers and manners
Density is on the order of American oak (FPL: properties “generally on par with those of U.S. oaks”). Janka commonly cited near 1,070 lbf, SG near 0.55–0.66 depending on source and plantation versus old-growth. Plantation teak can be lighter, paler, with wider rings and less oil. Old Burma teak is the folklore grade: tight, dark, greasy.
Workability: moderate, says FPL, with silica as the tax. Gluing and finishing may need the oil wiped back. Outdoor teak is often left unfinished to go silver; indoor teak in the 1950s was oiled to stay honey.
It is ring-porous. The face has a teak look — coarse pore, brown — that stain catalogues have chased onto other species for seventy years.
## Imperial furniture and the ship
Indian and Burmese teak was a British imperial timber: railways, harbors, the deck of a warship, the campaign chest that went to a hot station. Campaign furniture in mahogany and teak is a military-administrative style: brass corners, knockdown fittings, a wood that would not sulk in a hold. Dutch colonial furniture in Java used teak because the tree was there (and planted). Chinese shops in Southeast Asia used it. The furniture is older than Danish modern. Danish modern is why most buyers can spell the word.
Burmese teak extraction is a political and military story as well as a forest one. Later sanctions and logging bans belong in a buying note, not in a romance of the deck chair `[CITE NEEDED: a dated sanctions/logging-ban reference at publication]`.
## Danish modern and the suburb
After 1945, Danish and other Scandinavian designers used teak for dining chairs, sideboards, and the low tables that still fill estate sales. Finn Juhl, Arne Vodder, a hundred factories. Some of the best is solid; much is veneer on cheaper cores. The Danish-modern chapter returns to the mix with oak and rosewood. Teak was the tropical member of that triad.
American suburban “teak” of the 1960s includes true *Tectona*, and also print, and also other brown ring-porous woods. A lens on an unseen rail.
Outdoor furniture in the late 20th century made plantation teak a garden staple. The grey bench in the rain is doing what the wood does. Oil is a look, not a duty.
## Shop notes
Wipe with solvent before glue if the joint is oily. Sharp carbide. Stainless or bronze fasteners outdoors; teak and cheap steel can still make stains even if the wood is kinder than oak.
Sanding dust is an irritant for some people. So is the oil.
Do not strip a 1950s oiled teak sideboard and paint it without a long thought. The finish and the wood were a pair.
## Conservation
*Tectona grandis* is not a CITES appendix species in the rosewood sense; some populations and some export regimes are tightly controlled, and illegal logging in Southeast Asia is documented. Plantation teak in Africa and Latin America is a real supply (FPL already noted plantations). FSC and national export papers matter. “Burma teak” as a sales name should come with a legal path or be treated as a story.
Substitutes: iroko (*Milicia*), sometimes sold as “African teak,” is the next chapter. It is not *Tectona*.
## What to look for
Oil, ring-porous brown, silica-blunted planes in a shop, a campaign chest, a 1958 sideboard, a grey garden bench, a plantation board with wide rings. A “teak finish” on rubberwood: a stain.
Arkansas does not grow teak. A designer who wants teak’s outdoor manners in a domestic hardwood is looking at white oak or cypress, not at a stain. A designer who wants the 1960s interior color is looking at a named *Tectona* with papers, or at walnut, or at an honest iroko.
## Deck, campaign chest, and the imperial mill
*Tectona grandis* is a ring-porous tree of India, Burma (Myanmar), Thailand, and the old East Indies. British imperial timber practice wanted it for railways, harbors, and the deck of a warship because the heartwood does not corrode iron the way oak’s tannin does, and because the *Wood Handbook* still describes excellent dimensional stability and a very high natural durability. Furniture inherited those manners. Campaign chests with brass corners and knockdown fittings used mahogany and teak as woods that would not sulk in a hold. Dutch colonial furniture in Java used teak because the tree was there (and planted). Chinese shops in Southeast Asia used it. The furniture is older than Danish modern. Danish modern is why most buyers can spell the word.
Burmese teak extraction is a political and military story as well as a forest one. Later sanctions and logging bans belong in a buying note, not in a romance of the deck chair `[CITE NEEDED: a dated sanctions/logging-ban reference at publication]`. Do not invent a particular clipper or a price. The species, the colony, and the mill are enough history for a caption.
Silica in the fiber dulls tools. That is the shop tax FPL names when it calls workability moderate. The same silica is why a plane iron that just finished a cherry job will feel tired after twenty feet of teak. Carbide helps. So does accepting that teak is not mahogany under the iron.
## Numbers, plantation rings, and oil
Density is on the order of American oak (FPL: properties “generally on par with those of U.S. oaks”). Janka is commonly cited near 1,070 lbf, specific gravity near 0.55–0.66 depending on source and plantation versus old-growth. Plantation teak can be lighter, paler, with wider rings and less oil. Old Burma teak is the folklore grade: tight, dark, greasy. The folklore is not a permit.
The face is coarse-pored and brown. Stain catalogues have chased that look onto other species for seventy years. Rubberwood (*Hevea*) with a toner is an indoor plantation wood, not outdoor teak. Iroko (*Milicia*) is the next chapter: African, durable, sold as “African teak,” not *Tectona*. Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*) is a closer visual cousin and already CITES Appendix II. White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood of the tyloses story. It does not look like teak. It lasts if designed to drain.
Gluing and finishing may need the oil wiped back. Outdoor teak is often left unfinished to go silver; indoor teak in the 1950s was oiled to stay honey. Oil is a look, not a duty. A grey garden bench in the rain is doing what the wood does.
## Finn Juhl’s chair and the suburban sideboard
After 1945, Danish and other Scandinavian designers used teak for dining chairs, sideboards, and the low tables that still fill estate sales. Finn Juhl, Arne Vodder, a hundred factories. Some of the best is solid; much is veneer on cheaper cores. The Danish-modern chapter in this series returns to the mix with oak and rosewood. Teak was the tropical member of that triad.
American suburban “teak” of the 1960s includes true *Tectona*, and also print, and also other brown ring-porous woods. A lens on an unseen rail. A 1958 sideboard with an oiled face and a teak smell in a fresh scratch is one object. A 1968 suite with a printed grain that dies at the edge is another. Do not strip the first and paint it without a long thought. The finish and the wood were a pair.
Late-century garden furniture made plantation teak a patio staple — Africa and Latin America as well as Southeast Asia (FPL already noted plantations). FSC and national export papers matter. “Burma teak” as a sales name should come with a legal path or be treated as a story. *Tectona grandis* is not a CITES appendix species in the rosewood sense; some populations and some export regimes are tightly controlled, and illegal logging in Southeast Asia is documented `[CITE NEEDED: a named TRAFFIC or national-export note at publication]`. Lacey still wants the binomial and the harvest country.
## Working an oily, siliceous board
Wipe with solvent before glue if the joint is oily. Sharp carbide. Stainless or bronze fasteners outdoors; teak and cheap steel can still make stains even if the wood is kinder than oak. Sanding dust is an irritant for some people. So is the oil. Collection is not optional in a small shop.
Indoor oil finishes want maintenance the way a cutting board wants maintenance. A film finish is possible if the oil is cut back; it is a different object than a 1950s Danish piece. Outdoor design that traps water against end grain will fail in teak as surely as in oak. The durability is the heartwood’s, not the joint’s.
At the bench, ring-porous brown plus a greasy feel plus a blunted iron is the working ID. Smell is milder than juniper, not the kitchen-spice of eastern redcedar. Weight is oak’s neighbor, not western redcedar’s. A plantation board with wide rings is still *Tectona* if the anatomy agrees; it is not “Burma grade” because the tag says so.
Arkansas does not grow teak. A designer who wants teak’s outdoor manners in a domestic hardwood is looking at white oak or cypress, not at a stain. A designer who wants the 1960s interior color is looking at a named *Tectona* with papers, or at walnut, or at an honest iroko. The campaign chest and the Juhl chair share a species. They do not share a century, a port, or a finish schedule. Name the tree. Then decide whether the job is a deck, a sideboard, or a wish.
## Sources
USDA FPL, *Wood Handbook*, FPL-GTR-190 (teak). Kukachka FPL-125. Danish modern surveys (Fiell; museum collections). Campaign-furniture catalogues `[CITE NEEDED]`. CITES (negative: not listed as *Dalbergia* is); national Myanmar/Indonesia export rules `[CITE NEEDED]`.
See: `danish-modern-woods`, `iroko-teak-lookalikes`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Rosewood, ebony, and CITES
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Rosewood, ebony, and CITES
A piano from 1880 with a Brazilian rosewood case is a legal object in a living room and a paperwork object if you ship it across a border. *Dalbergia nigra* sits on CITES Appendix I. The rest of the rosewoods — the whole genus *Dalbergia* — went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, with Annotation #15 later revised so that finished musical instruments and small finished products (under a weight cap) would not freeze the concert hall (Taylor Guitars’ summary of the annotation; CITES notifications). Furniture, especially new furniture in sawn rosewood, is why the genus was listed. This chapter is species behavior and a trade history that ends in a permit.
## Rosewoods (*Dalbergia*)
Brazilian rosewood (*D. nigra*, jacaranda da Bahia) is the dark, fragrant, violet-brown wood of high Victorian pianos, of some French and English cabinet work, and of a forest in the Brazilian Atlantic that Warren Dean wrote as a destruction story. Appendix I: commercial trade in wild specimens is effectively shut.
East Indian rosewood (*D. latifolia*) is the other historic furniture and instrument wood: slightly more even, still a true palisander. Cocobolo (*D. retusa*), Honduras rosewood, Madagascar rosewoods, kingwood and tulipwood (separate chapter, same genus) — the family is a palette of dense, oily, colorful hardwoods.
Hardness is high; densities often above 0.8–1.0. They dull tools, they can be oily to glue, they take a polish that looks like stone. Dust is a sensitizer. Shop hygiene is not optional.
Worked as veneer more than as solid table tops, except in small pieces and in some mid-century Danish work (the Danish chapter). Solid rosewood dining tables that are truly *Dalbergia* are heavy, expensive, and now legally loud.
## Ebonies (*Diospyros*)
True ebonies are *Diospyros*: Ceylon ebony (*D. ebenum*), African ebonies including Gabon (*D. crassiflora*), Macassar (*D. celebica*) with its striped brown-black. They are the black of piano keys (when they were wood), of 17th-century cabinets, of Boulle’s counterpart to brass, of Art Deco accents. Madagascar *Diospyros* populations have been listed (CoP16 and after). Check Species+.
Much “ebony” furniture is ebonized pear, maple, or beech — a black stain or paint. That is a historic finish, not a fraud, if named. Victorian ebonized furniture is often a finish. A solid Gabon ebony chest would be a monster of weight and money.
## Furniture history
Ebony cabinets of the 17th century, Antwerp and Paris, are a luxury trade. Rosewood in English Regency and French Empire is a show veneer. Victorian parlor sets and pianos ate Brazilian rosewood in quantity. Art Deco used Macassar and other striped ebonies as a modern luxury.
Danish modern used rosewood for a smaller, sharper luxury than teak: a sideboard that was meant to look rare. After the 2017 listing, those pieces became more complicated to export. Owners of vintage *Dalbergia* furniture should learn the permit path before they sell abroad.
Colonial extraction — Brazil, India, Madagascar, West Africa — is the supply story. Enslaved and coerced labor sits in parts of that history as it does in mahogany. Do not tell the piano as a European object only.
## Substitutes
Walnut can look like a tired rosewood. Bubinga (*Guibourtia*, some species also listed with Annotation #15) was a stand-in. Wenge, stained oak, printed foil. The eye is easy to fool in a dark room. A lens and a weight test help. A lab test is what a customs officer may want.
## Shop notes
Do not machine rosewood without dust collection. Do not wash oily boards and then complain about glue. Do not refinish an Appendix I piano case as a casual weekend.
Repair with the same species is a permit question when the patch is imported. Repair with walnut or dyed pear is how shops have always faked a missing moulding.
## The law, short
- Appendix I: *D. nigra* (and other I species). Commercial new trade from the wild is not a furniture plan. - Appendix II: *Dalbergia* spp. (except I), with Annotation #15 as revised — finished musical instruments exempt; finished products under 10 kg of the listed wood per shipment exempt; sawn wood and veneer for furniture factories are not a casual import. - Madagascar ebonies and rosewoods: extra scrutiny, documented illegal trade. - U.S. Lacey Act sits on top: illegal under the source country’s law is illegal here. - Species+ and the national Management Authority are the living references. This draft is not a permit.
## What to look for
Smell (many *Dalbergia* are fragrant when cut), weight, pore, a piano, a 1960s Danish sideboard, ebonized vs ebony (look at a chip). A new “rosewood suite” from an unnamed exporter: walk away unless the papers are boringly complete.
Arkansas does not grow *Dalbergia*. The local dark hard woods are walnut and locust. They will not be rosewood. They do not need to be. The series includes this chapter so a buyer can enjoy an old piano and not commission a new one from a genus that is now a legal third rail.
## A piano case and a Bahia forest
A parlor piano from 1880 with a Brazilian rosewood case is a legal object in a living room and a paperwork object if you ship it across a border. *Dalbergia nigra* — jacaranda da Bahia — is the dark, fragrant, violet-brown wood of high Victorian pianos, of some French and English cabinet work, and of a forest in the Brazilian Atlantic that Warren Dean wrote as a destruction story (*With Broadax and Firebrand*). Appendix I: commercial trade in wild specimens is effectively shut.
The rest of the rosewoods — the whole genus *Dalbergia* — went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, with Annotation #15 later revised so that finished musical instruments and small finished products (under a weight cap, commonly described as 10 kg of the listed wood per shipment) would not freeze the concert hall (Taylor Guitars’ summary of the annotation; CITES notifications; verify against Species+). Furniture, especially new furniture in sawn rosewood, is why the genus was listed. A dining table is not a jewelry box.
East Indian rosewood (*D. latifolia*) is the other historic furniture and instrument wood: slightly more even, still a true palisander. Cocobolo (*D. retusa*), Honduras rosewood, Madagascar rosewoods, kingwood and tulipwood (separate chapter, same genus) — the family is a palette of dense, oily, colorful hardwoods. Hardness is high; densities often above 0.8–1.0. They dull tools, they can be oily to glue, they take a polish that looks like stone. Dust is a sensitizer. Shop hygiene is not optional.
Dean’s Atlantic-forest history is the ecological background for *D. nigra*. It is not a caption you can skip because the piano is pretty. Colonial extraction — Brazil, India, Madagascar, West Africa — is the supply story. Enslaved and coerced labor sits in parts of that history as it does in mahogany. Do not tell the piano as a European object only.
## Ebony cabinets, Boulle, and the black that is a finish
True ebonies are *Diospyros*: Ceylon ebony (*D. ebenum*), African ebonies including Gabon (*D. crassiflora*), Macassar (*D. celebica*) with its striped brown-black. They are the black of piano keys when the keys were wood, of 17th-century cabinets, of Boulle’s counterpart to brass, of Art Deco accents. The Wallace Collection’s Boulle pieces are the place to see brass and turtle and ebony in the same Paris luxury that later used kingwood as a leaf. Madagascar *Diospyros* populations have been listed (CoP16 and after). Check Species+.
Much “ebony” furniture is ebonized pear, maple, or beech — a black stain or paint. That is a historic finish, not a fraud, if named. Victorian ebonized furniture is often a finish. A solid Gabon ebony chest would be a monster of weight and money. Look at a chip. If the black is a skin, you have a finish. If the black goes through a dense, fine pore and the piece weighs like stone, you may have *Diospyros*. A lab test is what a customs officer may want.
Art Deco used Macassar and other striped ebonies as a modern luxury: a cabinet face, a clock case, an accent, not a farm table. English Regency and French Empire used rosewood as a show veneer. Danish modern used rosewood for a smaller, sharper luxury than teak: a sideboard that was meant to look rare. After the 2017 listing, those pieces became more complicated to export. Owners of vintage *Dalbergia* furniture should learn the permit path before they sell abroad.
## How a shop cuts an oily, listed wood
Do not machine rosewood without dust collection. The sensitizing dust is a known shop hazard; some people do not get a second chance at a first exposure `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`. Do not wash oily boards and then complain about glue. Wipe, then glue, then clamp longer than your mahogany habit. A scraper often beats a plane on interlock and on the polish the wood wants.
Do not refinish an Appendix I piano case as a casual weekend. The finish is part of the object’s legal and market identity; stripping it to “brighten the rosewood” is how a living-room piano becomes a different, lesser thing. Repair with the same species is a permit question when the patch is imported. Repair with walnut or dyed pear is how shops have always faked a missing moulding. Name the repair.
Solid rosewood dining tables that are truly *Dalbergia* are heavy, expensive, and now legally loud. Veneer was the historic furniture use more than solid tops, except in small pieces and in some mid-century Danish work. A new “rosewood suite” from an unnamed exporter is a walk-away unless the papers are boringly complete.
Walnut can look like a tired rosewood in a dark room. Bubinga (*Guibourtia*, some species also listed with Annotation #15) was a stand-in. Wenge, stained oak, printed foil. Weight, pore, and a fresh scratch smell (many *Dalbergia* are fragrant when cut) help. They do not replace a binomial on an invoice.
## The law in furniture language
Appendix I: *D. nigra* (and other I species). Commercial new trade from the wild is not a furniture plan.
Appendix II: *Dalbergia* spp. (except I), with Annotation #15 as revised — finished musical instruments exempt; finished products under the weight cap exempt; sawn wood and veneer for furniture factories are not a casual import.
Madagascar ebonies and rosewoods: extra scrutiny, documented illegal trade.
U.S. Lacey Act sits on top: illegal under the source country’s law is illegal here. APHIS Phase VII (1 December 2024) reaches more furniture codes. Species+ and the national Management Authority are the living references. This draft is not a permit.
Antique *Dalbergia* pieces already in the country are usually legal to own. They can be complicated to export. Ask before you ship a 1960s Danish sideboard. Appendix I objects are the sharpest case.
Arkansas does not grow *Dalbergia*. The local dark hard woods are walnut and locust. They will not be rosewood. They do not need to be. The series includes this chapter so a buyer can enjoy an old piano and not commission a new one from a genus that is now a legal third rail. The smell in a fresh kerf is a pleasure. The permit is the price of that pleasure crossing a border.
## Sources
CITES appendices and Annotation #15 (CoP17, CoP18 revisions; 2023+ notifications). CITES / TRAFFIC rosewood trade analyses. USFWS timber pages. Taylor Guitars CITES note (useful on annotations; verify against Species+). Dean, *With Broadax and Firebrand*. Wallace Collection / Boulle context. Danish modern catalogues.
See: `kingwood-tulipwood-ebeniste`, `danish-modern-woods`, `cites-lacey-buying`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`.

item.title: Satinwood
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Satinwood
Macquoid’s fourth age, from about 1770, is named for a yellow wood that takes a polish like a dry silk. Hepplewhite and Sheraton plates assume it: card tables, satinwood commodes, painted decoration on a golden ground, harewood and rosewood as the neighbours. Two trees, not one, carried the name. West Indian satinwood (*Zanthoxylum flavum*) was the earlier prize, a Caribbean citrus-family wood that was cut until it became a rumor. East Indian satinwood (*Chloroxylon swietenia*), from southern India and Sri Lanka, took the trade in the 19th century. They are not the same genus. They are both hard, lustrous, and yellow when the finish is kind.
## Two anatomies
Eric Meier’s Wood Database comparison (secondary, but careful) notes similar pore sizes and a useful tell: East Indian satinwood often shows ripple marks from storied rays; West Indian does not, and looks slightly freckled. Both sit in Rutaceae. Density is high relative to the later “satinwoods” of the plywood age (avodiré, movingui, obeche), which are lighter and were sold into the name.
Hardness is in the maple-and-above class `[CITE NEEDED: FPL or Kukachka numbers for both species]`. They work with a brittle, sometimes interlocked grain. They take a polish that is the point of the fashion. They were used mostly as veneer because the logs were not American-walnut generous.
*Chloroxylon swietenia* is IUCN Vulnerable (Asian Regional Workshop, 1998, still widely cited). *Z. flavum* is scarce in commercial sizes. Neither is a kitchen-island wood.
## Fashion
The English neoclassical shop — Adams’ interiors, Hepplewhite’s *Guide* (1788), Sheraton’s *Drawing-Book* (1793) — wanted pale, bright, classical. Satinwood did what gilding did, with grain. Painted swags sat on it. Marquetry sat in it. A whole commode in satinwood veneer is a luxury of the 1780s–1810s.
French taste used lighter woods in the late Louis XVI and Directoire years; satinwood appears, and so do other yellows. American Federal shops used satinwood when they could import it, and figured maple when they could not. A Connecticut piece with maple inlay is often a satinwood wish.
Victorian and Edwardian revivals brought satinwood back in display cabinets and Sheraton-revival desks. Some of that is *Chloroxylon*. Some is a dyed pale hardwood. A lens.
## Substitutes and the word
Avodiré (*Turraeanthus*), movingui (*Distemonanthus*), limba, even yellow birch with a toner — the 20th century sold “satinwood” as a color. Meier’s “Sorting Out Satinwoods” is the practical key. If the piece is not at least mid-19th-century and of quality, East Indian is the likelier true wood; if it is 1785 and English court-quality, West Indian is the romance and sometimes the fact.
## Shop notes
Old satinwood veneer is thin and brittle. It fades. A sun-bleached satinwood table looks like sad maple. Keep it out of the blast, or accept the fade.
Do not sand through a painted Sheraton panel to “find the satinwood.” The paint is the design.
## Conservation
*Chloroxylon* is vulnerable because it was good. *Z. flavum* was island-cut. Check CITES and IUCN at publication; listings move. New satinwood furniture is a specialist and permit question. Antique satinwood is the ethical supply for anyone who is not a museum.
Lacey still wants the name on a new import. “Satinwood” is not a binomial.
## What to look for
Yellow lustre, ripple or freckle, a 1790 card table, painted decoration, harewood beside it. A 1930s “satinwood” bedroom: maybe avodiré. A new yellow veneer: ask.
Arkansas has no satinwood tree. The Federal substitute on this continent was always maple. That is a complete sentence for a designer who likes the pale classical room and does not want a Vulnerable citrus-family log.
## A card table in a pale room
Macquoid’s fourth age, from about 1770, is named for a yellow wood that takes a polish like dry silk. A Hepplewhite or Sheraton card table — satinwood veneer, perhaps a harewood border, painted swags on a golden ground — is the object that taught English fashionable rooms to go pale after mahogany’s brown decades. Hepplewhite’s *Guide* (1788) and Sheraton’s *Drawing-Book* (1793) assume the color. The Adams’ interiors wanted classical light. Satinwood did what gilding did, with grain.
Two trees, not one, carried the name. West Indian satinwood (*Zanthoxylum flavum*) was the earlier prize, a Caribbean citrus-family wood that was cut until it became a rumor. East Indian satinwood (*Chloroxylon swietenia*), from southern India and Sri Lanka, took the trade in the 19th century. They are not the same genus. They are both hard, lustrous, and yellow when the finish is kind. They were used mostly as veneer because the logs were not American-walnut generous.
French taste used lighter woods in the late Louis XVI and Directoire years; satinwood appears, and so do other yellows. American Federal shops used satinwood when they could import it, and figured maple when they could not. A Connecticut piece with maple inlay is often a satinwood wish. That wish is a complete design history. It does not require a Vulnerable log.
Victorian and Edwardian revivals brought satinwood back in display cabinets and Sheraton-revival desks. Some of that is *Chloroxylon*. Some is a dyed pale hardwood. A lens.
## Two anatomies and a plywood-age crowd
Eric Meier’s Wood Database comparison (secondary, but careful) notes similar pore sizes and a useful tell: East Indian satinwood often shows ripple marks from storied rays; West Indian does not, and looks slightly freckled. Both sit in Rutaceae. Density is high relative to the later “satinwoods” of the plywood age — avodiré (*Turraeanthus*), movingui (*Distemonanthus*), obeche — which are lighter and were sold into the name.
Hardness is in the maple-and-above class `[CITE NEEDED: FPL or Kukachka numbers for both species]`. They work with a brittle, sometimes interlocked grain. They take a polish that is the point of the fashion. *Chloroxylon swietenia* is IUCN Vulnerable (Asian Regional Workshop, 1998, still widely cited). *Z. flavum* is scarce in commercial sizes. Neither is a kitchen-island wood.
Meier’s “Sorting Out Satinwoods” is the practical key for a 20th-century tag. If the piece is not at least mid-19th-century and of quality, East Indian is the likelier true wood; if it is 1785 and English court-quality, West Indian is the romance and sometimes the fact. Avodiré, movingui, limba, even yellow birch with a toner — the last century sold “satinwood” as a color. A 1930s bedroom suite in “satinwood” is often that color, not *Zanthoxylum*.
Harewood — sycamore or maple stained a grey-green — sat beside satinwood in the same neoclassical palette. Rosewood sat as the dark neighbour. The marquetry chapter in this series is the picture-making version of that palette. A whole commode in satinwood veneer is a luxury of the 1780s–1810s. A painted Sheraton panel is a design; do not sand through the paint to “find the satinwood.”
## Ports, islands, and the later mill
West Indian satinwood came from the same Caribbean basin that sent mahogany, in smaller quantities and for a different fashion. Do not invent a particular packet or a price. The species and the islands are the facts; a named customs line that separates *Zanthoxylum* from *Swietenia* is still a research note `[CITE NEEDED]`. East Indian satinwood rode the later imperial timber trade from southern India and Ceylon (Sri Lanka) into Victorian and Edwardian shops that wanted a Sheraton revival and had exhausted the island prize.
Check CITES and IUCN at publication; listings move. New satinwood furniture is a specialist and permit question. Antique satinwood is the ethical supply for anyone who is not a museum. Lacey still wants the name on a new import. “Satinwood” is not a binomial.
At the bench the wood is brittle compared with mahogany. Thin old veneer chips. Sun fades the yellow toward a sad maple. Keep a card table out of the blast, or accept the fade. A polish that looks like dry silk is the historic point; a thick plastic film is a different object.
## Federal maple and the Arkansas sentence
American Federal shops solved the pale-room problem with what they had. Figured maple — tiger, bird’s-eye, a quiet curl — did the satinwood job in Connecticut, Massachusetts, and the Mid-Atlantic when the imported leaf was scarce or dear. Holly and a little imported exotic turned up as inlay. The object is still Federal. The wood is not a failed satinwood. It is the continental answer.
Biedermeier shops in the German-speaking lands made a virtue of pale birch, pear, and cherry after the Napoleonic wars. That is another pale-room tradition, not Macquoid’s Age of Satinwood, and it has its own chapter. A designer who likes classical light has more than one tree.
Arkansas has no satinwood tree. The Federal substitute on this continent was always maple. That is a complete sentence for a designer who likes the pale classical room and does not want a Vulnerable citrus-family log. Specify *Acer saccharum*, or an antique *Chloroxylon* piece already in the country, or a named modern yellow — avodiré, maple, a dyed pear — with the name on the invoice. A new “satinwood” kitchen from an unnamed mill is a color. Ask which genus. Then look at the ripple, the freckle, or the missing both.
A Sheraton-revival display cabinet of 1905 may still be *Chloroxylon* veneer over a deal or oak carcase; a 1930s bedroom in the same yellow is likelier avodiré or a toner. The date on the piece is half the identification. The other half is the ray ripple under a raking light.
## Sources
Macquoid, *Age of Satinwood*. Hepplewhite; Sheraton. Wood Database, “Sorting Out Satinwoods”; *Chloroxylon* / *Zanthoxylum* pages. IUCN *C. swietenia*. Federal furniture literature (maple as substitute).
See: `sycamore`, `maple`, `biedermeier-pale-woods`, `marquetry-picture-of-trees`.

item.title: Kingwood, tulipwood, and the ébéniste
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Kingwood, tulipwood, and the ébéniste
Paris in the 17th and 18th centuries bought color by the leaf. The men who glued those leaves were *ébénistes* — the name from ebony, the job from a whole tropical palette. Kingwood (*Dalbergia cearensis*), once “princes wood,” is a violet-brown striped Brazilian rosewood of small dimension, almost only an inlay and banding wood. Tulipwood (*D. decipularis*, *D. frutescens*, and the trade’s overlapping names) is pink and yellow and loud. Together with bois de rose, violetwood, holly, box, stained sycamore, and pewter or brass, they made furniture that was a picture. The Wallace Collection’s Riesener notes are the place to see how many pieces of veneer sit in a single flower.
This chapter is the ébéniste’s palette, not a dining-table species. The marquetry chapter is the technique. The rosewood/CITES chapter is the law. Read the three together.
## Kingwood
Restricted to a small Brazilian range, *D. cearensis* is dense, hard, fine-striped, spectacular under a polish, and available only in small sizes (the old encyclopedias and the trade agree). Seventeenth-century Paris used it when it was the most expensive furniture wood in general use — the “princes wood” of the inventories. It turns for small objects. It blunts tools. It is a banding on a secrétaire, not a carcase.
## Tulipwood
Not *Liriodendron*. The Brazilian *Dalbergia* tulipwoods are streaked pink-cream, used for parquetry grounds, for small boxes, for the loudest edges on a Louis XV piece. They are still rosewoods in the legal sense. Appendix II, Annotation #15. Small finished objects may fall under the weight exemption; a factory’s sawn stock does not.
## The shop
André-Jacob Roubo’s *L’Art du menuisier* (1769–75) is the period encyclopedia of the French wood shop. Jean-Henri Riesener’s pictorial marquetry for the French crown is the high-water mark: sand-shaded edges, engraved detail, mastics, a palette that has since faded to brown (Wallace Collection). When new, the furniture was a garden. Time and light ate the dyes and some of the natural pinks.
Boulle work is brass and turtle and ebony more than kingwood; it belongs in the same Paris. German and English shops imported the taste and the woods. English seaweed marquetry of the 1690s is a related, quieter cousin, often in walnut and holly.
## America
Federal inlay used holly, maple, cherry, and a little imported exotic. It is not Riesener. A Baltimore painted-and-inlaid table is a different school. Southern and New England shops did not keep kingwood in the rack.
## Shop notes
These woods are oily, hard, and small. They are also listed. A restorer replacing a lost band should document the antique source of the scrap or use a legal substitute (dyed pear, walnut, a documented old piece). Do not order a new log of *D. cearensis* as if it were walnut.
Faded marquetry should not be “brought back” with aniline on a guess. Conservators photograph, then stop.
## Conservation
All *Dalbergia*: CITES as in the rosewood chapter. Brazilian Atlantic forest history (Dean) is the ecological background. New kingwood and tulipwood furniture is a luxury that now has to justify itself on paper. Antique Paris furniture is the museum and the market that already exists.
## What to look for
Violet stripes in a 3 mm band. Pink parquetry. A Riesener flower that is now brown. A small Brazilian box. A “tulipwood” American chest that is poplar: the other tulip.
Arkansas has no *Dalbergia*. The ébéniste’s lesson for a domestic shop is the idea of a palette — holly and walnut and cherry as colors — not a hunt for princes wood.
## A flower on a Riesener secrétaire
The Wallace Collection’s notes on Jean-Henri Riesener are the place to see how many pieces of veneer sit in a single flower: sand-shaded edges, engraved detail, mastics, a trellis of stringing, knife marks where a leaf breaks a border. When new, the furniture was a garden. Time and light ate the dyes and some of the natural pinks. The brown you see on a 1780 secrétaire now is not the garden it was.
Paris in the 17th and 18th centuries bought color by the leaf. The men who glued those leaves were *ébénistes* — the name from ebony, the job from a whole tropical palette. Kingwood (*Dalbergia cearensis*), once “princes wood,” is a violet-brown striped Brazilian rosewood of small dimension, almost only an inlay and banding wood. Tulipwood (*D. decipularis*, *D. frutescens*, and the trade’s overlapping names) is pink and yellow and loud. Together with bois de rose, violetwood, holly, box, stained sycamore, and pewter or brass, they made furniture that was a picture.
André-Jacob Roubo’s *L’Art du menuisier* (1769–75) is the period encyclopedia of the French wood shop: saws, presses, the hot hide glue, the sand box for a shadow. Riesener’s pictorial marquetry for the French crown is the high-water mark the Wallace notes keep returning to. Boulle work is brass and turtle and ebony more than kingwood; it belongs in the same Paris. German and English shops imported the taste and the woods. English seaweed marquetry of the 1690s is a related, quieter cousin, often in walnut and holly.
This chapter is the ébéniste’s palette, not a dining-table species. The marquetry chapter is the technique. The rosewood/CITES chapter is the law. Read the three together.
## Princes wood and the pink that fades
*D. cearensis* is restricted to a small Brazilian range: dense, hard, fine-striped, spectacular under a polish, and available only in small sizes (the old encyclopedias and the trade agree; the 1905 *New International* is the shop-lore citation, not a forest inventory). Seventeenth-century Paris used it when it was the most expensive furniture wood in general use — the “princes wood” of the inventories. It turns for small objects. It blunts tools. It is a banding on a secrétaire, not a carcase.
Tulipwood is not *Liriodendron*. The Brazilian *Dalbergia* tulipwoods are streaked pink-cream, used for parquetry grounds, for small boxes, for the loudest edges on a Louis XV piece. They are still rosewoods in the legal sense. Appendix II, Annotation #15. Small finished objects may fall under the weight exemption; a factory’s sawn stock does not. The pink fades. Conservators photograph, then stop. Faded marquetry should not be “brought back” with aniline on a guess.
Warren Dean’s Atlantic-forest history is again the ecological background. New kingwood and tulipwood furniture is a luxury that now has to justify itself on paper. Antique Paris furniture is the museum and the market that already exists. Do not order a new log of *D. cearensis* as if it were walnut.
## How an ébéniste’s leaf behaves in a modern shop
These woods are oily, hard, and small. They are also listed. A restorer replacing a lost band should document the antique source of the scrap or use a legal substitute (dyed pear, walnut, a documented old piece). Dust collection is the same rule as for the larger rosewoods: sensitizing dust, no casual sanding at an open bench `[CITE NEEDED: a named occupational-health note]`.
Glue wants a wiped surface and patience. A scraper and a fine polish are the historic finish, not a thick film that wants to be a piano. Book-matching a tulipwood ground is a design choice; the pink will not stay the pink you saw on the day you opened the packet. Plan for fade the way you plan for mahogany’s shift from pink to brown.
Federal American inlay used holly, maple, cherry, and a little imported exotic. It is not Riesener. A Baltimore painted-and-inlaid table is a different school. Southern and New England shops did not keep kingwood in the rack. A “tulipwood” American chest that is yellow-poplar is the other tulip — *Liriodendron tulipifera* — a secondary wood of Philadelphia high chests, not a Brazilian *Dalbergia*. Keep the words apart.
## Palette without a Brazilian log
The ébéniste’s lesson for a domestic shop is the idea of a palette. Holly and walnut and cherry are colors. Pear, stained, can stand in for a lost black line. Maple can stand in for a lost yellow. None of these are kingwood. They do not need to be. A shop that thinks in leaves — a 3 mm band, a flower of a dozen pieces, a ground that will fade — is thinking like Roubo’s reader even when the rack is Arkansas hardwood.
CITES for all *Dalbergia* is the rosewood chapter’s law: Appendix II, Annotation #15 as revised; *D. nigra* separately on Appendix I. Species+ at publication. Lacey on top. A small antique box already in the country is one object. A new factory parquetry floor in unnamed “tulipwood” is another.
Density in these Brazilian *Dalbergia* banding woods sits well above mahogany; compiled figures put kingwood and tulipwood in the 0.9–1.2 specific-gravity range, hard enough to blunt a moulding plane that just finished a walnut job `[CITE NEEDED: Kukachka or a measured table for *D. cearensis* and *D. decipularis*]`. That hardness is why a 3 mm band holds a polish like stone and why a shop does not treat a leftover offcut as kindling for a practice cut without dust collection.
Violet stripes in a 3 mm band. Pink parquetry. A Riesener flower that is now brown. Those are the things to look for. Arkansas has no *Dalbergia*. The useful borrow is the floating picture, not a hunt for princes wood. The Wallace flower is still the teacher. The dye that left is part of the lesson.
## Sources
Wallace Collection, Riesener marquetry. Roubo. Macquoid / Edwards. Dean. CITES *Dalbergia*. Old encyclopedias on kingwood (New International, 1905). Wood Database species pages (secondary).
See: `marquetry-picture-of-trees`, `rosewood-ebony-cites`, `walnut`, `boxwood`.

item.title: Khaya, sapele, and African “mahogany”
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Khaya, sapele, and African “mahogany”
By the time a 20th-century American factory stamped MAHOGANY on a dining suite, the tree behind the stamp was often West African. *Khaya* (true African mahogany to the trade) and *Entandrophragma* — sapele, utile, sipo — filled the hole that Cuban *Swietenia mahagoni* had left and that Honduran *S. macrophylla* could not fill at every price. They are Meliaceae, like *Swietenia*. They are not *Swietenia*. A ribbon-striped quartered sapele door is one of the best furniture faces of the last hundred years. It is still a substitute name when the invoice says mahogany.
## Khaya
*Khaya ivorensis* and its cousins are the woods FPL compares to American mahogany: similar color range, often a bit more interlocked, easy enough to work, a staple of the 20th-century trade. Janka commonly near 830 lbf. They carve. They veneer. They were the “mahogany” of a great deal of interwar and postwar case work.
Some *Khaya* populations have been under IUCN and harvest pressure `[CITE NEEDED: current IUCN / listing status per species]`. They have not all followed *Swietenia* onto Appendix II in the same way. Check Species+ at publication.
## Sapele (*Entandrophragma cylindricum*)
Sapele is the designer’s African wood of the last generation: a pronounced ribbon stripe on the quarter, a cedar-ish smell, Janka often cited near 1,410 lbf — harder than *Swietenia*, closer to hard maple. Interlocked grain is the price. A plane chatters. A scraper and a sharp belt save the face.
It finishes well. It is more stable than its hardness suggests if quartered. It has been used for doors, boat interiors, guitar necks, and furniture that wanted mahogany’s color with more flash.
Utile (*E. utile*) and sipo (*E. utile* / *E. cylindricum* trade confusion — use the binomial) are related, often a bit quieter. The shop that wants ribbon asks for quartered sapele.
## How the name slipped
Philippine mahogany was lauan (next chapter but one). Gaboon was okoume. “Santos mahogany” is *Myroxylon*, a different, denser wood. The word mahogany became a color and a hope. Bowett’s 18th-century Jamaica wood did not consent.
Honest specification: *Khaya ivorensis*, *Entandrophragma cylindricum*, country, cut (quartered / crown). A client who wants Chippendale should hear that the splat will be harder to carve in sapele and historically wrong in species, even if the color sings.
## Furniture history
African mahoganies enter European and American shops in volume in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, as colonial concessions opened West African forests. The furniture is Edwardian, then factory Colonial Revival, then mid-century commercial. Some excellent work is in *Khaya*. A lot of mediocre veneer is too.
Late-century architectural millwork made sapele a default “modern mahogany.” Hotels, offices, the boardroom table that is a quartered ribbon. That is a legitimate aesthetic. Name it.
## Shop notes
Interlocked grain: read the direction, take light cuts, do not chase tear-out with stain. Sapele dust irritates some people.
Color: fresh sapele can be salmon; it oxidizes toward brown-red. Like cherry, it will change after installation.
## Conservation
West African hardwood concessions are a long controversy: legality, community rights, old-growth. FSC and national documents are the minimum. Some *Entandrophragma* and *Khaya* have been discussed for CITES; afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*), sometimes in the same showroom, is already Appendix II. Do not assume “African mahogany” is unlisted. Look up the binomial.
Lacey Phase VII wants the scientific name on more furniture. This is exactly the category where “mahogany” on a crate fails.
## What to look for
Ribbon stripe, hardness above true mahogany, a cedar smell, a 1920s suite, a 2010s office door. A Chippendale reproduction in sapele: say so. A “solid mahogany” that is *Khaya*: say so.
Arkansas shops meet these woods as imports. The local lesson is labeling. Cherry and walnut will not be sapele. They also will not require a West African concession map.
## A ribbon door and a crate stamped MAHOGANY
By the time a 20th-century American factory stamped MAHOGANY on a dining suite, the tree behind the stamp was often West African. *Khaya* (true African mahogany to the trade) and *Entandrophragma* — sapele, utile, sipo — filled the hole that Cuban *Swietenia mahagoni* had left and that Honduran *S. macrophylla* could not fill at every price. They are Meliaceae, like *Swietenia*. They are not *Swietenia*. A ribbon-striped quartered sapele door is one of the best furniture faces of the last hundred years. It is still a substitute name when the invoice says mahogany.
Bowett’s 18th-century Jamaica wood did not consent. The Naval Stores Act of 1721 made British West Indian *Swietenia* cheap enough to carve in the solid. The West African concession map of the late 19th and early 20th centuries made *Khaya* and sapele ordinary enough to veneer a factory suite. Those are different statutes, different ports — Lagos, Takoradi, the Congo mouth, then Liverpool and Hamburg — and a different century. Do not invent a particular steamer. The colonial forest concession is the evidence `[CITE NEEDED: a named concession or port-statistic source for Khaya exports]`.
Edwardian shops, then Colonial Revival factories, then mid-century commercial case work: some excellent work is in *Khaya*. A lot of mediocre veneer is too. Late-century architectural millwork made sapele a default “modern mahogany.” Hotels, offices, the boardroom table that is a quartered ribbon. That is a legitimate aesthetic. Name it.
## Khaya’s manners, sapele’s fight
*Khaya ivorensis* and its cousins are the woods FPL compares to American mahogany: similar color range, often a bit more interlocked, easy enough to work, a staple of the 20th-century trade. Janka commonly near 830 lbf. They carve. They veneer. They were the “mahogany” of a great deal of interwar and postwar case work. Some *Khaya* populations have been under IUCN and harvest pressure `[CITE NEEDED: current IUCN / listing status per species]`. They have not all followed *Swietenia* onto Appendix II in the same way. Check Species+ at publication.
Sapele (*Entandrophragma cylindricum*) is the designer’s African wood of the last generation: a pronounced ribbon stripe on the quarter, a cedar-ish smell, Janka often cited near 1,410 lbf — harder than *Swietenia*, closer to hard maple. Interlocked grain is the price. A plane chatters. A scraper and a sharp belt save the face. It finishes well. It is more stable than its hardness suggests if quartered. It has been used for doors, boat interiors, guitar necks, and furniture that wanted mahogany’s color with more flash.
Utile (*E. utile*) and sipo (trade confusion with *E. cylindricum* — use the binomial) are related, often a bit quieter. The shop that wants ribbon asks for quartered sapele. Fresh sapele can be salmon; it oxidizes toward brown-red. Like cherry, it will change after installation. Tell the client.
Philippine mahogany was lauan. Gaboon was okoume. “Santos mahogany” is *Myroxylon*, a different, denser wood. The word mahogany became a color and a hope. Honest specification: *Khaya ivorensis*, *Entandrophragma cylindricum*, country, cut (quartered / crown). A client who wants Chippendale should hear that the splat will be harder to carve in sapele and historically wrong in species, even if the color sings.
## Working interlock
Read the grain direction. Take light cuts. Do not chase tear-out with stain; you will only darken the torn fibers. A scraper, a high cutting angle, sometimes a belt with a fresh grit — those are the tools. Sapele dust irritates some people. Collection is not optional.
*Khaya* is kinder, closer to *Swietenia* under the plane, still more interlocked than a straight Honduran board. Moulding profiles will take. A rococo splat in sapele is a fight the 1754 *Director* did not ask you to have.
Glue is ordinary if the surface is clean. Finish: oil and film both work; the ribbon will flash under a polish the way quartered sapele is supposed to flash. That flash is why architects specify it. It is also why a flatsawn sapele table looks busier than the door you saw in the millwork catalogue.
Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*), sometimes in the same showroom, is already Appendix II. Do not assume “African mahogany” is unlisted. Look up the binomial. West African hardwood concessions are a long controversy: legality, community rights, old-growth. FSC and national documents are the minimum.
