Lacey Phase VII wants the scientific name on more furniture. This is exactly the category where “mahogany” on a crate fails.
## The Arkansas label problem
Arkansas shops meet these woods as imports. The local lesson is labeling. Cherry and walnut will not be sapele. They also will not require a West African concession map. A southern shop that wants mahogany’s color in a domestic wood is looking at cherry after ten years of sun, or at walnut, or at a named *Khaya* with papers.
On a 1920s suite: probably *Khaya* or a mix, a redder factory finish, secondary poplar or pine. On a 2010s office door: probably quartered sapele, and that is fine if the invoice says so. On a Chippendale reproduction in sapele: say so. On a “solid mahogany” that is *Khaya*: say so. The ribbon, the hardness above true mahogany, a cedar smell in a fresh cut — those are the bench tells.
The 2003 Appendix II listing for neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* did not automatically list *Khaya*. That gap is why the word mahogany kept working as a sales tag after the true genus needed a permit. The gap is not a reason to keep the tag. Write the binomial. The door will still stripe.
## Sources
USDA FPL imported woods (*Khaya*, *Entandrophragma*). Kukachka FPL-125. CITES Species+ (*Pericopsis*; check *Khaya*). TRAFFIC five-taxa paper (context). Wood Database (secondary Janka). Bowett (on what mahogany meant in 1750).
See: `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `lauan-meranti-okoume`, `cites-lacey-buying`, `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`.

item.title: Iroko and the teak lookalikes
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Iroko and the teak lookalikes
Iroko (*Milicia excelsa*, *M. regia*) is a West and Central African hardwood that shops sell when they want teak’s outdoor manners without teak’s price or papers. Ring-porous, yellow-brown to brown, durable, a Janka often cited near 1,260 lbf — oak’s neighbor. It has been called African teak in catalogues. It is not *Tectona*. The pore and the color rhyme; the oil and the smell do not quite.
This chapter is the honest substitute: what iroko does, what other brown outdoor woods do, and when the substitution is a good shop decision rather than a dodge.
## Iroko in the shop
It works with a moderate fight, sometimes with a dust that irritates (chlorophorin and related compounds are shop-lore allergens `[CITE NEEDED: a medical or FPL dust note]`). It glues better than oily teak. It finishes well. Outdoors it weathers grey. Indoors it can look like a quieter teak or a brown ash.
Furniture: garden chairs, kitchen worktops in European shops, church pews, lab benches, the late-20th-century “teak” patio set that was not. Some contemporary indoor furniture uses it as a show wood on purpose.
## Other lookalikes
Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*) is a closer visual cousin to teak for furniture, finer, and CITES Appendix II. Do not treat it as an unlisted bargain.
Cumaru, ipe, and the South American deck woods are harder, heavier, and a different aesthetic — more iron than oil. They make furniture that feels like a deck. Fine if wanted.
Robinia (black locust, *Robinia pseudoacacia*) is a temperate outdoor hardwood of high durability, yellow-green when fresh, grown in Europe and America. It is a true alternative for benches, not a teak clone.
White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood of the tyloses story. It does not look like teak. It lasts if designed to drain.
Rubberwood (*Hevea*) is a plantation indoor wood, often stained “teak.” It is not outdoor-durable.
## History
Iroko enters European trade with the same colonial concession map as *Khaya*. It was a decking and joinery wood, then a furniture wood as teak fashion outran teak supply. It has no 18th-century London age. It has a 1960s–2000s garden-center age.
African furniture traditions used *Milicia* locally long before the export name “iroko” sat on a Dutch pallet `[CITE NEEDED: a specific West African furniture-history source]`. The export story is not the only story.
## Shop notes
Iroko can stain metal and skin in the same tannin family as oak. Wet cloth and steel leave marks.
Quartered stock is less wild. The ring-porous face will telegraph through a thin paint.
## Conservation
*Milicia* has been logged hard in parts of West Africa. IUCN and national statuses vary by species and country. Not as legally famous as *Dalbergia*. Still a Lacey name problem if the crate says “teak.” FSC exists. Ask.
Afrormosia is the lookalike that can get you a seizure at the border if you ignore Appendix II.
## What to look for
Teak color without teak oil, African origin, garden furniture, a worktop, a crate that says African teak. A domestic outdoor bench in locust or white oak: the better named choice if you live in Arkansas.
The series includes iroko so teak’s chapter does not have to carry every brown garden chair, and so a buyer can say the binomial instead of the wish.
## A garden chair that wanted to be teak
Iroko (*Milicia excelsa*, *M. regia*) is a West and Central African hardwood that shops sell when they want teak’s outdoor manners without teak’s price or papers. Ring-porous, yellow-brown to brown, durable, a Janka often cited near 1,260 lbf — oak’s neighbor. It has been called African teak in catalogues. It is not *Tectona*. The pore and the color rhyme; the oil and the smell do not quite.
The *Wood Handbook* and Kukachka’s FPL-125 treat *Milicia* as an imported utility hardwood with genuine durability, not as a mahogany substitute and not as a true teak. Compiled specific-gravity figures sit in the oak neighborhood `[CITE NEEDED: the exact FPL or Kukachka row]`. It works with a moderate fight, sometimes with a dust that irritates (chlorophorin and related compounds are shop-lore allergens `[CITE NEEDED: a medical or FPL dust note]`). It glues better than oily teak. It finishes well. Outdoors it weathers grey. Indoors it can look like a quieter teak or a brown ash.
Furniture: garden chairs, kitchen worktops in European shops, church pews, lab benches, the late-20th-century “teak” patio set that was not. Some contemporary indoor furniture uses it as a show wood on purpose. That is a good shop decision when the binomial is on the invoice. It is a dodge when the crate says teak.
Iroko enters European trade with the same colonial concession map as *Khaya*. It was a decking and joinery wood, then a furniture wood as teak fashion outran teak supply. It has no 18th-century London age. It has a 1960s–2000s garden-center age. African furniture traditions used *Milicia* locally long before the export name “iroko” sat on a Dutch pallet `[CITE NEEDED: a specific West African furniture-history source]`. The export story is not the only story. Do not invent a particular voyage.
## The lookalike rack
Afrormosia (*Pericopsis elata*) is a closer visual cousin to teak for furniture, finer, and CITES Appendix II. Do not treat it as an unlisted bargain. A seizure at the border is a real outcome if you ignore the listing. Species+ at publication.
Cumaru, ipe, and the South American deck woods are harder, heavier, and a different aesthetic — more iron than oil. They make furniture that feels like a deck. Fine if wanted. They will not oil up like *Tectona* and they will eat tools.
Robinia (black locust, *Robinia pseudoacacia*) is a temperate outdoor hardwood of high durability, yellow-green when fresh, grown in Europe and America. It is a true alternative for benches, not a teak clone. White oak is the domestic outdoor furniture wood of the tyloses story. It does not look like teak. It lasts if designed to drain. Rubberwood (*Hevea*) is a plantation indoor wood, often stained “teak.” It is not outdoor-durable.
The honest substitute is the one you name. Iroko for a garden chair that must live in rain. Locust or white oak for an Arkansas bench. Afrormosia only with the permit path. *Tectona* when the papers are boring and the job wants the oil. A stain on mixed hardwood is none of these.
## Working a tannin-brown outdoor wood
Iroko can stain metal and skin in the same tannin family as oak. Wet cloth and steel leave marks. Stainless or bronze outdoors. Quartered stock is less wild. The ring-porous face will telegraph through a thin paint.
Dust collection is the same rule as for the allergenic tropicals. Some shops treat iroko dust as they treat western redcedar or cocobolo: not a wood for a first-day apprentice at an open sander. Glue is kinder than teak’s oily habit. Finish: oil indoors if you want a quieter teak look; leave it raw outdoors if you accept grey. Design that drains beats a finish that claims immortality.
At the bench, ring-porous brown without teak’s grease, African origin if the tag is honest, a hardness near oak — those are the tells. A crate that says African teak is a crate that failed the noun test. Write *Milicia excelsa* or *M. regia*, country, cut.
*Milicia* has been logged hard in parts of West Africa. IUCN and national statuses vary by species and country. Not as legally famous as *Dalbergia*. Still a Lacey name problem if the crate says “teak.” FSC exists. Ask.
## An Arkansas bench and the wish
The series includes iroko so teak’s chapter does not have to carry every brown garden chair, and so a buyer can say the binomial instead of the wish. Arkansas does not grow *Milicia*. It grows white oak and, in places, black locust. Those are the better named choices for a bench that will sit in rain beside a Delta cypress or an Ozark oak house.
A designer who wants teak’s outdoor manners without teak’s papers is looking at iroko (named), locust, white oak, or cypress — not at a stain. A designer who wants the 1960s interior honey is looking at a named *Tectona* or at walnut, not at iroko pretending. The garden-center age made iroko ordinary. Ordinary is fine. The word teak on that ordinary chair is not.
A European kitchen worktop in iroko — the late-century fashion in British and Dutch shops — is a useful object lesson. The wood takes the knife and the wet cloth better than beech; it is not a butcher-block maple and it is not a teak oil advertisement. Church pews and lab benches used the same durability without asking the board to look like a 1958 Danish sideboard. Those jobs are why a mill kept *Milicia* on the rack after the patio set went out of fashion.
Ports that handled the export — the same West African coast that sent *Khaya* and sapele — do not make the wood Jamaican mahogany and do not make it Burmese teak. Bowett’s 1721 Act is a different statute. CITES 2017 is a different genus. Iroko lives in the gap those two famous dates do not cover. The gap still wants a binomial.
## Sources
FPL / Kukachka imported woods (*Milicia*, *Pericopsis*). CITES (*Pericopsis elata*). Wood Database (secondary). Teak chapter sources for comparison. `[CITE NEEDED: allergen; West African use]`.
See: `teak`, `african-mahogany-sapele-khaya`, `oak-european-and-american`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Huanghuali and zitan
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Huanghuali and zitan
A Ming yoke-back chair in huanghuali is not an English oak chair in another climate. The joinery (mitered bridle joints, floating panels, no glue as a religion), the finish (wax and hand, not French polish), and the trees belong to a Chinese classical tradition that was already mature when Macquoid’s Age of Oak was young. Western collecting in the late 20th century made these woods fashionable in New York and London. The trees — *Dalbergia odorifera* (huanghuali, Hainan and related trade) and the dark dense woods sold as zitan (often *Pterocarpus santalinus*, red sandalwood, and other heavy dark hardwoods) — were already scarce. This chapter is a comparative frame: another 500-year furniture culture, and the names a buyer will meet in a catalogue.
## Huanghuali
The word names a look as much as a species: a warm, translucent brown-orange, a ghostly figure, a sweet smell in the cut. *Dalbergia odorifera* is the Hainan rosewood at the center of the modern botanical identification. Trade has also used related *Dalbergia* and lookalikes; connoisseurship (Wang Shixiang; Handler; the Museum of Classical Chinese Furniture literature) argues from objects more than from bills of lading.
It is a rosewood in the CITES sense. Appendix II (or I if a given species is listed separately — check). New furniture in true huanghuali is a legal and ethical knot. Antique furniture is the supply that scholars trust.
## Zitan
Zitan is the dark, almost black-purple, extremely dense imperial wood of Qing court taste, earlier used more sparingly. *Pterocarpus santalinus* (red sandalwood) is the species most often attached; other heavy dark woods have been sold under the name. *P. santalinus* is listed (CITES — verify appendix and annotation). The furniture is late, courtly, and heavy in the hand.
Do not confuse zitan with ebonized beech or with wenge. Weight and pore tell.
## Why it belongs in this series
Because 500 years of furniture woods is not only the North Atlantic. Because American and European designers now specify “rosewood” and meet Chinese classical pieces in the same auction week as a Stickley chair. Because the conservation lesson is the same genus story as Brazilian rosewood, with a different shop tradition.
Because the joinery is a lesson: a floating panel in a mitered frame is the same physics as a 17th-century English oak panel, solved with different proportions.
## Shop notes
Do not refinish a classical Chinese hardwood piece with a film finish that wants to be a piano. The surface is part of the object.
Do not accept a new “huanghuali” dining table from an unnamed factory. The word is too expensive to be casual.
Identification of old pieces is a specialist’s job. This series will not pretend a blog chapter replaces a scholar.
## Conservation
Hainan *D. odorifera* is rare. Red sandalwood has been a smuggling species. Madagascar and Southeast Asian lookalikes have their own crises. Buy antiques with provenance, or buy other woods. The Lacey Act and CITES both apply to new trade.
## What to look for
In a museum: the chair, the incense stand, the wax, the join. In a market: papers, weight, smell, a price that makes sense only if the wood is true — or a price that makes sense only if it is not. In a design studio: the idea of a hardwood chair without upholstery, not a raid on Hainan.
Arkansas walnut and oak will not be huanghuali. They can still teach a floating panel. That is the useful borrow.
## A yoke-back chair and a different canon
A Ming yoke-back chair in huanghuali is not an English oak chair in another climate. The joinery — mitered bridle joints, floating panels, no glue as a religion — the finish (wax and hand, not French polish), and the trees belong to a Chinese classical tradition that was already mature when Macquoid’s Age of Oak was young. Wang Shixiang’s *Connoisseurship of Chinese Furniture* and Sarah Handler’s *Austere Luminosity of Chinese Classical Furniture* are the books this chapter leans on. The Museum of Classical Chinese Furniture literature argues from objects more than from bills of lading.
Western collecting in the late 20th century made these woods fashionable in New York and London. The trees — *Dalbergia odorifera* (huanghuali, Hainan and related trade) and the dark dense woods sold as zitan (often *Pterocarpus santalinus*, red sandalwood, and other heavy dark hardwoods) — were already scarce. A 500-year survey that stopped at satinwood and Danish teak would have left a parallel canon in a footnote. The series will not.
The horseshoe armchair, the continuous-yoke official’s chair, the incense stand, the recessed-leg table: those are the object types a reader will meet in a catalogue. Proportions are not Chippendale’s. A floating panel in a mitered frame is the same physics as a 17th-century English oak panel, solved with different sections. Hoadley’s movement lesson still applies. The shop that refuses glue is making a choice about repair and about humidity, not a mysticism.
## Huanghuali as a look and a listing
The word names a look as much as a species: a warm, translucent brown-orange, a ghostly figure, a sweet smell in the cut. *Dalbergia odorifera* is the Hainan rosewood at the center of the modern botanical identification. Trade has also used related *Dalbergia* and lookalikes. Connoisseurship argues from the object: the figure, the scent, the tool marks, the construction. A bill of lading from Hainan is a rare gift, not the usual evidence.
It is a rosewood in the CITES sense. The whole genus *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 as revised; check whether a given species is listed separately. New furniture in true huanghuali is a legal and ethical knot. Antique furniture is the supply that scholars trust. Hainan *D. odorifera* is rare. Do not accept a new “huanghuali” dining table from an unnamed factory. The word is too expensive to be casual.
Do not refinish a classical Chinese hardwood piece with a film finish that wants to be a piano. The surface is part of the object. Wax, hand, a sheen that is not a plastic skin — Handler and Wang keep returning to that surface. A belt sander is how a chair becomes a different, lesser thing.
Identification of old pieces is a specialist’s job. This series will not pretend a blog chapter replaces a scholar. Weight, smell, pore, and construction are the amateur’s first filter. A lab test and a provenance file are what a serious sale wants.
## Zitan, court taste, and the heavy dark woods
Zitan is the dark, almost black-purple, extremely dense imperial wood of Qing court taste, earlier used more sparingly. *Pterocarpus santalinus* (red sandalwood) is the species most often attached; other heavy dark woods have been sold under the name. *P. santalinus* is listed (CITES — verify appendix and annotation at publication). The furniture is late, courtly, and heavy in the hand.
Do not confuse zitan with ebonized beech or with wenge. Weight and pore tell. A solid zitan piece should feel like a dense tropical, not like a stained temperate hardwood. Red sandalwood has been a smuggling species. Madagascar and Southeast Asian lookalikes have their own crises. Buy antiques with provenance, or buy other woods. The Lacey Act and CITES both apply to new trade.
Dean’s Atlantic-forest book is a parallel extractive story, not a Chinese forest history. The Chinese hardwoods have their own depletion literature in the connoisseurship books and in the listing files. Quote those. Do not invent a particular tribute voyage or a palace price.
## What a North Atlantic shop can borrow
Because American and European designers now specify “rosewood” and meet Chinese classical pieces in the same auction week as a Stickley chair. Because the conservation lesson is the same genus story as Brazilian rosewood, with a different shop tradition. Because the joinery is a lesson.
Arkansas walnut and oak will not be huanghuali. They can still teach a floating panel, a mitered frame that lets a panel move, a chair that is hardwood without upholstery. That is the useful borrow. The idea of a hardwood chair that is all joinery and wax is older than the New York collecting boom. It does not require a raid on Hainan.
In a museum: the chair, the incense stand, the wax, the join. In a market: papers, weight, smell, a price that makes sense only if the wood is true — or a price that makes sense only if it is not. This draft will not invent those prices. In a design studio: specify *Juglans nigra* or *Quercus alba* for a new chair in that spirit, or buy an antique with a scholar’s file. The 2017 *Dalbergia* listing and the red-sandalwood files are the legal third rail. Species+ is the living page.
Handler keeps returning to luminosity: a hardwood that reads as light in the room even when the species is dense. That is a finish and a figure fact, not a metaphor. Wang’s connoisseurship pages teach the same objects from construction — the miters, the floating panel, the absent glue as a habit. A reader who has just come from the oak and mahogany chapters will recognize the physics and miss the proportions if they only look for a splat.
Macquoid gave English furniture four ages of timber. China’s classical hardwoods were already a canon. The series puts them in the same 500 years so a reader walking from a yoke-back to a splat-back can see two answers to the same physics.
## Sources
Wang Shixiang, *Connoisseurship of Chinese Furniture*. Handler, *Austere Luminosity*. Museum of Classical Chinese Furniture catalogues. CITES Species+ (*D. odorifera*, *P. santalinus*). Dean (Atlantic forest as parallel extractive story).
See: `rosewood-ebony-cites`, `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`, `cites-lacey-buying`, `five-centuries-of-furniture-wood`.

item.title: Twentieth-century plywoods and face veneers
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Twentieth-century plywoods and face veneers
The V&A’s plywood history makes a point that flat-board people forget: between about 1850 and 1890 the innovative plywood was molded. Chair seats, backs, the factory furniture that was not Thonet’s solid beech bend — laminated veneer in curves. Then modernists in the 1920s and 1930s took the industrial sheet as a badge. Then the war taught compound curves to a couple in Los Angeles, and the Eames DCM went onto a thousand drawing boards (Robin Day’s remark, via the V&A). The species on the face could be walnut, teak, or birch. The species in the core could be something the catalogue hoped you would not ask about.
This chapter is the 20th-century veneer economy. Finnish birch and the tropical cores have their own essays. Engineered particle panels have theirs. Here is the habit of hiding a tree behind a tree.
## Rotary versus sliced
A log on a lathe, peeled like a paper towel: rotary veneer. Wide, wild cathedrals, cheap, the look of a 1950s dresser side. Lauan, yellow-poplar, Douglas-fir. A log sliced on a leaf: crown-cut or quarter-cut decorative veneer. Walnut crotch, quartered oak flake, mahogany crown. Furniture that wants to look like solid show wood uses sliced faces. Furniture that wants to be cheap uses rotary faces. Furniture that wants to be honest modern sometimes shows the ply edge.
Adhesives moved from animal glue to casein (Aalto’s factory still used casein for some cold bends, Klim 1990) to urea-formaldehyde and phenol-formaldehyde. Phenolic films in the 1930s made waterproof ply for aircraft and boats (Klim). Interior furniture ply is often a different, cheaper glue. Water still finds it.
## Faces of fashion
Art Deco liked exotic sliced faces on cheap cores: Macassar, burl, palisander. The core might be alder or gaboon. Bauhaus and early modern liked the idea of ply even when the famous chairs went to metal. Aalto made the ply the chair. Eames and Saarinen’s 1940 MoMA “Organic Design” experiments wanted a compound-curved shell; the war interrupted, then supplied the splint contract (1942) that taught the moulds.
Postwar American suites: a walnut-look rotary face on lauan, a printed grain that is not even veneer. The printed-and-papered board is the ancestor of foil-wrapped MDF. Look at a chip.
## Why ply is not a sin
Cross-banding cancels movement. A shaped seat that would split in solid flatsawn oak can live in five layers of birch. A table top that stays flat in a heated apartment is often ply. The 18th-century frame-and-panel was the old answer to the same physics. Plywood is the industrial answer.
The sin is the name. “Walnut dining table” for a 0.6 mm face on a void-core of mixed tropicals is a sentence that needs more nouns.
## Shop notes
Void-core cheap ply will telegraph and will lose a screw. Baltic birch and apple-ply grades will not. Count plies. Weigh the board.
Old furniture ply delaminates when the protein glue gives up in a damp room. Clamping and the right adhesive save some of it. A belt sander does not.
Veneer matching — book, slip, radial — is a design choice as old as the 17th century. Plywood factories automated it and then abandoned it for random rotary.
## Conservation
Decorative faces in rosewood and mahogany sit under CITES when the species does. Cores in lauan and okoume sit under the tropical-forest argument of those chapters. Formaldehyde in old urea glues is an indoor-air story (the engineered chapter). Buying vintage Eames and Aalto is reuse of an already-cut tree. Buying new “walnut ply” is a specification: face species, core species, glue, certification.
## What to look for
An edge. A void. A printed grain that does not continue around a corner. A moulded seat. A splint in a museum. A 1930s radio with a burl face and a cheap back.
The 500-year series needs this chapter because more people own ply than own joined oak. The physics is old. The factory is new. The label is where the trouble lives.
## Molded seats before the modern badge
The V&A’s plywood history makes a point that flat-board people forget: between about 1850 and 1890 the innovative plywood was molded. Chair seats, backs, the factory furniture that was not Thonet’s solid beech bend — laminated veneer in curves. Michael Thonet’s No. 14 (V&A W.31-2011) is a solid-beech object; the parallel factory problem was how to make a seat or a back from leaves of wood glued in a mould. Then modernists in the 1920s and 1930s took the industrial sheet as a badge. Then the war taught compound curves to a couple in Los Angeles, and the Eames DCM went onto a thousand drawing boards. Robin Day’s remark, via the V&A, is the short version of that afterlife.
Charles and Ray Eames’s 1940 MoMA “Organic Design” experiments with Eero Saarinen wanted a compound-curved shell. The war interrupted, then supplied the 1942 splint contract that taught the moulds (Engelbrecht on the 1946 chair; Kirkham, *Charles and Ray Eames*). The species on the face could be walnut, teak, or birch. The species in the core could be something the catalogue hoped you would not ask about. Aalto’s Finnish birch laminations — casein glue in some cold bends (Klim, WAG 1990) — are the other modern lineage. Finmar sold Aalto in Britain in the 1930s. The Finnish-birch chapter returns to that mill.
None of this fits Macquoid’s Age of Mahogany. It is still furniture wood. Cross-banding cancels movement. A shaped seat that would split in solid flatsawn oak can live in five layers of birch. The 18th-century frame-and-panel was the old answer to the same physics. Plywood is the industrial answer.
## Rotary cathedrals and sliced faces
A log on a lathe, peeled like a paper towel: rotary veneer. Wide, wild cathedrals, cheap, the look of a 1950s dresser side. Lauan, yellow-poplar, Douglas-fir. A log sliced on a leaf: crown-cut or quarter-cut decorative veneer. Walnut crotch, quartered oak flake, mahogany crown. Furniture that wants to look like solid show wood uses sliced faces. Furniture that wants to be cheap uses rotary faces. Furniture that wants to be honest modern sometimes shows the ply edge.
Adhesives moved from animal glue to casein to urea-formaldehyde and phenol-formaldehyde. Phenolic films in the 1930s made waterproof ply for aircraft and boats (Klim). Interior furniture ply is often a different, cheaper glue. Water still finds it. Old furniture ply delaminates when the protein glue gives up in a damp room. Clamping and the right adhesive save some of it. A belt sander does not.
Art Deco liked exotic sliced faces on cheap cores: Macassar, burl, palisander. The core might be alder or gaboon. Bauhaus and early modern liked the idea of ply even when the famous chairs went to metal. Postwar American suites: a walnut-look rotary face on lauan, a printed grain that is not even veneer. The printed-and-papered board is the ancestor of foil-wrapped MDF. Look at a chip.
Veneer matching — book, slip, radial — is a design choice as old as the 17th-century ébéniste. The Wallace Collection’s Riesener notes are the handmade version: a flower of a dozen leaves. Plywood factories automated matching and then abandoned it for random rotary. A 1930s radio with a burl face and a cheap back is the object that holds both habits in one box.
## Why the name is the sin
“Walnut dining table” for a 0.6 mm face on a void-core of mixed tropicals is a sentence that needs more nouns. Cross-banding is honest physics. The sin is the name. Void-core cheap ply will telegraph and will lose a screw. Baltic birch and apple-ply grades will not. Count plies. Weigh the board.
Decorative faces in rosewood and mahogany sit under CITES when the species does. *Dalbergia* went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15; neotropical *Swietenia macrophylla* went onto Appendix II on 15 November 2003 for logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood. Cores in lauan and okoume sit under the tropical-forest argument of those chapters. Formaldehyde in old urea glues is an indoor-air story the engineered chapter takes up. Buying vintage Eames and Aalto is reuse of an already-cut tree. Buying new “walnut ply” is a specification: face species, core species, glue, certification.
Hoadley’s veneer pages still teach the difference between a leaf and a board. A shop that repairs a delaminated 1950s dresser is doing hide-or-PVA work on a protein or early synthetic glue line. A shop that specifies a new table is doing a bill of materials. Both jobs fail when the only noun is walnut.
## An edge in the room
Look at an edge. A void. A printed grain that does not continue around a corner. A moulded seat. A splint in a museum. A 1930s radio with a burl face and a cheap back. The 500-year series needs this chapter because more people own ply than own joined oak.
Arkansas shops meet ply as imported faces on imported cores, and as domestic yellow-poplar and pine rotary for paint-grade work. Bradley Brand’s hardwoods are the solid side of that rack. The useful sentence for a designer is still the long one: face *Juglans nigra*, core birch, phenolic, FSC — or face rotary lauan, void, urea, no papers. Those are different objects. The Eames DCM and a printed suburban suite share a century. They do not share a glue, a mould, or a noun.
The V&A’s ten-object history is the reading. Klim 1990 is the conservator’s adhesive timeline. Kirkham and Engelbrecht are the Eames file. Ostergard is the bent-wood shelf. None of them will save a specification that says only wood. The physics is old. The factory is new. The label is where the trouble lives.
## Sources
V&A, “A short history of plywood in ten-ish objects.” Klim, WAG 1990. Engelbrecht on Eames 1946. Kirkham, *Charles and Ray Eames*. Ostergard, bent wood. Hoadley (veneer).
See: `finnish-birch-aalto`, `lauan-meranti-okoume`, `engineered-wood-honest`, `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`.

item.title: Finnish birch and the laminated chair
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Finnish birch and the laminated chair
Alvar Aalto designed a chair for the Paimio tuberculosis sanatorium with a seat that looks like a scroll of paper and is a bent laminate of Finnish birch. The V&A tells the object as a plywood milestone; Artek’s factory (Korhonen, then the Artek system) made the bends a product. Finmar sold them into Britain in the 1930s, and the UK was Finland’s largest furniture export market in those years (Finmar study). The wood is the same genus as Biedermeier birch. The technology is Thonet’s cousin and Eames’s elder. The forest is boreal.
## Why birch
Northern birch peels well, glues well, and is pale in a way that modern interiors wanted. It is not as silica-hard as teak, not as tannic as oak. Thin leaves of it, stacked with the grain alternated or aligned depending on the part, will take a bend that solid oak of the same thickness will not. Aalto’s “bent knee” legs and scroll seats are that fact made polite.
Solid Finnish birch furniture exists too — stools, tables — but the famous objects are laminates. Baltic birch plywood, the many-ply clear core, is the shop descendant: jigs, modern cabinets with exposed edges, the honest ply aesthetic.
## The line from Thonet
Thonet bent solid beech in moulds. Aalto bent stacks of veneer. Both used heat, moisture, and a form. Both needed a forest next to a factory. Moravia had beech; Finland had birch. The café chair and the sanatorium chair are answers to shipping and to sitting, a century apart.
Casein’s slow, water-resistant glue in Artek’s cold-bend processes (Klim) is a reminder that “plywood glue” is not one chemistry. Later production moved. Conservators of Aalto have to ask which.
## Influence
Charles and Ray Eames knew this work. The 1940 MoMA shell and the 1942 splint are American wartime industrializations of a laminated idea. English designers (Day and others) pinned up the DCM. The Finnish chair taught a generation that wood could be modern without being painted metal.
It also taught a market that “Scandinavian” meant pale wood, even when Danish factories were shipping teak.
## Shop notes
Exposed birch ply edges want a finish that does not leave them fuzzy. Water raises the grain of those end-plies with enthusiasm.
Repairs to a broken Aalto knee are specialist work. Do not sister a pine block onto a laminate scroll and call it conservation.
New “Aalto-style” chairs in mixed ply from unnamed mills are a shape, not a forest. The birch chapter and this one both ask you to count plies.
## Conservation
Boreal birch is a managed industrial forest, tied to paper as much as to Artek. Old-growth arguments in Finland and Russia are real and are not solved by a stool. Certification exists. Vintage Artek is reuse. The species is not CITES.
## What to look for
A scroll seat, a bent knee, pale laminates, a 1930s Finmar label, a many-ply edge. A stained “walnut” version of the same shape: a different sentence.
Arkansas has no *Betula pendula* forest. The lesson a southern shop takes is the laminate: poplar and oak veneers can bend too. The species credit for the famous chair stays Finnish.
## The Paimio chair in a room
The Paimio tuberculosis sanatorium, in the pine and birch country southwest of Turku, opened in 1933. Alvar Aalto and Aino Aalto designed the building and the furniture as one argument: pale rooms, washable surfaces, a chair that would not feel like hospital iron. The armchair now called 41, or the Paimio chair, was drawn in 1931–32 and made by Otto Korhonen’s Huonekalu- ja Rakennustyötehdas in Turku. Two closed birch loops form the arms and the runners. Between them a single scroll of laminated birch — seat and back in one sheet — hangs like a piece of paper that learned to hold a person. The V&A’s plywood history treats that scroll as a milestone: molded ply as furniture, not as a hidden core. The museum’s own Aalto holdings (among them a Finmar-imported birch chair, W.41-1987, and related Korhonen-Aalto stacking types) let you walk around the grain instead of reading a caption.
Patients sat in those loops. The wood is cool in a Finnish winter room and warm compared with tubular steel. That is not a slogan. It is why Aalto kept arguing with Marcel Breuer’s metal chairs in the early 1930s. Birch was the local answer to metal fashion.
## Korhonen, Artek, Finmar
Otto Korhonen had been bending and stacking chairs in Turku since the 1910s. Aalto met him on the Southwestern Agricultural Cooperative building and then on Paimio. The factory, not the drawing board, is where the closed loop and the later “bent knee” or “Doric” leg were made repeatable. Aalto later called the standard L-leg a column. The shop called it a sawn and bent laminate that had to come out of the mould without spring-back that would ruin a stool.
Artek was founded in Helsinki in 1935 by Alvar Aalto, Aino Aalto, Maire Gullichsen, and Nils-Gustav Hahl, to sell the furniture as a system and to keep the art-and-industry talk attached to actual invoices. Korhonen kept making the pieces. The brand and the benches were not the same thing.
Britain saw the work before Artek existed as a company. Philip Morton Shand, who wrote for the *Architectural Review* and had met Aalto at the Stockholm Exhibition of 1930, put Aalto’s plywood furniture into Fortnum & Mason in November 1933 under the title *Wood Only*, timed with an English-Finnish trade week. Orders from that show were enough that Shand and Geoffrey Boumphrey formed Finmar Ltd in 1934 as the UK importer. Heal’s and Bowman’s sold the chairs. Jack Pritchard of the Venesta plywood company walked the Korhonen shop and Paimio in 1935 and went home to found Isokon. The Finmar study still used by architectural historians says the UK was Finland’s largest furniture export market in those years. A stamp on the underside — FINMAR LTD / MADE IN FINLAND — is the object-level proof. Look for it before you believe a dealer’s “1930s Aalto.”
## What birch is, as a number
The peeler logs behind those chairs are European silver birch and downy birch, *Betula pendula* and *B. pubescens*: pale sap, fine diffuse-porous texture, a tree that paper mills already knew how to peel. The USDA *Wood Handbook* (FPL-GTR-190) tables the American cousins, not a single Finnish mill run. Yellow birch (*B. alleghaniensis*) sits at specific gravity about 0.62 and Janka about 1,260 lbf at 12 percent moisture — near hard maple, a little kinder, and it “shrinks considerably” in the kiln. Paper birch (*B. papyrifera*) is lighter (SG about 0.55, Janka about 910 lbf). Finnish furniture birch behaves in that neighborhood: hard enough for a stool rail, pale enough for a modern room, and — this is the industrial fact — it peels into long, even leaves. A published FPL-equivalent Janka for *B. pendula* as a Finnish furniture grade is not the number shops quote `[CITE NEEDED]`. The genus credit is safe.
Birch is not oak. It has no tyloses story and no ray flake. It is not teak: no oil, no silica tax of that kind. It glues. It takes a clear film that yellows toward cream, which is why mid-century owners either loved the honey or fought it with water-white varnish. Water raises the end-grain of a plywood edge as if the board were a brush.
Karelian or masur birch — the marble figure of Biedermeier luxury — is a growth peculiarity, not a separate order. Aalto’s factory chairs are ordinary, clear birch, stacked. The luxury is the bend, not the figure.
## Glue, heat, and the bent knee
Thonet’s No. 14, from 1859, is solid beech, steamed and forced into an iron mould. Aalto’s scroll and L-leg are stacks of veneer, glued, then bent. Both need heat, moisture, and a form. Both need a forest next to a factory. Moravia and the Austrian beech woods fed Thonet; the Finnish boreal belt fed Korhonen. The café chair and the sanatorium chair are answers to shipping and sitting, a century apart.
Susan Klim’s 1990 Wooden Artifacts Group paper still helps a conservator more than a catalogue essay: protein glues, then casein, then the cheap ureas. Artek’s cold-bend work used casein — slow, reasonably water-resistant, a dairy chemistry, not a formaldehyde one. Later production moved. A broken knee on a 1930s stool and a broken knee on a 1980s reissue are not the same repair. Ask which glue. The V&A plywood history is the public version of that timeline; Klim is the bench version.
The L-leg, standardized on Stool 60 in 1933, is a closed birch loop sawn so that the grain of the upright turns into the grain of the seat rail. It looks like a solid piece that changed its mind. It is a laminate that was taught a corner. Later Y-legs (1947) and X-legs (1954) are the same idea cut into a fan. A shop that sisters a pine block onto a failed knee has not conserved the chair. It has changed the sentence.
## Shop behavior
Count the plies on an exposed edge. Baltic birch of the jig-and-cabinet grade is many thin, clear leaves, few voids — often thirteen plies in an 18 mm sheet, though mills vary and you should count, not recite. A “birch” plywood with a pretty face and a core of mixed rotary tropicals is a different product. Weigh the board. Tap it. A void sounds like a drum.
When you cut Baltic birch, the saw fuzzes the end-plies. A light sanding and a finish that does not raise the grain again is the whole edge ritual. Water-based finishes are enthusiastic about that fuzz. Oil darkens the edge lines and makes the sandwich readable, which is the honest modern look.
Do not belt-sand a vintage Aalto scroll. The face veneer is thin. The curve is the object. A white ring from a wet glass is a finish problem; a delaminated leaf is a glue problem. Protein and casein failures can sometimes be re-adhered with the right adhesive and a form. A home-center yellow glue and a C-clamp across a scroll will telegraph forever.
New “Aalto-style” chairs from unnamed mills arrive in mixed ply, often a tropical core, often a stain that wants to be walnut. The shape is not a forest. The birch chapter and this one both ask you to count plies and to read the underside stamp.
## After 1940
Charles and Ray Eames knew this work. The 1940 MoMA “Organic Design in Home Furnishings” experiments with Eero Saarinen wanted a compound-curved shell; the war interrupted, then supplied the 1942 molded-plywood splint contract for the U.S. Navy that taught the moulds. The 1946 DCM and LCW are American industrializations of a laminated idea that Aalto had already made polite. Robin Day and other English designers pinned up the DCM. The Finnish chair had already taught a generation that wood could be modern without being painted metal.
It also taught a market that “Scandinavian” meant pale wood, even when Danish factories in the 1950s were shipping teak. Aalto’s birch and Wegner’s oak are cousins. Juhl’s teak is a refusal of that pale as much as a continuation of the craft. The Danish chapter returns to that argument.
Vintage Artek and Finmar pieces are reuse of an already-cut tree. The species is not CITES-listed. Boreal birch is a managed industrial forest, tied to paper as much as to furniture. Old-growth arguments in Finland and in Russian Karelia are real and are not solved by a stool. Certification exists. A new birch ply from a named mill with a grade stamp is a specification. A crate that says only “wood” is the lauan problem in a northern accent.
## Sources
V&A plywood history; Paimio chair. Finmar / Aalto UK sales paper. Klim 1990 (casein). Artek production histories. Birch chapter (FPL; Biedermeier).
See: `birch`, `beech`, `plywood-veneers-twentieth`, `danish-modern-woods`.

item.title: Lauan, meranti, okoume
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Lauan, meranti, okoume
Open a hollow-core door from 1974. The skin is a pink-brown rotary veneer that the hardware store called Philippine mahogany. The tree was likely a *Shorea* or a cousin — lauan, meranti, seraya, the dipterocarp forest of the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia. Open an older aircraft or a cheap French panel: the pink might be okoume (*Aucoumea klaineana*) from Gabon, the peelers’ favorite, light, cooperative, the core of a lot of decorative ply. These woods furnished the hidden 20th century. They are why “mahogany” on a motel dresser is a joke, and why Southeast Asian and Central African forests took a furniture-shaped hole.
## Lauan and meranti (*Shorea* and allies)
A cluster of species, not one. Density varies from light utility to something that can pretend to be a show wood. Rotary-cut, they built the postwar world’s cheap faces and cores. “Philippine mahogany” was a trade name that Bowett’s Jamaica wood would not recognize.
Furniture: the entire middle market of 1950–1990. Drawer bottoms, case backs, the veneer under a printed walnut photograph. Some solid meranti doors and outdoor furniture exist; durability varies by species and sapwood. Do not treat meranti as teak.
Conservation: dipterocarp forests are one of the planet’s serious loss stories — logging, oil palm, fire. CITES listings have applied to some *Shorea* (e.g. ramin is *Gonystylus*, a different genus, Appendix II; do not confuse). Many merantis are unlisted and still a Lacey/due-care problem if illegally cut. FSC and national bans matter. The TRAFFIC five-taxa paper’s world is next door.
## Okoume / gaboon (*Aucoumea klaineana*)
Light, salmon-pink, peels into long, even veneers. Aviation in the early 20th century and decorative ply afterward. Gabon and neighboring forests. It works like a dream and dents like a softwood. A show surface in okoume wants a finish and a gentle life.
Okoume has been the subject of sustainability fights and certification drives in Central Africa `[CITE NEEDED: a current ITTO or FSC note]`. It is not a rosewood. It is a peeler tree whose forest is not infinite.
## Why they sat in the core
Cheap, large, peelable logs. Glue likes them. The face could be anything: walnut, a photograph of walnut, a paper foil. The 20th-century furniture factory is a sandwich machine. These species are the filling.
Hollow doors and void-core ply made the filling thinner. The lauan skin got thinner too. A chip shows a paper.
## Shop notes
Screws in cheap lauan ply crumble the core. Use inserts or go to birch ply.
Okoume dust and the pink stain on clothes are shop folklore. Finish soon; the color shifts.
Do not restore a printed-lauan suite by sanding. There is nothing under the print.
## What to look for
Pink rotary faces, “Philippine mahogany,” a 1970s credenza, an aircraft ply, a void. A new meranti garden bench sold as teak: weigh it and look at the pores.
Arkansas shops use these woods as imported ply, not as local logs. The local substitute for a cheap core is poplar ply or, if you want the good core, birch. The tropical peeler forest is not a southern hardwood story. It is the story of the furniture most people already own.
## A name that never was a tree
“Philippine mahogany” was a hardware-store sentence, not a binomial. Adam Bowett’s work on Jamaica wood and the 18th-century London trade is the reminder: mahogany, in English, once meant *Swietenia* from the Caribbean. By 1974 the word had been stretched over a pink rotary leaf from a dipterocarp. The pores are different. The weight is different. The smell is different. A motel dresser that says mahogany on the hangtag and shows a wild cathedral grain on a paper-thin face is this chapter, not the Chippendale one.
Lauan (also lauan, red lauan, white lauan in older U.S. yard talk) and meranti and seraya are trade clusters inside *Shorea*, *Parashorea*, and their neighbors — the dipterocarp canopy of the Philippines, Borneo, Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula. Light red meranti, dark red meranti, white meranti, yellow meranti: four colors that are not four species. Density runs from a light utility peeler you can dent with a thumbnail to a heavier board that can pretend to be a show wood. The USDA imported-woods sheets and Kukachka’s FPL-125 tradition treat them as a range, not a single Janka. Secondary compilations put light red meranti near SG 0.40–0.54 and a soft Janka; dark red meranti sits higher `[CITE NEEDED: pin one FPL/Chudnoff line per trade group if the editor tables it]`. Do not treat meranti as teak. Teak is oily, silica-hard, and a different family. Meranti outdoors is a species-and-sapwood question. Some heartwoods last. A lot of garden-center “meranti benches” do not.
The logs left through Manila, then through Sandakan and Tawau on the east coast of Sabah, through Balikpapan and Samarinda, through Singapore as a sorting port. Postwar American and Japanese mills wanted wide, cheap, peelable stems. The furniture factory wanted a face it could print. The two wants met in a rotary lathe.
## Okoume at Port-Gentil
*Aucoumea klaineana*, okoume or gaboon, is a Burseraceae tree of Gabon and neighboring forests, not a dipterocarp. The Chudnoff / FPL African sheet gives a basic specific gravity (ovendry weight / green volume) of 0.37 and an air-dry density around 28 pounds per cubic foot — a lightweight hardwood, salmon-pink, that peels into long, even veneers. Janka numbers in the compilations sit in a soft band, often cited near 270–400 lbf; confirm against a primary FPL table before you publish a single figure `[CITE NEEDED]`. It works like a dream and dents like a softwood. Silica is low compared with teak, but the face can still go woolly under a dull knife.
Aviation wanted that combination before furniture did. Early 20th-century aircraft ply — and later a great deal of decorative European panel — used okoume because the leaf was wide, the glue line behaved, and the sheet was light. Port-Gentil and Libreville were the names on the bills of lading. French and later multinational mills made “gaboon ply” a specification. A show surface in okoume wants a finish and a gentle life. A core of okoume under a walnut face is the 20th-century sandwich in its polite form.
Okoume has been the subject of sustainability fights and certification drives in Central Africa `[CITE NEEDED: a current ITTO or FSC note]`. It is not a rosewood. It is not CITES-listed as of the last check this draft made. It is a peeler tree whose forest is not infinite.
## The factory as a sandwich machine
Cheap, large, peelable logs. Glue likes them. The face could be anything: walnut, a photograph of walnut, a paper foil. Klim’s 1990 WAG paper is again the glue timeline: protein, casein, phenolics for wet work, cheap ureas for interior furniture. Interior lauan ply is often a urea sandwich. Water finds it. A kitchen splash that swells a 1970s drawer side is that chemistry, not a mystery.
Hollow-core doors and void-core ply made the filling thinner. The lauan skin got thinner too. A chip on a 1974 door shows a paper, then air, then a cardboard honeycomb or a few slats. The “Philippine mahogany” was never the door. It was the costume.
Drawer bottoms, case backs, the unseen sides of a credenza — this is where most people already own *Shorea*. Some solid meranti doors and outdoor furniture exist. Durability varies by species and sapwood. A new meranti garden bench sold as teak should be weighed. Look at the pores. Teak’s ring-porous face and oily feel are not meranti’s.
Ramin (*Gonystylus* spp.) is a different genus, a pale utility wood that went onto CITES Appendix II, and a standing confusion in yard talk. Do not fold ramin into meranti. Some *Shorea* have carried listings or national bans; many merantis remain unlisted and are still a Lacey due-care problem if illegally cut. The TRAFFIC / Chatham House five-taxa paper sits next door. FSC and national export bans matter. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care — that argument belongs to the Lacey chapter, but it starts in this forest.
## Shop behavior
Screws in cheap lauan ply crumble the core. The rotary leaf is thin; the inner plies are often voids dressed as wood. Use inserts, or go to birch ply, or design the joint so the fastener lives in a solid rail. A confirmat screw in furniture-grade birch is a different conversation from a drywall screw in a 1970s stereo cabinet.
Okoume dust is fine and pink. It stains clothes. Finish soon; the salmon shifts toward brown in light. A clear film yellows. Oil makes it look like a cheap mahogany, which is how a lot of boat interiors were sold.
Do not restore a printed-lauan suite by sanding. There is nothing under the print. A 0.4 mm rotary face under a walnut photograph is not a veneer you can “take down to fresh wood.” You will take it down to glue.
When you specify new ply, write the face species and the core species. “Walnut ply” is not a specification. *Juglans nigra* face, birch core, interior glue, CARB/TSCA Title VI, is a specification. *Shorea* core, paper-foil oak, urea glue, is also a specification. The honest shop names both.
## What the forest paid
Dipterocarp forests are one of the planet’s serious loss stories — logging, oil palm, fire, the conversion of a peeler stand into a plantation that will never make a 1974 door again. Central African okoume stands have their own pressure and their own certification politics. Buying vintage furniture in these woods is reuse. Buying new meranti with no harvest country on the invoice is how the Lacey Act got a furniture phase.
Arkansas did not grow these trees. Southern shops meet them as imported sheets and as the insides of furniture clients already own. The local substitute for a cheap core is yellow-poplar ply or, if you want the good core, Baltic birch. The tropical peeler forest remains the hidden 20th century. Most living rooms still sit on it.
## Sources
V&A plywood history. Klim 1990. FPL imported woods (okoume, *Shorea* where tabled). TRAFFIC / CITES (ramin; context). ITTO market notes `[CITE NEEDED]`. Bowett (on the word mahogany).
See: `plywood-veneers-twentieth`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `engineered-wood-honest`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Engineered wood, told honestly
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Engineered wood, told honestly
Most of the furniture alive in the world right now is not a joined oak chest. It is a panel: veneered plywood, particleboard, medium-density fiberboard, a paper foil, a plastic edge. This chapter will not sneer. It will say what those panels do well, where they die, and how a buyer can tell a named tool from a costume.
Bradley Brand works solid hardwoods. That is a choice, not a license to lie about the other choice.
## What the panels are
Plywood: layers of veneer, grain crossed. Already treated in the ply chapters. The good stuff (Baltic birch, proper hardwood ply) is a furniture wood with a species list. The cheap stuff is a void and a smell.
Particleboard (chipboard): chips in glue, pressed. Heavy, cheap, swells in a wet kitchen like a bread sponge. Holds a cam lock if you do not sit on the shelf. Invented for a reason: small wood, waste wood, a flat sheet. European kitchens after the 1950s ran on it. So did a lot of “walnut wall units.”
Medium-density fiberboard (MDF): refined fiber, usually with urea-formaldehyde or a newer resin, pressed smooth. Machines like a dream. Edges are the tell: fuzzy, brown, homogeneous. Takes paint. Swells if you leave a cup on a raw edge. A walnut-veneered MDF door is a standard, respectable kitchen door if the invoice says so.
OSB: oriented strand, a sheathing board. Rare in show furniture, common in the back of something you should not have bought.
LVL and other structural laminates: beams. They appear as live-edge-look tables when someone slabs a laminated beam and calls it rustic. That is a look. Name the glue.
## What they do better than solid wood
They stay flat. A six-foot cabinet door in flatsawn oak is a season of movement. The same door in MDF with a veneer is a rectangle in January and in July. The 18th-century shop used frame-and-panel to get that rectangle. The 21st-century shop uses a press.
They use trees that solid furniture would reject: small stems, waste, plantation thinnings. That can be a conservation good if the glue and the forest are decent.
They are cheap enough that more people have a place to put a plate.
## What they do worse
Water. A leak under a sink is a particleboard obituary. Solid oak would have stained and lived.
Screws in the edge. MDF holds a well-designed fastener and drops a careless one. Particleboard is worse.
Repair. A chipped foil cannot be planed. A broken cam-lock carcase is often landfill. Hide-glue mahogany can be taken apart. That is not nostalgia. It is a joinery fact.
Heat and cheap foil: the dining table that blisters under a casserole.
Formaldehyde: urea-formaldehyde resins emit. Standards (CARB, TSCA Title VI in the U.S., E1/E0 in Europe) exist because people live with these boards. Old unlabelled particleboard in a closed room is the worst of the story. Ask for certified low-emission boards. This is not a scare paragraph. It is a specification.
## History
Klim’s 1990 WAG paper still helps: protein glues, then phenolics for wet work, then cheap ureas for interior furniture. Particleboard’s European industrial rise is postwar. MDF’s American and European rise is late 20th century. IKEA and its peers did not invent the panel; they perfected the cam lock and the flat box.
Printed grain and vinyl wraps are the late costume. A 1970s lauan print and a 2010s paper-foil oak are the same idea with better ink.
## How to buy without being a snob
Read the edge. Ask for the core. A “solid walnut front, engineered carcase” is a normal, honest kitchen. A “solid walnut collection” that is foil on particleboard is a catalogue crime.
Pay for the right panel: moisture-resistant MDF in a bath, plywood in a wet-adjacent cabinet, particleboard only where the budget and the dryness agree.
If you want repairable furniture that can be recut, buy solid or honest ply. If you want a wall of cheap storage you will not move, buy the cam lock and do not wet it.
## Conservation
Engineered wood can be the least romantic and the most efficient use of a log. It can also be a tropical core with a temperate photograph on top (lauan chapter). Certification and the resin matter. Landfill of failed particleboard is the end of the efficiency story. Design for a life that matches the glue.
## What to look for
Homogeneous brown edges. Cam locks. Foil that does not turn a corner with the grain. A CARB label. A veneered door with a plywood core (good) versus a paper-wrapped chip (know it). A swollen kickboard.
The 500-year series ends its materials run here so that oak and mahogany do not pretend they are the only furniture left. They are not. The honest shop names the panel. The honest buyer reads the edge.
## A kitchen in 1962, and one in 2012
Walk a West German or Swedish kitchen from the early 1960s. The doors may be painted, or a thin teak face, or a printed wood. The carcase is particleboard: chips in urea glue, pressed flat, edged in a strip of real wood or a painted banding. The plates live. The sink leak is the enemy. Max Himmelheber and the German postwar mills did not invent waste-wood board as a thought experiment; they industrialized a sheet that could be a wall of storage for people who were not going to commission a joined oak dresser. IKEA did not invent the panel either. Gillis Lundgren’s 1956 flat-pack idea — take the legs off a table so it fits in a car — and the later cam-lock carcase are distributions of a board that already existed.
Walk the same kitchen type in 2012. The door is often MDF, veneered or foil-wrapped, machined on a CNC as if it were cheese. The edge is a 0.4 mm ABS or a thicker wood lipping. The core is brown and fuzzy and homogeneous. A confirmat screw holds if the hole was drilled for it. A drywall screw in the edge does not. The physics did not change. The costume got better ink.
A shop that works solid hardwoods has made a choice about repair and about a forest it can name. That is not a license to sneer at the wall of storage. This chapter keeps that line.
## What the Wood Handbook and Hoadley actually give you
The *Wood Handbook* is a book about trees as engineering material. Engineered panels have their own chapters and their own ASTM and EN standards; they do not get a Janka the way *Quercus alba* does. What you can steal from FPL and from R. Bruce Hoadley’s *Understanding Wood* is the reason the panel was invented: solid wood moves. Tangential shrinkage in oak is on the order of 8–10 percent from green to ovendry; radial is less; longitudinal is a rounding error. A six-foot flatsawn oak door is a season of cup and a year of argument. Frame-and-panel was the 18th-century answer. Cross-banded plywood is the 20th-century answer. MDF is the 21st-century answer if you want a painted rectangle and you accept the water rule.
Hoadley is also the reminder that glue is a material. A hide-glue mahogany carcase can be taken apart with heat and moisture. A urea-formaldehyde particleboard carcase cannot. That is not nostalgia. It is a joinery fact. Phenol-formaldehyde, the dark glue of exterior ply and of some older marine sheets, is a different chemistry: darker line, better wet behavior, still not a solid-wood repair culture. Methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) and other newer resins show up in some moisture-resistant and no-added-formaldehyde boards. Ask. The invoice should say.
Formaldehyde emission is a specification, not a ghost story. Urea-formaldehyde resins emit. The California Air Resources Board’s ATCM, then the U.S. EPA’s TSCA Title VI, set composite-wood formaldehyde limits for hardwood ply, particleboard, and MDF sold in the United States. Europe’s E1 and the tighter E0 / CARB NAF / ULEF labels are the same conversation in different stamps. Old unlabelled particleboard in a closed room is the worst of the story. Ask for the stamp. This is not a scare paragraph.
## How a panel dies
Water. A leak under a sink is a particleboard obituary. The chips swell, the glue lets go, the edge crumbles into a brown pastry. Solid oak would have stained and lived. Moisture-resistant MDF (often green-dyed in the core, a factory habit) lasts longer in a bath than standard MDF and still hates a standing puddle on a raw edge. Plywood in a wet-adjacent cabinet is the better of the cheap choices if the glue is the right glue.
Heat. A foil-wrapped dining table under a casserole blisters. The photograph of oak lifts in a bubble. There is no plane that fixes a bubble. A solid top would have a white ring you might revive. The foil table is a different object.
Fasteners. MDF holds a well-designed fastener — confirmat, insert, a screw into the face rather than the edge — and drops a careless one. Particleboard is worse. Cam locks are honest if you do not sit on the shelf. They are not a mortise and tenon. A broken cam-lock carcase is often landfill because the holes have gone oval and the board has no long fiber to grab.
Repair. A chipped foil cannot be planed. A dented MDF edge can be filled and painted if the door was painted to begin with. A walnut veneer on MDF can be patched by a specialist; the patch will be a leaf, not a recut of the door. Hide-glue mahogany can be taken apart. Choose the life you want before you choose the board.
## Shop behavior
Read the edge before you read the catalogue. A homogeneous brown fuzz is MDF. Chips in a pale glue are particleboard. Thin dark lines, many of them, are ply. A void behind a 0.6 mm face is cheap ply. A paper that does not turn the corner with the grain is a print. A veneer that does turn the corner, with book-matched leaves on a door pair, is a different invoice.
When you machine MDF, the dust is fine and the cut is clean. Seal the raw edge the same day if the door will see a kitchen. When you machine particleboard, the chips tear. When you machine cheap lauan ply, the core crumbles and the screw story begins.
LVL and other structural laminates appear as “live-edge” tables when someone slabs a laminated beam and calls it rustic. Name the glue. Name the species in the lamstock if you can. A beam is not a walnut tree.
OSB is a sheathing board. It shows up as the back of something you should not have bought, or as a “rustic” headboard. It is oriented strand, waxed, structural. It is not furniture grade. Say so.
## Conservation, without romance
Engineered wood can be the least romantic and the most efficient use of a log: small stems, mill waste, plantation thinnings, a flat sheet. That can be a conservation good if the glue and the forest are decent. It can also be a tropical core with a temperate photograph on top — the lauan chapter — and a landfill of failed particleboard at the end of the efficiency story. Design for a life that matches the glue.
Certification (FSC, PEFC) is a risk tool for the face and the core. It is not a finding that the Lacey Act has been met. CARB / TSCA Title VI is an emission stamp, not a forest stamp. You want both conversations on the same purchase order if the board is imported or mixed.
## Sources
Klim, WAG 1990. Hoadley. CARB / EPA TSCA Title VI public pages. V&A plywood history (for the ply subset). Manufacturer technical sheets for MDF/particleboard (generic).
See: `plywood-veneers-twentieth`, `lauan-meranti-okoume`, `reading-furniture-wood`, `cites-lacey-buying`.

item.title: Windsor chairs
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Windsor chairs
A Windsor is a mixed-wood machine. The seat is a thick plank, often elm in England, often pine or poplar or elm in America. The legs are turned, often maple in America, ash or beech in England. The bow and the spindles want a wood that bends and does not snap — ash, oak, hickory, sometimes yew. Nancy Goyne Evans’s *Windsor-Chair Making in America* is the long proof that the label “maple Windsor” is a half-sentence. The chair is a system of jobs.
This chapter is a comparative frame. The species chapters (elm, ash, maple, oak, pine, yew, hickory) are the parts list.
## Why mix
No one wood wants every job. Elm’s interlocked seat does not split when you drive four tapered legs and a row of spindles into it. Maple turns a crisp bead and wears at the foot. Ash takes a steam bend for a continuous-arm bow. Oak will bow too, and quartersawn oak was used. Pine seats are light and cheap and split more readily; American shops used them anyway, and painted.
Green woodworking — shrinking a dry tenon in a wetter seat, or the reverse depending on the shop — is part of the vernacular. Factory Windsors of the 19th century used drier stock and glue and paint.
## England and America
English Windsors from the Thames valley and the Midlands are a type with elm seats as a cliché that is often true. Yew-wood Windsors are the collector’s prize (yew chapter). Painted beech and ash chairs sit in the cheaper line.
American Windsors, from Philadelphia outward, become a national industry: Rhode Island, New York, New England, later the Midwest. Evans tracks woods by part and by region. Paint is common. Fancy Windsors pick up bamboo turnings and color. The species mix remains a job mix.
## Fashion
18th-century garden and tavern seating; then the polite American parlor; then the 19th-century factory; then the Colonial Revival; then the craft revival of the late 20th century (Dunbar and others) that taught a new generation to rive oak and steam ash. The Windsor never needed Macquoid’s mahogany age. It outlived it.
## Shop notes
Do not replace an elm seat with a flatsawn oak plank and expect the same life. If you restore, match the job, not the romance.
Paint layers are history. Stripping a Philadelphia Windsor to “show the maple” is a 1960s idea.
A new craft Windsor in white oak and maple is a correct American sentence. A new “Windsor” in stained rubberwood from a container is a shape.
## What to look for
Seat thickness, interlocked grain, turned legs that do not match the seat species, a bent bow, paint in the spindle holes, a wedge through a through-tenon. Weight. A pine seat’s dents.
Arkansas woods — oak, ash, hickory, maple if shipped or found, pine, elm if any remains — are a complete Windsor palette. A southern shop can build the system without a tropical crate. That is the point of a mixed-wood chapter in this series.
## High Wycombe, and a Philadelphia shop in 1765
English Windsors gather around the Thames valley and the Chiltern beech woods, with High Wycombe as the factory town of the 19th century. The cliché is an elm seat, ash or yew bow, ash or beech sticks, turned legs in beech or fruitwood. It is often true. Victor Chinnery’s oak book is not the Windsor book, but the English vernacular chair literature still sits thin in American shops `[CITE NEEDED: name the English monograph the editor wants beside Evans]`. Yew-wood Windsors — the bow a ribbon of orange heart and pale sap — are the collector’s prize. The yew chapter is the anatomy. Painted beech and ash chairs sat in the cheaper line and still do in the leftovers of pub rooms.
In Philadelphia, by the 1740s and 1750s, the same job-mix had become an urban export. Joseph Henzey, the Tracys of Connecticut (Ebenezer Tracy’s shop in Lisbon is the named New England case), and a long list Evans tracks by account book and by wood sample, made chairs that went south and west in coasting vessels. The seat might be eastern white pine, poplar, or elm. The legs were often hard maple. The spindles and the bow wanted hickory or oak or ash — whatever would rive and bend. Paint was not an apology. Philadelphia green, a mustard, a black, a red — the chair was a painted object. Fancy Windsors of the early 19th century picked up bamboo turnings and more color. The species mix remained a job mix.
Nancy Goyne Evans’s *Windsor-Chair Making in America* (2006) is the long proof that “maple Windsor” is a half-sentence. She sorts woods by part and by region. Forman’s earlier seating book (*American Seating Furniture, 1630–1730*) is the prehistory: joined chairs and board chairs before the stick chair takes the tavern.
## Why each wood, in numbers
No one wood wants every job. That is the whole chapter.
Elm (*Ulmus* spp.): interlocked grain, a seat that does not split when you drive four tapered legs and a row of spindles into it. The *Wood Handbook* puts American elm at SG about 0.50 and Janka about 830 lbf at 12 percent — softer than oak, tough rather than hard. Dutch elm disease (U.S. introduction in the 1930s) emptied the urban elm. English elm seats of the 18th century are a different forest that also thinned. A restorer who puts a flatsawn red-oak plank in place of an elm seat has changed the physics.
Hard maple (*Acer saccharum*): SG 0.63, Janka 1,450 lbf (FPL-GTR-190). It turns a crisp bead and wears at the foot. American shops used it for legs because the lathe likes it and the floor does not erase it in a year. Soft maple will turn. It will not wear the same.
Ash (*Fraxinus americana*, and European *F. excelsior*): white ash at SG 0.60, Janka 1,320 lbf. Ring-porous, pale, the textbook steam-bend. A continuous-arm bow in ash is the American sentence. Oak will bow too; quartersawn oak was used; hickory will bow and come back like a tool. Shagbark hickory sits at Janka about 1,820 lbf, SG about 0.72 — the hardest of the ordinary eastern hardwoods. Spindles in hickory can be thinner than spindles in oak for the same nerve.
Pine seats (*Pinus strobus* in the northeast): SG about 0.35, Janka about 380 lbf. Light, cheap, they dent and they split more readily than elm. American shops used them anyway, and painted. Poplar (*Liriodendron tulipifera*) is the southern and mid-Atlantic cousin of that cheap seat: a servant wood, as in 1760.
Green woodworking — a drier tenon in a wetter seat, so the seat shrinks onto the leg — is part of the vernacular. The reverse, or a fully dry joint with glue, appears as shops industrialized. Factory Windsors of the 19th century used drier stock and glue and paint. Michael Dunbar and the late-20th-century craft revival taught a new generation to rive oak and steam ash and to argue about moisture again. Use Dunbar as practice, not as an archive.
## Paint, wedges, and the 1960s mistake
Paint layers are history. Pigment in the spindle hole, a drip under the seat, a wear-through on the crest that shows an earlier green — those are the object. Stripping a Philadelphia Windsor to “show the maple” is a 1960s idea. The maple was not the face. The paint was the face.
Through-tenons on the legs, wedged from above, are a tell if the seat is thick enough. A wedge in a different wood is common. A seat that is too thin for the tradition is often a later replacement or a factory economy.
Weight is a tell. A pine-seat chair feels like a pine-seat chair. An elm seat has a duller heft. A container “Windsor” in stained rubberwood has a slick turnery and no job-mix at all: one species trying to be four. Look at the underside. Look at the bow: steam-bent long grain, or sawn from a wide board and hoping.
## Shop behavior
If you restore, match the job, not the romance. Do not replace an elm seat with a flatsawn oak plank and expect the same life. Oak will split along the ring if you bore a row of spindle holes across the growth like a dotted line. Quartered oak is kinder. Elm is kinder still.
If you build new, a craft Windsor in white oak and maple is a correct American sentence. Hickory spindles and an oak bow are a correct American sentence. A continuous arm in ash is a correct American sentence. Arkansas woods — oak, ash, hickory, maple if shipped or found, pine, elm if any remains — are a complete palette. A southern shop can build the system without a tropical crate.
Steam-bending is not a mystery and is not a weekend. The stick wants straight grain. A run-out bow is a broken bow. The box wants a thermometer you believe. Spring-back is a number you learn on scrap.
Do not stain a new maple leg to “look old” and then sell it as a 1790 Philadelphia chair. The turning profile and the tool marks will argue with you. Evans is full of profiles. Use them.
## Fashion without mahogany
18th-century garden and tavern seating; then the polite American parlor; then the 19th-century factory; then the Colonial Revival; then the craft revival. The Windsor never needed Macquoid’s mahogany age. It outlived it. That is why this series gives it a chapter among the style frames: it is the mixed-wood machine that kept running while fashion went to Jamaica, to Burma, and to a printed lauan.
## Sources
Evans, *Windsor-Chair Making in America* (2006). Forman, seating. English vernacular chair literature `[CITE NEEDED]`. Species chapters (FPL numbers). Dunbar and craft-revival manuals (practice, not archives).
See: `elm`, `ash`, `maple`, `oak-european-and-american`, `yew`, `hickory-and-pecan`.

item.title: Shaker woods
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Shaker woods
The Shaker list is short on purpose. Maple for the parts that must stay true and take a turning. Cherry for the face that will darken in the meetinghouse light. Pine for the broad, painted or clear boards that do not need to be heroes. Occasional butternut, occasional walnut, a little figured maple. John Kassay’s *Book of Shaker Furniture* and Rieman and Burks’s *Complete Book* are the measured catalogues. The theology of simplicity has been written to death. The species list is the furniture fact.
## Why these trees
New England and New York communities sat in the white pine and hard maple forest. Kentucky’s Pleasant Hill sat in a different mix and the woods shift — more walnut and cherry, more southern secondary woods. The Shakers bought and sold timber; they were not only forest hermits. They still preferred a small set because a small set can be finished with one vocabulary: a clear wash, a light stain, a red or yellow paint on pine, a chair that can be hung on a peg.
Maple chairs: the slat-back, the tape seat, the pommel. Cherry stands and cases. Pine cupboards and built-ins. The famous oval boxes are often maple sides with pine tops, fingers swallow-tailed, copper tacks — a mixed-wood object like a Windsor, quieter.
## What they did not use
Mahogany appears when they made goods for sale to “the world” or when a piece is not as Shaker as the dealer hopes. Heavy Renaissance Revival walnut is not their hour. Tropical inlay is not their hour. The absence is a specification.
## Finish
Milk paint, distemper, later industrial paints, clear varnish, oil. The orange “Shaker finish” of late reproductions is often a toner that the historic piece did not wear. Cherry was allowed to darken. Maple was allowed to stay pale. Pine was painted or left, depending on the room.
## The reproduction problem
20th-century factory “Shaker” is a stain and a tape seat on mixed hardwoods. Some is decent maple. Some is beech or birch from a chair plant. Look at the turning and the underside. A Hancock-quality cherry stand has thin, exact legs and a top that moved and was allowed to.
## Shop notes
If you build in this vocabulary, use the list. A “Shaker” table in sapele is a confusion. A Shaker-style table in Arkansas cherry and maple is a geographic shift of the same idea — Pleasant Hill already made that shift.
Do not distress. The originals wore.
## What to look for
Maple, cherry, pine. Tape. Pegs. A cupboard interior as careful as the face. Lightness. A reproduction’s thick legs.
The series includes Shaker woods as a comparative frame so the American hardwood chapters have a shop that chose them as a set, not as leftovers from mahogany.
## Mount Lebanon, Hancock, Pleasant Hill
The United Society of Believers furnished rooms the way they furnished theology: a short list, repeated until it became a vocabulary. Mount Lebanon, New York — the central ministry — ran a chair industry that sold to “the world.” The slat-back chair with a tape seat and a pommel finial is that industry’s object. Hancock, Massachusetts, and Sabbathday Lake, Maine, and Canterbury, New Hampshire, and Enfield, Connecticut, sat in the white-pine and hard-maple forest. Kentucky’s Pleasant Hill sat in a different mix: more walnut, more cherry, more southern secondary woods. The Shakers bought and sold timber. They were not only forest hermits. They still preferred a small set because a small set can be finished with one vocabulary: a clear wash, a light stain, a red or yellow paint on pine, a chair that can be hung on a peg rail.
John Kassay’s *The Book of Shaker Furniture* (1980) is the measured-drawing book. Timothy Rieman and Jean Burks’s *The Complete Book of Shaker Furniture* (1993) is the catalogue raisonné habit: community, wood, date range, construction. Read them before you believe a dealer’s “Shaker.” A lot of country slat-backs are just country slat-backs.
The oval box is the mixed-wood object that sits beside the Windsor in this series. Maple sides, steamed and fingered in a swallow-tail, copper tacks, a pine top and bottom. The maple takes the bend. The pine stays light. The tacks are the fasteners you can see. A box in all walnut is a different community or a later fancy. A box in sapele from a weekend class is a shape.
## Why these numbers
Hard maple (*Acer saccharum*): SG 0.63, Janka 1,450 lbf (FPL-GTR-190). The chair wood. It turns a pommel that stays crisp. It stays true if it was dried. It takes a tape seat’s holes without crumbling. Figured maple appears; it is not required. The theology of simplicity has been written to death. The Janka number is why the slat does not fuzz.
Black cherry (*Prunus serotina*): SG 0.50, Janka 950 lbf. The *Wood Handbook* still says machining is “very good” and the wood is “very dimensionally stable after drying.” Heartwood goes from light to dark reddish brown in the sun — the meetinghouse window is a finish. Gum flecks stay. A Hancock-quality cherry stand has thin, exact legs and a top that moved and was allowed to. The orange “Shaker finish” of late reproductions is often a toner the historic piece did not wear.
Eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*): SG about 0.35, Janka about 380 lbf. The cupboard wood, the built-in, the painted case. Soft enough to dent, cheap enough to be a wall of storage, clear enough in old-growth boards that a door can be one leaf. Second-growth pine is knotty. Paint was not a cover-up. It was the specification for a lesser room or a wet one.
Occasional butternut (*Juglans cinerea*), occasional black walnut (*J. nigra*), a little yellow-poplar as a secondary wood — the list grows at Pleasant Hill and in pieces made for sale. Mahogany appears when they made goods for the world or when a piece is not as Shaker as the dealer hopes. Heavy Renaissance Revival walnut is not their hour. Tropical inlay is not their hour. The absence is a specification.
## Pegs, tape, and the underside
A Shaker cupboard interior is as careful as the face: shelves that fit, a pin that holds, no slush of leftover stain. That is a shop habit you can still read. The peg rail is not a decorative row. It is how a chair leaves the floor so the floor can be cleaned. Look at the wear on the peg and at the hole in the chair finial.
Chair tape — cotton or wool, later a synthetic — is a seat, not a brand. A 20th-century factory “Shaker” is often a stain and a tape seat on mixed hardwoods. Some is decent maple.
