Some is beech or birch from a chair plant that also made hotel stock. Look at the turning. Look at the underside. A pommel that is fat and vague is not a Mount Lebanon pommel. Kassay’s plates are the comparison.
Milk paint, distemper, later industrial paints, clear varnish, oil. Cherry was allowed to darken. Maple was allowed to stay pale. Pine was painted or left, depending on the room. Do not “age” a new piece with a chain. The originals wore.
## Shop behavior
If you build in this vocabulary, use the list. A “Shaker” table in sapele is a confusion. A Shaker-style table in Arkansas cherry and maple is a geographic shift of the same idea — Pleasant Hill already made that shift, and the walnut belt of Kentucky is not a Massachusetts maple grove. Name the community you are thinking of, even if you are only thinking of it.
Keep the legs thin. The historic stands are lighter than the reproduction houses want them. A thick leg is the tell of a factory that insured itself against freight damage.
Do not distress. Do not add a fake peg rail to a piece that never hung. Do not stain maple to cherry and call it Hancock.
When you repair an oval box, match the swallow-tail and the tack. A steel nail in place of a copper tack is a different object. Hide glue is the historic adhesive for a lot of the case work; later shops used what the hardware store sold. Ask before you soak a joint.
The Mount Lebanon chair lists — numbers stamped or written under a slat, a #7 rocking chair as the famous size — are commercial marks, not monastery poetry. Communities sold chairs by the dozen. A surviving label or a stencil on the underside is worth more than a dealer’s adjective. Sabbathday Lake still holds a living community and a furniture memory; Hancock is a museum village. Walk the rooms before you copy a finial from a photograph.
## What the series needs this frame for
The American hardwood chapters — maple, cherry, pine, walnut — need a shop that chose them as a set, not as leftovers from mahogany. The Shakers are that shop. They sat in the forest this series keeps recommending to a southern designer: local woods, a short list, a finish that can be renewed, a chair you can hang on a wall. Fashion went to *Swietenia* and to teak. They mostly did not. That is the furniture fact. The rest is theology, and it has been written.
## Sources
Kassay, 1980. Rieman and Burks, 1993. Community histories (Hancock, Sabbathday Lake, Pleasant Hill). FPL on the three species. Cherry, maple, pine chapters.
See: `maple`, `cherry`, `pine-country-furniture`, `windsor-mixed-wood`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Arts and Crafts oak
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Arts and Crafts oak
Gustav Stickley put quartersawn white oak in the American living room and fumed it. Ammonia vapor and the tree’s tannin made a brown that is not a pigment sitting in the pores but a reaction in the fiber. The ray flake went darker or lighter than the ground, depending on the board, and the catalogues called it honest. William Morris had already argued, in *Hopes and Fears for Art* and in the practice of Morris & Co., that oak and the visible joint were a moral alternative to ebonized mahogany pretence. English shops (Barnsley, Voysey’s designs, Gimson) and American ones (Stickley, Limbert, Roycroft, the lesser Mission factories) made oak fashionable again for the first time since Macquoid’s first age — and they made the quartered face the badge.
This chapter is a style frame. The oak chapter and the sawing chapter are the anatomy.
## Why oak, why quartered
They wanted a northern hardwood that was not mahogany’s empire and not walnut’s Victorian parlor. Oak was local (or could be), tannic, visible in the grain, and old in the English floor. Quartersawn stock showed the ray — “silver grain” — and moved less in the wide boards they liked for settles and library tables. Flatsawn Mission exists; it was the cheaper line. Collectors still sort by flake.
Fuming works because oak is tannic. Maple will not fume the same way. A “fumed” maple is a stain. Red oak fumes less dramatically than white; the shops that cared specified white.
## England and America
Morris & Co. and the English craft furniture makers used oak in a range of finishes, not only fume. The American Craftsman movement industrialized a version: mortise-and-tenon through-tenons with visible pins, corbels, a brown that photographed well in *The Craftsman* magazine (1901–1916). Limbert’s cutouts and the Michigan factories made a broader, sometimes lighter oak. The Prairie school overlapped.
Golden oak of the 1890s — often quartersawn, often a yellow-brown varnish — is a cousin, more factory, more fill. Do not collapse it into Stickley, or vice versa.
## Finish myths
Not every brown oak chair is fumed. Many were stained and shellacked. A true fume has color in the wood, not only in the pore. A scratch that stays pale is a stain. A scratch that stays brown is in the fiber — or a deep dye.
Original finishes are thin. Restoration that pours polyurethane on a 1905 settle is a different object.
## Shop notes
If you fume now: ammonia is dangerous, the color keeps changing after the tent, and clients must be told that sunlight will still move the brown. Test boards.
If you build Mission in Arkansas white oak, you are in the right genus and the right cut. Specify quartered. Specify white. The 1905 mill in Eastwood, New York, was not the only oak forest.
## What to look for
Flake, through-tenons, a brown that is a reaction, a 1910 settle, a factory Mission with decals, a golden-oak sideboard with filled pores. Red oak pretending to be the catalogue.
The series places this chapter after the species essays so the fashion of 1900 can be seen as a sawing choice and a chemistry choice, not as a vague “return to craft.”
## Eastwood, Sapperton, East Aurora
Gustav Stickley’s Craftsman Workshops at Eastwood, New York — Syracuse’s edge — made the American object most people mean by Mission: a settle or a library table in quartersawn white oak, through-tenons with visible pins, corbels under a top, a brown that photographed well in *The Craftsman* (1901–1916). The mill was not a cottage. It was a factory that wanted to look like a guild. The catalogues are the proof: models, prices, a finish called “fumed” as if the reader already knew the tent.
In the Cotswolds, Ernest Gimson and Sidney and Ernest Barnsley at Sapperton were closer to the Morris argument and farther from a mail-order settle. English oak (*Quercus robur*, *Q. petraea*), visible joints, a finish that was not always a fume. C. F. A. Voysey’s designs — the owl suite is the postcard — used oak as a northern moral wood. Morris & Co. had already, in *Hopes and Fears for Art* (1882) and in the firm’s practice, set oak and the visible joint against ebonized mahogany pretence. William Morris’s sentence is the English one. Stickley’s magazine is the American broadcast.
Charles Limbert’s factory in Grand Rapids and then Holland, Michigan, cut cutouts into oak that was sometimes lighter, sometimes more Mackintosh than Eastwood. Elbert Hubbard’s Roycroft shops at East Aurora, New York, made a heavier, more hammered oak. The Prairie school overlapped: oak interiors that were architecture, not only furniture. Lesser Mission factories from Indiana to the Pacific coast flooded the catalogues after 1905. Collectors still sort by flake, by hardware, by the red decal on the drawer.
Golden oak of the 1890s — often quartersawn, often a yellow-brown varnish, pores filled — is a cousin, more factory, more Renaissance-revival leftover. Do not collapse it into Stickley, or vice versa. A filled golden-oak sideboard and a fumed 1910 settle are both oak. They are not the same finish religion.
## Why oak, in the handbook’s numbers
They wanted a northern hardwood that was not mahogany’s empire and not walnut’s Victorian parlor. Oak was local (or could be), tannic, visible in the grain, and old in the English floor.
White oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group): SG about 0.68, Janka about 1,360 lbf at 12 percent (FPL-GTR-190, table 5–3a). Tyloses plug the heartwood pores. That is why tight cooperage and a certain outdoor manners attach to white oak, and why a fume — ammonia vapor plus the tree’s tannin — has something to react with. The brown is a reaction in the fiber, not only a pigment sitting in the pore.
Northern red oak (*Q. rubra*): SG about 0.63, Janka about 1,290 lbf. Open pores. You can blow through a straight red-oak end grain. Stain floods. Fuming is less dramatic; the shops that cared specified white. Red oak pretending to be the 1905 catalogue is a common floor.
European oak sits in the same hardness neighborhood; published Janka figures vary by source and ring width `[CITE NEEDED for a single FPL-equivalent on Q. robur]`. Slow-grown English or Baltic oak is often finer than a wide-ringed second-growth American board. The binomial does not tell you the ring count. The quartersawn chapter tells you why the ray — “silver grain” — became the badge. Flatsawn Mission exists. It was the cheaper line.
Maple will not fume the same way. A “fumed” maple is a stain. Ash will take a brown; it is not oak’s tannin story.
## The tent, and the scratch test
Ammonia vapor and tannin. The shop hung the piece, or the boards, in a tent or a chamber with aqueous ammonia. The color kept changing after the tent came down. Sunlight still moves the brown. Clients who want a 1905 settle matched to a new leaf must be told that the next two years are part of the finish.
Not every brown oak chair is fumed. Many were stained and shellacked. A true fume has color in the wood. A scratch that stays pale is a stain. A scratch that stays brown is in the fiber — or a deep dye. Original finishes are thin. Restoration that pours polyurethane on a 1905 settle is a different object. The pore that Stickley left open is a 1910 idea, against the filled golden-oak pore of 1892.
Museum holdings — the Art Institute of Chicago, the Dallas Museum of Art, Winterthur’s Mission pieces — are where you go to see an unstripped surface. A dealer’s “refinished Stickley” is often a darker, thicker thing than Eastwood shipped.
## Shop behavior
If you fume now: ammonia is dangerous. Ventilation is not a suggestion. Test boards from the same tree if you can. The latewood and the ray will not go the same brown. That is the point, and also the complaint.
If you build Mission in Arkansas white oak, you are in the right genus and the right cut. Specify quartered. Specify white. Specify the pin in the through-tenon as a piece of oak or of walnut, not as a steel dowel with a wood cap unless you say so. Draw-boring is older than Stickley; he made it visible on purpose.
Through-tenons that are proud of the post will get knocked. Historic ones often sit flush or a hair proud. A tenon that looks like a hat is a reproduction flourish.
Do not stain red oak with a yellow-brown toner and sell it as fumed white oak. The pore will argue. The ray will argue. The weight may not.
Hardware: hammered copper and iron are part of the American object. English pieces often used quieter iron. A bright brass knob on a 1910 settle is usually a replacement.
## Fashion as a sawing choice
The series places this chapter after the species essays so the fashion of 1900 can be seen as a sawing choice and a chemistry choice, not as a vague return to craft. Quartersawn white oak, tannin, a visible pin: that is the specification. Morris supplied the English sentence. Stickley supplied the American mill. The tree was already here. Arkansas still grows it.
## Sources
Stickley, *The Craftsman*. Morris, *Hopes and Fears for Art*. Oak chapter (FPL; Chinnery for the older oak). Quartersawn chapter. Museum collections (Art Institute, Dallas, Winterthur Mission holdings).
See: `oak-european-and-american`, `quartersawn-versus-flatsawn`, `ash`, `shaker-woods`.

item.title: Biedermeier pale woods
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Biedermeier pale woods
After Napoleon, the Central European bourgeois interior went pale. Birch with a butter polish, pear like a closed silk, cherry a little warmer, maple, a black inlay line, columns and lyres and a commode that looked expensive without looking imperial. The name Biedermeier is later and half-mocking. The woods are local. This is Macquoid’s satinwood age translated off the ship and onto the northern tree.
## The palette
Birch — often *Betula pendula* and its figured forms, including Karelian masur — is the frequent face. Pear is the finer, even face. Cherry when a rose heat was wanted. Ebonized pear or stained hardwood for the black. Walnut appears, especially later and in darker rooms, but the postcard Biedermeier is pale.
They used veneer on cheaper grounds, like everyone else. They also used solid in smaller forms. The polish is high. The grain is quiet compared with oak.
## Compared with England and America
English satinwood rooms of 1780–1810 are the fashionable cousin: more yellow, more imported, more painted swag. American Federal pale is often figured maple and cherry, mahogany still at the top of the house. Biedermeier is what a Viennese or Berlin shop did with the forest it had when mahogany was a political and a money problem.
The birch chapter and the fruitwood chapter are the anatomy. This chapter is the room.
## Afterlife
Museums in Vienna, Munich, Prague, and Berlin hold the type. 20th-century collectors made it expensive. Reproductions in pale birch ply are a shape. A true pear commode has weight and a surface like stone.
Scandinavian pale modern (Aalto, later IKEA’s better lines) is not Biedermeier, but a northern taste for light wood runs through both. Danish teak is a refusal of that pale as much as a continuation of the craft.
## Shop notes
Do not sand a faded Biedermeier veneer to “fresh gold.” The surface is the object. Black lines are often ebonized pear — repair in kind.
A new “Biedermeier” in stained maple from a container is a poster.
## What to look for
Pale silk grain, black stringing, columns, a Viennese commode, Karelian figure, pear’s evenness. A mahogany Empire piece in the same decade: the other political color.
The series includes this frame so satinwood does not stand as the only pale classical story, and so birch and pear have a room to sit in.
## Vienna after the Congress, Berlin after the army
The Congress of Vienna closed in 1815. The Central European bourgeois interior, for a generation, went pale. The name Biedermeier is later — a half-mocking coinage from the 1850s satirical figure Gottlieb Biedermaier (the spelling wandered) — and it stuck to furniture that was already thirty years old. The dates shops use, 1815–1848, run from the peace to the revolutions. The woods did not wait for the name.
Josef Danhauser’s Vienna manufactory is the named shop everyone cites and then under-documents in English `[CITE NEEDED: a specific Danhauser workshop inventory or MAK object list the editor wants]`. Berlin, Prague, Munich, and a string of smaller residences made the same argument with local trees: birch, pear, cherry, maple, a black line, columns and lyres and a commode that looked expensive without looking imperial. Museums in those cities hold the type. A Viennese commode in figured birch with ebonized colonnettes is the postcard. A Prague secretary in pear is the quieter cousin.
They used veneer on cheaper grounds, like everyone else — pine, beech, a local oak. They also used solid in smaller forms: chairs, a work table, a sewing stand. The polish is high. The grain is quiet compared with oak. The room wanted silk, not a ray flake.
## The pale list, with numbers
Birch — often *Betula pendula* and its figured forms, including Karelian masur from Finnish and Russian Karelia — is the frequent face. The *Wood Handbook* tables the American cousins (yellow birch SG about 0.62, Janka about 1,260 lbf). European furniture birch sits in that neighborhood: fine, diffuse-porous, pale, a butter color under a spirit polish. Karelian figure is a growth peculiarity, almost marble, a luxury veneer from particular trees. You cannot order it by the cubic meter and mean it.
Pear (*Pyrus communis* and related orchard woods) is the finer, even face — closed silk, almost no pore to the fingernail. Fruitwood chapters in this series give the shop manners: dense, often twisted, specific gravity commonly cited near 0.65–0.75, Janka in the hard-maple neighborhood, but orchard wood varies so wildly that a handbook average is a rumor `[CITE NEEDED: FPL does not table orchard pear as a commercial lumber]`. Ebonized pear is the black line and the black capital. Repair in kind. A painted maple line is a different sentence.
Cherry, here mostly European wild cherry (*Prunus avium*, Kirsche, cerisier), when a rose heat was wanted. American black cherry (*P. serotina*, SG 0.50, Janka 950 lbf) is the New World cousin, not the Viennese default. Both darken in light. A Biedermeier cherry that is still pale may have lived behind a curtain, or may have been refinished.
Maple (*Acer* spp., including the European sycamore maple *A. pseudoplatanus*) for a colder pale. Walnut appears, especially later and in darker rooms. The postcard Biedermeier is still birch and pear.
Black is usually ebonized local wood, not Gabon ebony. Pewter and brass turn up as line inlay. The ébéniste’s tropical palette — kingwood, tulipwood, satinwood — is not this room’s shopping list. That is the political and money fact: mahogany after the Napoleonic wars was a problem of supply and of taste. Local pale woods were the answer a Berlin shop could write on an invoice.
## Satinwood’s cousin, not satinwood
English satinwood rooms of 1780–1810 are the fashionable cousin: more yellow, more imported (*Chloroxylon* and the West Indian woods of that chapter), more painted swag. Macquoid’s *Age of Satinwood* is the English periodization. Hepplewhite and Sheraton plates are the English grammar. Biedermeier is what a Viennese or Berlin shop did with the forest it had when mahogany was a political and a money problem.
American Federal pale is often figured maple and cherry, mahogany still at the top of the house. A Baltimore card table with holly stringing is a linear art, not a Viennese commode. The birch chapter and the fruitwood chapter are the anatomy. This chapter is the room.
Do not sand a faded Biedermeier veneer to “fresh gold.” The surface is the object. The butter color is a polish and a century of light, not a stain you can get back with a belt. Black lines are often ebonized pear. A later PVA fill in a missing line is a conservation event.
## Shop behavior
A true pear commode has weight and a surface like stone. Reproductions in pale birch ply are a shape. A new “Biedermeier” in stained maple from a container is a poster: thick legs, a lyre laser-cut, a finish that looks like candy. Look at the underside. Look at the ground. A pine ground with hide glue and a birch face that has moved and been allowed to is the historic sandwich. An MDF ground with a paper birch print is the engineered chapter wearing a column.
When you repair, support the ground first. Central heating has cracked more Biedermeier faces than bad taste. Protein glue lets go in a damp room and in a dry one it can go brittle. A specialist. Not a kitchen-table refinisher with a dark wax.
Karelian figure is expensive and often veneer for a reason. Solid masur birch in large sizes is a unicorn. Do not plane it to “even out” the marble. The marble is the point.
Spirit varnish and a French-polish habit gave the butter surface. A later polyurethane is a different object: thicker, colder, a plastic skin on a pale face. When a client wants “that Viennese glow,” they want the thin film and the wood’s own yellowing, not a candy coat. Columns and lyres are the fashionable hardware of the type; a shop that machines them from a CNC file and glues them onto a box has made a poster. Look at how the capital meets the frieze. A knife-cut mitre in ebonized pear is the historic join. A blob of black filler is not.
## Afterlife
20th-century collectors made the type expensive. Dealers in Vienna and New York taught a generation to say Biedermeier the way an earlier generation said Chippendale. Scandinavian pale modern — Aalto’s birch, later IKEA’s better lines — is not Biedermeier, but a northern taste for light wood runs through both. Danish teak is a refusal of that pale as much as a continuation of the craft. The Aalto chapter and the Danish chapter return to that argument.
The series includes this frame so satinwood does not stand as the only pale classical story, and so birch and pear have a room to sit in. A designer who specifies a pale dining room in Arkansas maple and cherry is not making Biedermeier. They are making the American Federal and Pleasant Hill version of the same wish: local trees, a quiet grain, a dark line if you want one. Name the wish. Do not name the wrong city.
## Sources
Biedermeier museum catalogues. Birch and fruitwood chapters. Macquoid *Age of Satinwood* (for the English parallel). Sheraton/Hepplewhite (English pale).
See: `birch`, `fruitwoods`, `satinwood`, `maple`, `danish-modern-woods`.

item.title: Danish modern woods
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Danish modern woods
Hans Wegner’s Wishbone (CH24) is usually oak. Finn Juhl’s more sculptural chairs are often teak, sometimes walnut. A rosewood sideboard from a Copenhagen factory in 1962 is a third luxury. Danish modern is not “teak furniture.” It is a small set of woods — oak, teak, rosewood, walnut, a little beech — used with joinery that shows and a finish that is oil or a thin film. The magazines flattened it to a honey brown. The shops did not.
## Oak
Northern oak, often pale, sometimes smoked, the chair wood of Wegner and of many dining sets that were never photographed. It connects Danish work to a local forest and to the Arts and Crafts idea of a visible hardwood, without fuming as a religion. A 1950s oak chair is as Danish as a teak one.
## Teak
The tropical member, the export look, the suburban American living room. Solid and veneer. The teak chapter covers the tree and the plantations. Danish factories made teak a Scandinavian word, which it is not botanically. They also made some of the best teak furniture in the record.
## Rosewood
Sharper, darker, rarer, now a CITES object. The rosewood chapter is required reading before you ship a 1960s sideboard. Danish rosewood was often *Dalbergia latifolia* and related, not only Brazilian. Still a listed genus.
## Walnut and others
American black walnut appears in some lines, especially those aimed at the U.S. Beech appears in lesser chairs. Teak-on-oak mixes exist: a teak face and oak where the shop saved.
## Finish and the copy
Oil that can be renewed is part of the object. A thick polyurethane on a Wegner is a mistake you can see from the door. Taiwanese and later global copies used rubberwood, printed veneer, and a shape. Look at the joint and the underside.
## Shop notes
If you specify “Danish modern” in a new commission, pick a wood. Oak is the local-ethic choice in a hardwood region. Teak is a paper-trail choice. Rosewood is a no for new work. Walnut is the American cousin.
Arkansas oak and walnut sit comfortably in this vocabulary. Teak does not grow there. The style does not require it.
## What to look for
A Wishbone in oak, a teak sideboard with a thin oil, a rosewood grain that is not a print, dowels and tenons, a copy’s rounded nothing.
The series puts this chapter near the end so teak, oak, and rosewood have already been met as trees.
## Copenhagen, the Guild, and a chair with a name
The Copenhagen Cabinetmakers’ Guild exhibitions, from the 1920s into the 1960s, are the public record of the shops: Kaare Klint’s teaching at the Furniture School, then the generation that magazines flattened to a honey brown. Hans J. Wegner’s Round Chair — “The Chair” after the 1960 Nixon–Kennedy broadcast sat it in American living rooms — is usually oak or walnut, sometimes teak, a joined crown and a woven seat. The Wishbone, CH24, designed 1949 and put into production by Carl Hansen & Søn in 1950, is usually oak: a steam-bent back, a Y of splats, a paper-cord seat. Finn Juhl’s Chieftain (1949) and the more sculptural chairs are often teak, sometimes walnut, a carver’s attitude toward a slab. Børge Mogensen’s hunting chair and his oak cases are the sober line. Arne Jacobsen’s wood is often the secondary story beside the metal and the leather; the Series 7 is not this chapter. Poul Kjærholm is even less a wood story.
Danish modern is not “teak furniture.” It is a small set of woods — oak, teak, rosewood, walnut, a little beech — used with joinery that shows and a finish that is oil or a thin film. The shops did not flatten it. The magazines did.
## Oak as the local ethic
Northern oak, often pale, sometimes smoked, the chair wood of Wegner and of many dining sets that were never photographed. European oak (*Quercus robur*, *Q. petraea*) and, in later and export work, American white oak. The *Wood Handbook* puts white oak at SG about 0.68, Janka about 1,360 lbf. European oak sits in the same neighborhood `[CITE NEEDED for a single FPL-equivalent on Q. robur]`. It connects Danish work to a local forest and to the Arts and Crafts idea of a visible hardwood, without fuming as a religion. A 1950s oak chair is as Danish as a teak one. The Wishbone in oak is the object to keep in your head when a catalogue tries to sell you “Danish” as a color.
Smoked oak — ammonia or a related fume, a darker brown — appears in later and in revival work. It is chemistry the Stickley chapter already explained. It is not a different tree.
## Teak as the export look
*Tectona grandis*, the tropical member, the suburban American living room of 1962. Solid and veneer. FPL puts teak’s properties “generally on par with those of U.S. oaks”; Janka is commonly cited near 1,070 lbf, SG near 0.55–0.66 depending on plantation versus old-growth. Silica dulls tools. Oil in the fiber wants wiping before glue and finish. Indoor teak in the 1950s was oiled to stay honey. Outdoor teak goes silver if you let it.
The logs, in the years the Copenhagen factories wanted them, came out of Burma (Rangoon as the old port name), Thailand, and later Indonesian plantations. Danish factories made teak a Scandinavian word, which it is not botanically. They also made some of the best teak furniture in the record. The teak chapter covers the tree, the imperial deck, and the plantation. This chapter covers the oil can on a Copenhagen bench.
Paper-trail teak is the only new teak a specifier should write. Plantation, country, certificate number. A “solid teak suite” at a funny price is the meranti problem in a honey costume.
## Rosewood, and the 2017 line
A rosewood sideboard from a Copenhagen factory in 1962 is a third luxury. Sharper, darker, rarer, now a CITES object. Danish rosewood was often East Indian *Dalbergia latifolia* and related, not only Brazilian *D. nigra*. The whole genus went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15 later revised so finished musical instruments and small finished products (wood of the listed species up to 10 kg per shipment) would not freeze concerts and jewelry boxes. A rosewood dining table is not a jewelry box. *D. nigra* was already Appendix I.
Densities in the *Dalbergia* group often sit above 0.8–1.0. They dull tools, they can be oily to glue, they take a polish that looks like stone. Dust is a sensitizer. The rosewood chapter is required reading before you ship a 1960s sideboard. Antique pieces already in the country are usually legal to own. They can be complicated to export. Ask.
## Walnut, beech, and the mix
American black walnut (*Juglans nigra*, SG 0.55, Janka 1,010 lbf) appears in some lines, especially those aimed at the U.S. Beech (*Fagus sylvatica*) appears in lesser chairs and in parts. Teak-on-oak mixes exist: a teak face and oak where the shop saved. That is honest if you can see it. A teak print on a beech carcase is the engineered chapter.
## Oil, copies, and the underside
Oil that can be renewed is part of the object. A thick polyurethane on a Wegner is a mistake you can see from the door. The paper cord on a Wishbone is a seat, not a brand; it wears and is meant to be replaced. Look at the joint: a dowel and a tenon that meet as if someone cared, or a rounded nothing from a copy mill.
Taiwanese and later global copies used rubberwood (*Hevea brasiliensis*), printed veneer, and a shape. Rubberwood is a plantation utility hardwood. It is not oak. It is not teak. Look at the underside. Look at the tool marks on the inside of a rail. Carl Hansen’s and the other named shops’ model woods are in the catalogues. Fiell’s *Scandinavian Design* is a picture book with a spine; use it to find the object, then go to the maker’s sheet for the species.
## Shop behavior
If you specify “Danish modern” in a new commission, pick a wood. Oak is the local-ethic choice in a hardwood region. Teak is a paper-trail choice. Rosewood is a no for new work. Walnut is the American cousin.
Arkansas oak and walnut sit comfortably in this vocabulary. Teak does not grow there. The style does not require it. A new dining chair in quartersawn white oak with a paper-cord seat and a thin oil is a correct sentence. A new “Danish” credenza in foil-wrapped MDF with a honey print is a catalogue crime.
When you restore, clean and re-oil before you sand. The thin film is the object. A white ring from a glass is often recoverable. A belt sander is how a 1962 teak top becomes a 1990s one. Keep the original oil can’s logic: wipe, wait, wipe again. Do not pour a gel stain into the pore and call it teak.
The series puts this chapter near the end so teak, oak, and rosewood have already been met as trees. The magazines sold a color. The shops sold a joint.
## Sources
Fiell, *Scandinavian Design*. Maker catalogues (Carl Hansen, etc.) for model woods. Teak, oak, rosewood chapters. Kirkham / Eames (for the parallel ply modern).
See: `teak`, `oak-european-and-american`, `rosewood-ebony-cites`, `finnish-birch-aalto`.

item.title: Marquetry
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Marquetry
Marquetry is a picture whose pigments grew. A saw, a knife, a bundle of dyed and natural veneers, a ground of oak or deal or poplar, hide glue, hot sand for a shadow, an engraving tool and a mastic for a vein. The Wallace Collection’s notes on Riesener are exact: a flower of a dozen pieces, a trellis of stringing, knife marks where a leaf breaks a border. The brown you see on a 1780 secrétaire now is not the garden it was. Dyes fade. Some pink tulipwood goes quiet. The technique does not.
This chapter is a comparative frame for the woods already met: box, holly, walnut, kingwood, tulipwood, satinwood, pewter, brass, turtle in Boulle, straw in poorer work, later celluloid in sad copies.
## Kinds
Marquetry: pictorial or floral veneers assembled like a puzzle. Parquetry: geometry — cubes, diamonds, the tumbling-block floors of a table top. Inlay: a recess cut into a solid and a piece let in (Federal holly in mahogany). Boulle: brass and turtle (and pewter, and ebony) sawn together and swapped — a première-partie and contre-partie. Oyster veneer: transverse slices, not a picture but a related luxury of the walnut age.
English seaweed marquetry of the 1690s is fine, dark, acanthus-like, often on walnut. Dutch and Flemish floral marquetry is a garden. French pictorial work is the court. American Federal inlay is a quieter, often linear art. Islamic and Indian inlaid furniture are other schools; this series notes them and does not pretend to cover them.
## Woods as colors
Pale: box, holly, maple, satinwood, bone. Dark: ebony, ebonized pear, walnut burl. Red: cherry, some dyed woods, padauk in later work. Green: dyed sycamore (the famous faded greens). Purple: kingwood, plum. The ébéniste’s palette chapter is the shopping list. Roubo describes the shop.
Sand-shading: dip the edge of a leaf-shaped veneer in hot sand, get a burn that reads as volume. Engraving: cut a vein, fill it. None of this is a printer’s trick. It is a wood trick.
## Grounds and time
The picture is as stable as the ground and the glue. A deal or oak ground that moves will split a face. Central heating has cracked more marquetry than bad taste. Protein glue lets go in damp. A later PVA repair is a conservation event.
Do not sand a picture. Do not “oil it back to life” with a dark polish that fills the engraving. Photograph, support, a specialist.
## Law
A new floral panel in *Dalbergia* tulipwood and kingwood is a CITES object. Antique marquetry is the ethical picture. Holly and walnut still make a Federal fan without a permit.
## What to look for
A flower that has escaped its panel, a sand-shaded edge, a fade from green to brown, oysters on a William-and-Mary box, holly stringing on a Baltimore table, a Boulle clock. A laser-cut “marquetry” from a gift shop: even, dead, often paper.
The series ends its style frames here because marquetry is the place all the minor woods were doing a job at once. A buyer who can read a Riesener flower can read a kitchen edge.
## A flower on a secrétaire, 1780
Jean-Henri Riesener’s pictorial marquetry — the Wallace Collection’s notes are the exact public version — is a flower of a dozen pieces, a trellis of stringing, knife marks where a leaf breaks a border. The brown you see on a 1780 secrétaire now is not the garden it was. Dyes fade. Some pink tulipwood goes quiet. A green sycamore leaf goes brown. The technique does not. Stand in front of the piece and count the woods before you count the ormolu.
André-Jacob Roubo’s *L’Art du menuisier* (1769–1775) is the shop manual: the saw, the donkey, the bundle of dyed and natural veneers, the ground, the hot sand, the engraving tool, the mastic. Paris is the court school. André-Charles Boulle, a century earlier, had already made the metal-and-turtle version: brass and turtle (and pewter, and ebony) sawn together and swapped — a première-partie and a contre-partie. English seaweed marquetry of the 1690s — Gerrit Jensen’s circle, the William-and-Mary walnut age — is fine, dark, acanthus-like. Dutch and Flemish floral marquetry is a garden. American Federal inlay is a quieter, often linear art: holly in mahogany on a Baltimore table, a fan, a string. Islamic and Indian inlaid furniture are other schools; this series notes them and does not pretend to cover them.
Oyster veneer — transverse slices of walnut, laburnum, olive — is not a picture. It is a related luxury of the walnut age: a cut across the branch that makes a ring like a shell. Parquetry is geometry: cubes, diamonds, the tumbling-block floors of a table top. Inlay is a recess cut into a solid and a piece let in. Marquetry is a puzzle assembled on a sheet and then laid. Keep the words apart. Dealers do not.
## Woods as a palette
Pale: boxwood (*Buxus sempervirens*), holly (*Ilex*), maple, satinwood, bone. Dark: ebony (*Diospyros*), ebonized pear, walnut burl. Red: cherry, some dyed woods, padauk in later work. Green: dyed sycamore maple (*Acer pseudoplatanus*) — the famous faded greens of French work. Purple: kingwood (*Dalbergia cearensis*), plum. The ébéniste’s palette chapter is the shopping list. Tulipwood (*D. decipiens* and kin) is the pink stripe. None of these is a stain catalogue. They are trees, or they are trees plus a dye.
Sand-shading: dip the edge of a leaf-shaped veneer in hot sand, get a burn that reads as volume. Engraving: cut a vein, fill it with mastic. None of this is a printer’s trick. It is a wood trick. A laser-cut “marquetry” from a gift shop is even, dead, often paper. The sand-shaded edge is the tell you want. The fade from green to brown is the tell that the piece lived.
Boxwood and holly are the pale line-woods because they are fine, hard, and take a cut. The boxwood chapter and the holly-in-the-Federal-shop habit are the anatomy. Walnut is the dark ground of the 1690s. Mahogany is the dark ground of the 1780s. Oak or deal or poplar is the hidden ground under the picture.
## Grounds, glue, and central heating
The picture is as stable as the ground and the glue. A deal or oak ground that moves will split a face. Hoadley’s movement numbers — tangential shrinkage in oak on the order of 8–10 percent from green to ovendry, radial less — are why an 18th-century shop used a quartered or a framed ground when it could, and why a 20th-century apartment with the heat on splits a flower at the border. Protein glue (hide) lets go in damp and can go brittle in dry. A later PVA repair is a conservation event. It does not reverse with the same heat and moisture as hide.
Do not sand a picture. The veneer is thin. A leaf is a leaf. Do not “oil it back to life” with a dark polish that fills the engraving. Photograph, support, a specialist. The Wallace Collection’s conservation notes on Riesener are the public standard of that caution `[CITE NEEDED: a specific AIC paper on dyed veneer fade if the editor wants a journal cite beside the museum]`.
A ground of yellow-poplar in American Federal work is the servant wood again. A ground of MDF in a new “marquetry” table is the engineered chapter wearing a flower. The flower may be real leaves. The ground will not move like 1780. Say so.
## Law on the palette
A new floral panel in *Dalbergia* tulipwood and kingwood is a CITES object. The whole genus went onto Appendix II on 2 January 2017. Brazilian rosewood, if someone still tries it as a ground or a flower, is Appendix I. Antique marquetry is the ethical picture: the trees are already cut, the dyes have already faded, the object is already a museum or a living room. Export is a different question from ownership. Holly and walnut still make a Federal fan without a permit. Boxwood is not a *Dalbergia*. Dyed sycamore is a maple.
Ivory and turtle are not woods and are their own legal and ethical wall. This chapter names them because Boulle and some Federal work used them. It does not recommend a new supply.
## Shop behavior
If you commission a new picture, write the binomials. Holly, walnut, maple, cherry, pear: a Federal fan or a simple floral that does not need a permit. If the designer wants kingwood and tulipwood, the file needs the permit path. If the designer wants a lasered paper on MDF, that is a poster. Charge poster money.
When you restore, do not replace a faded green with a bright new dye and call it original. The fade is the 1780–2020 sentence. Infill in kind, slightly quieter than the old, is the conservation habit. A dark wax rubbed into every joint is how a picture becomes a brown rectangle.
Look for a flower that has escaped its panel — a lift at the border, a sand-shaded edge still readable, oysters on a William-and-Mary box, holly stringing on a Baltimore table, a Boulle clock with a contre-partie still paired somewhere in the literature. A gift-shop “marquetry” chessboard with even squares and a glossy film is parquetry’s distant cousin, often stained birch.
The series ends its style frames here because marquetry is the place all the minor woods were doing a job at once. A buyer who can read a Riesener flower can read a kitchen edge: which leaf is a tree, which leaf is a print.
## Sources
Wallace Collection, Riesener. Roubo. Macquoid / Edwards. Kingwood and satinwood chapters. CITES *Dalbergia*. Conservation literature on dyed veneers `[CITE NEEDED: a specific AIC paper]`.
See: `kingwood-tulipwood-ebeniste`, `boxwood`, `walnut`, `satinwood`, `rosewood-ebony-cites`.

item.title: CITES, Lacey, and a clean buy
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# CITES, Lacey, and a clean buy
A dining table is a tree with a paper trail, or it is a tree without one. This chapter is for the buyer and the specifier, not for a lawyer. The living references are Species+ (CITES), the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service’s timber pages, and USDA APHIS’s Lacey Act declaration pages. Listings and annotations change. Check the date.
## CITES in furniture language
Appendix I: commercial trade in wild specimens is not a furniture plan. Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) is the famous I. Some ebonies and other woods join it.
Appendix II: trade is allowed with permits and a non-detriment finding. Big-leaf mahogany (*Swietenia macrophylla*, neotropical populations) went on II in 2003 (in force 15 November 2003), typically for logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood — Annotation #6. Finished furniture may sit outside that annotation; the mill that imported the sawn wood does not. The whole *Dalbergia* genus went on II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15, later revised so finished musical instruments and small finished products (wood of the listed species up to 10 kg per shipment) would not freeze concerts and jewelry boxes. A rosewood dining table is not a jewelry box.
Appendix III: a country asks others to help control a species. Some cedars and others have sat here. Always look up the current appendix.
Annotations decide whether a finished chair needs a permit. They are the fine print. Guitar companies learned this the hard way (Taylor’s public CITES note is a clear industry walkthrough; verify against the text). Furniture companies have less excuse.
## Lacey, 2008 and Phase VII
The Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.), amended by the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 §8204, makes it illegal to trade plants taken in violation of U.S. or foreign law. It is the first comprehensive U.S. ban of that kind on illegal wood. Importers file a declaration: scientific name, country of harvest, quantity, value. Enforcement of declarations was phased. Phase VII, 1 December 2024, extends declarations to remaining plant-product HTS codes that are not 100 percent composite, including more furniture (APHIS).
Due care is the standard. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care. FSC is a useful risk tool. It is not a finding that Lacey has been met (APHIS and FSC both say versions of this).
Composite exemptions and special-use designations exist for some mixed or unidentifiable cases. They are not a blanket for a solid “mahogany” table.
## What a designer can actually do
Write binomials on the specification. *Quercus alba*, United States. *Tectona grandis*, plantation, country, certificate number. *Swietenia macrophylla* only with the permit path in the file.
Prefer domestic hardwoods when the job allows: oak, walnut, cherry, maple, hickory, ash (while it lasts), pine. The Arkansas chapter is that preference without a sermon.
For tropicals: old furniture already in the country, or new wood with boring paperwork. If the price of a “solid rosewood suite” is funny, the wood is funny.
For engineered goods: still ask the face species and the core species. Lauan cores have a forest. Foil has a name.
## Antiques
Antique *Dalbergia* and *Swietenia* pieces are usually legal to own. They can be complicated to export. Ask before you ship a 1960s rosewood sideboard to another country. Appendix I objects are the sharpest case.
## What this series will not do
It will not issue a permit. It will not update itself when CoP20 changes an annotation. It will not treat FSC as a halo. It will not treat domestic wood as automatically innocent (stolen walnut trees exist). It will say: names, countries, papers, edges.
## What to look for
A binomial on an invoice. A harvest country. A Species+ printout in a project file. An APHIS declaration if you import. An edge that matches the name. A crate that says only “wood.”
The 500-year story ends, for a buyer, in this dull chapter. The interesting trees are in the other chapters. The dullness is the point. Fashion without a paper trail is how *Swietenia* and *Dalbergia* got to the appendices.
## A crate on a dock, and a dining table in a drawing
A container lands at Long Beach or Savannah. The packing list says “wood furniture.” The HTS code is a furniture code. Until Phase VII, a lot of those codes did not require a Lacey declaration. On 1 December 2024 they did, unless the product is 100 percent composite or sits in a remaining exemption APHIS still lists. The Federal Register notice of 31 May 2024 is the dated instrument. USDA APHIS’s Lacey Act declaration pages are the living ones. Check the date. This chapter will not update itself when the next phase or the next Conference of the Parties moves a line.
The Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. §3371 et seq.), amended by the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 §8204, makes it illegal to trade plants taken in violation of U.S. or foreign law. It is the first comprehensive U.S. ban of that kind on illegal wood. Importers file a declaration: scientific name, country of harvest, quantity, value. Due care is the standard. A certificate on a website is not automatically due care. FSC is a useful risk tool. It is not a finding that Lacey has been met — APHIS and FSC both say versions of this. Composite exemptions and special-use designations exist for some mixed or unidentifiable cases. They are not a blanket for a solid “mahogany” table.
Stolen walnut trees exist. Domestic wood is not automatically innocent. A Boone County walnut log with a cloudy chain of custody is a Lacey problem if it crossed a line to get to the mill. The Arkansas chapter is a preference, not a halo.
## CITES, said as furniture
CITES is a trade convention. Species+ is the lookup. The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service’s timber pages are the permit office in American language.
Appendix I: commercial trade in wild specimens is not a furniture plan. Brazilian rosewood (*Dalbergia nigra*) is the famous I. Some ebonies and other woods join it. A new dining table in *D. nigra* is a fantasy or a crime.
Appendix II: trade is allowed with permits and a non-detriment finding. Big-leaf mahogany (*Swietenia macrophylla*, neotropical populations) went on II in 2003 (in force 15 November 2003), typically for logs, sawn wood, veneer, plywood — Annotation #6. Finished furniture may sit outside that annotation; the mill that imported the sawn wood does not. The whole *Dalbergia* genus went on II on 2 January 2017, Annotation #15, later revised so finished musical instruments and small finished products (wood of the listed species up to 10 kg per shipment) would not freeze concerts and jewelry boxes. A rosewood dining table is not a jewelry box. Taylor Guitars’ public CITES note is a clear industry walkthrough; verify against the text. Furniture companies have less excuse.
Appendix III: a country asks others to help control a species. Some cedars and others have sat here. Always look up the current appendix.
Annotations decide whether a finished chair needs a permit. They are the fine print. Guitar companies learned this the hard way. A specifier who writes “*Dalbergia latifolia*, finished sideboard, 80 kg” has written a permit problem. A specifier who writes “*Quercus alba*, United States, quartersawn” has written a dining table.
TRAFFIC and Chatham House’s five-taxa paper is the trade-analysis neighbor of this chapter. It is not a permit. It is why the permits exist.
## What a designer can actually put on a sheet
Write binomials. *Quercus alba*, United States. *Juglans nigra*, United States. *Prunus serotina*, United States. *Tectona grandis*, plantation, country, certificate number. *Swietenia macrophylla* only with the permit path in the file. *Shorea* spp. as a core only if you know the harvest country and you are willing to defend due care.
Prefer domestic hardwoods when the job allows: oak, walnut, cherry, maple, hickory, ash (while the dry stock lasts), pine. The Arkansas chapter is that preference without a sermon.
For tropicals: old furniture already in the country, or new wood with boring paperwork. If the price of a “solid rosewood suite” is funny, the wood is funny. If the hangtag says mahogany and the pore looks like *Shorea*, the lauan chapter already told you.
For engineered goods: still ask the face species and the core species. Lauan cores have a forest. Foil has a name. CARB / TSCA Title VI is an emission stamp, not a harvest stamp. You want both conversations on the same purchase order.
## Antiques, exports, and the sideboard that cannot fly
Antique *Dalbergia* and *Swietenia* pieces are usually legal to own in the U.S. They can be complicated to export. Ask before you ship a 1960s rosewood sideboard to another country. Appendix I objects are the sharpest case. A 1880 Brazilian rosewood piano is a living-room object and a paperwork object at the border. Pre-convention certificates and antique annotations exist; they are not a postcard you write yourself. USFWS will tell you. A dealer’s shrug will not.
Within the country, a 1962 Danish rosewood credenza can be bought and sold. Take a photograph of the grain. Keep the invoice. If you later want to send it to London, the file starts then, not at the airport.
## Shop behavior
Keep a Species+ printout in the project file, dated. Keep the harvest country on the invoice. If you import, keep the APHIS declaration. If you do not import, keep the mill’s chain-of-custody sheet anyway. An edge that matches the name is the object-level check: tyloses in white oak, the oily pore of teak, the tight diffuse face of maple, the printed cathedral that does not turn the corner.
A crate that says only “wood” is a refusal. A salesperson who says “it’s all mahogany” is a refusal. A funny price on a listed genus is a refusal.
This series will not issue a permit. It will not update itself when CoP20 changes an annotation. It will not treat FSC as a halo. It will not treat domestic wood as automatically innocent. It will say: names, countries, papers, edges.
The 500-year story ends, for a buyer, in this dull chapter. The interesting trees are in the other chapters. The dullness is the point. Fashion without a paper trail is how *Swietenia* and *Dalbergia* got to the appendices.
## Sources
CITES appendices; 2003 mahogany press release; Annotation #15 notifications. Species+. USFWS timber pages. USDA APHIS Lacey Act; Phase VII (1 Dec. 2024); Federal Register 31 May 2024. TRAFFIC/Chatham House five-taxa paper. Taylor Guitars CITES note (industry; verify). Forest Policy / Lacey summaries.
See: `rosewood-ebony-cites`, `mahogany-and-substitutes`, `engineered-wood-honest`, `arkansas-hardwoods-500y`.

item.title: Arkansas hardwoods in a five-hundred-year frame
item.dc:creator: editor
item.content:encoded:
# Arkansas hardwoods in a five-hundred-year frame
The Ozark and Ouachita hardwood stands are not a footnote to London. They are the same genera that furnished American shops when Philadelphia still bought mahogany at the wharf and the backcountry used what grew. White oak and red oak, hickory and pecan, black walnut, cherry in the cooler coves, ash where the beetle has not finished, shortleaf and loblolly pine, baldcypress in the Delta, eastern redcedar on the glades, yellow-poplar in the east of the state. Bradley Brand works those woods. This chapter is a map, not a catalogue.
## Where the 500 years sit
Before 1800 the timber of this region was a Native woodland economy and then a settler one: buildings, fences, a press, a table, tanbark, fuel. It does not have a Chippendale archive. It has the same physics as a Rhode Island shop: oak that quarters, walnut that planes, pine that paints.
In the 19th century the lower Mississippi and the railroads took the best logs toward cities. Heart pine and cypress from the wet south, oak and hickory from the hills. Furniture factories elsewhere ate some of it. Local furniture stayed vernacular: pine and poplar painted, oak when the piece had to last.
In the 20th century Arkansas was a hardwood state in the national tally — flooring, pallets, the unglamorous grades — and a pine state in the south. Furniture-grade walnut and cherry were always the minority log. They still are.
In the present, a shop that quarters white oak here is doing what a Gdansk splitter and a Stickley mill did, on a second-growth ring count. The Baltic wainscot story does not have to be imported for the ray to be real.
## What the woods want
White oak: tyloses, flake, outdoor manners if designed to drain, the Arts and Crafts face. Red oak: open pores, stain, the 1980s kitchen, still a valid furniture wood if you like it. Hickory: tools and shock, a hard table, not a delicate moulding. Walnut: the Central States gift, sap and heart, no permit. Cherry: the sun will finish it; gum flecks stay. Ash: use the dry stock, do not pretend the living forest is what it was in 1990. Pine: paint, dents, country. Cypress: wet sites, pecky honesty. Cedar: chests, knots, a smell.
Yellow-poplar: the servant wood, as in 1760.
## What not to pretend
This is not Honduran mahogany and should not be stained to lie. It is not Burma teak. It is not huanghuali. It can do Windsor, Shaker, Mission, a Danish-modern oak chair, a walnut dining table, a painted pine cupboard. It cannot do a Riesener flower without imported scraps, and it does not need to.
Second-growth rings are wider than the old Baltic oak. Say so. Kiln schedules are better than a 1710 shed. Say so. The forest is managed and also pressured — oak decline, land use, the ash borer. Say so.
## Buying from this belt
Binomials still help: *Quercus alba* versus *Q. rubra*. Cut: quartered, rift, flat. Grade: the clear wide board is the expensive one because the trees are not old-growth cathedrals. A knot in a country piece is correct. A knot in a formal table is a conversation.
No CITES on these mains. Lacey still applies if the shop ever mixes in an imported ply core. The engineered chapter still applies if a “solid oak collection” is a foil.
## A last walk
Walk a new white-oak table from this timber with the series in your head. End grain: rings and tyloses. Face: flake or cathedral. Finish: is the pore filled like 1890 or open like 1910 or 2020. Movement: how is the top held. Secondary wood: poplar or pine, as in Philadelphia. Compare it, in memory, to a linenfold chest, a fumed settle, a Wegner oak chair. Same genus. Different rooms.
That is the whole education the series was for. Fashion moved. The trees in this state kept making furniture wood. A designer who knows the difference between a ray and a print, a *Swietenia* and a *Khaya*, a cam lock and a draw-bored pin, can use Arkansas hardwoods without costume and without apology.
## Ozarks, Ouachitas, and the river
The Ozark Plateau and the Ouachita Mountains are oak-hickory country with pine on the south slopes and in the plantations. The Mississippi Alluvial Plain — the Delta — is where baldcypress and the wet-site hardwoods sat, and where the best 19th-century logs went onto the water toward New Orleans and the railheads. Michael Williams’s *Americans and Their Forests* is the geography book. Hurst and Prown’s *Southern Furniture 1680–1830* is the reminder that the backcountry used what grew, and that a Chippendale archive is a coastal and a money fact, not a physics fact. The same genera that furnished Philadelphia when the wharf still took Jamaica mahogany furnished a press and a table in a highland county: oak that quarters, walnut that planes, pine that paints.
Bradley Brand works those woods. The shop’s job in this series is to teach species behavior, not to sell a line. One sentence is enough: the boards come from this belt, and the essays are how to read them.
In the 19th century the lower Mississippi and the railroads took the best logs toward cities. Heart pine and cypress from the wet south, oak and hickory from the hills. Furniture factories elsewhere ate some of it. Local furniture stayed vernacular. In the 20th century Arkansas was a hardwood state in the national tally — flooring, pallets, the unglamorous grades — and a pine state in the south. Furniture-grade walnut and cherry were always the minority log. They still are. A clear wide walnut board is expensive because the trees are not old-growth cathedrals.
## The list, with the handbook open
White oak (*Quercus alba* and the white group): SG about 0.68, Janka about 1,360 lbf (FPL-GTR-190). Tyloses, flake on the quarter, outdoor manners if designed to drain, the Arts and Crafts face. A shop that quarters white oak here is doing what a Gdansk splitter and a Stickley mill did, on a second-growth ring count. The Baltic wainscot story does not have to be imported for the ray to be real. Say the rings are wider than the old Riga oak. Say so.
Red oak (*Q. rubra* and the red group): SG about 0.63, Janka about 1,290 lbf. Open pores, stain, the 1980s kitchen, still a valid furniture wood if you like it. Do not fume it and call it Eastwood.
Hickory (*Carya* spp.): shagbark Janka about 1,820 lbf, SG about 0.72 — the hardest of the ordinary eastern hardwoods. Tools and shock, a hard table, not a delicate moulding. Pecan (*C. illinoinensis*) is the sweeter-named cousin, a bit more furniture-facing, still a tough ring-porous wood. Factory “pecan” of the 1960s was often a finish color.
Black walnut (*Juglans nigra*): SG 0.55, Janka 1,010 lbf. The Central States gift. FPL still said about three-quarters of the commercial wood comes from that belt. Arkansas sits on it. Sap and heart, no permit, a plane that behaves. The walnut chapter is the love letter. This chapter is the map.
Black cherry (*Prunus serotina*): SG 0.50, Janka 950 lbf. Cooler coves, a minority log. The sun will finish it. Gum flecks stay. Pleasant Hill already used the southern version of this idea.
Ash (*Fraxinus americana*): SG 0.60, Janka 1,320 lbf. Use the dry stock. The emerald ash borer, found near Detroit in 2002, did not spare this state. Do not pretend the living forest is what it was in 1990.
Eastern white pine is not the Arkansas default. Shortleaf (*Pinus echinata*) and loblolly (*P. taeda*) are the southern pines: louder latewood, paint, dents, country. Longleaf heart pine is a different, older grade, mostly reclaimed. Baldcypress (*Taxodium distichum*): SG about 0.46, Janka about 510 lbf — wet sites, pecky honesty. Eastern redcedar (*Juniperus virginiana*): SG about 0.47, Janka about 900 lbf — chests, knots, a smell, the glades. Yellow-poplar (*Liriodendron tulipifera*): the servant wood, as in 1760, in the east of the state.
## What a shop here can build
Windsor: oak, ash, hickory, maple if shipped or found, pine, elm if any remains. Shaker: cherry, maple, pine, walnut at the Pleasant Hill end of the list. Mission: quartersawn white oak, fumed if you have a tent and a warning. Danish-modern oak chair: yes. Walnut dining table: yes. Painted pine cupboard: yes. Aalto’s birch laminate: the lesson is the bend, not the species. Marquetry of Riesener’s kind: not without imported scraps, and it does not need to.
This is not Honduran mahogany and should not be stained to lie. It is not Burma teak. It is not huanghuali. Second-growth rings are wider. Kiln schedules are better than a 1710 shed. The forest is managed and also pressured — oak decline, land use, the ash borer. Say so.
## Buying from this belt
Binomials still help: *Quercus alba* versus *Q. rubra*. Cut: quartered, rift, flat. Grade: the clear wide board is the expensive one. A knot in a country piece is correct. A knot in a formal table is a conversation.
No CITES on these mains. Lacey still applies if the shop ever mixes in an imported ply core. The engineered chapter still applies if a “solid oak collection” is a foil. Stolen walnut trees exist; ask the mill how the log arrived.
When you walk a new white-oak table from this timber, use the series. End grain: rings and tyloses. Face: flake or cathedral. Finish: is the pore filled like 1890 or open like 1910 or 2020. Movement: how is the top held. Secondary wood: poplar or pine, as in Philadelphia. Compare it, in memory, to a linenfold chest, a fumed settle, a Wegner oak chair. Same genus. Different rooms.
Fashion moved. The trees in this state kept making furniture wood. A designer who knows the difference between a ray and a print, a *Swietenia* and a *Khaya*, a cam lock and a draw-bored pin, can use Arkansas hardwoods without costume and without apology.
